subject: Physics
question_text: Which type of lens is used to correct myopia (nearsightedness)?
option_b: A flat lens with no curvature
explanation_short: Myopia (nearsightedness) is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens.
explanation_long: In myopia, the eye focuses light in front of the retina (images converge too early); a concave (diverging) lens spreads the incoming light out slightly before it enters the eye, pushing the focal point back onto the retina.
explanation_trick: Myopia (near-sighted, focuses too early) needs a DIVERGING (concave) lens; hyperopia (far-sighted, focuses too late/behind the retina) needs a CONVERGING (convex) lens instead — the opposite correction for the opposite problem.

explanation_options.a: A convex (converging) lens is used to correct hyperopia (far-sightedness), not myopia.
explanation_options.b: A flat lens with no curvature provides no corrective optical power at all.
explanation_options.c: A cylindrical lens specifically corrects astigmatism, not simple myopia.
explanation_options.d: Correct — a concave (diverging) lens corrects myopia.

subject: Physics
question_text: Dispersion of white light through a prism occurs because:
option_a: Different wavelengths of light travel at different speeds within the prism, refracting by different amounts
option_b: All wavelengths refract by exactly the same amount
option_c: The prism absorbs all colors except white
option_d: Light does not interact with the prism material
explanation_short: Dispersion occurs because different wavelengths travel at different speeds (and thus refract differently) within the prism.
explanation_long: A prism's refractive index varies slightly with wavelength (a property called dispersion of the material itself); since different colors of white light have different wavelengths, they travel at slightly different speeds inside the glass and refract by slightly different angles — spreading white light into its constituent spectrum of colors.
explanation_trick: This wavelength-dependence of refractive index (and hence speed) inside the material is called 'dispersion' — the same underlying phenomenon that also causes chromatic aberration in lenses.

explanation_options.a: Correct — different wavelengths refract by different amounts due to differing speeds in the prism material.
explanation_options.b: If all wavelengths refracted identically, no color separation (dispersion) would occur at all — white light would just bend as one beam.
explanation_options.c: A prism transmits (doesn't absorb) the visible spectrum — that's how dispersion is visibly observed in the first place.
explanation_options.d: Light very much interacts with (refracts through) the prism material — that interaction is the entire basis of dispersion.

subject: Physics
question_text: A convex lens has a focal length of 20 cm. An object is placed 40 cm from the lens. Using 1/f = 1/v - 1/u (with sign convention u = -40 cm, f = +20 cm), what is the image distance v?
explanation_trick: This is the classic 'object at 2F' case for a convex lens: when the object sits at exactly twice the focal length, the image also forms at 2F on the other side, real, inverted, and the same size — a useful benchmark case to recognize instantly.

explanation_options.a: Correct — solving the lens equation gives v=40 cm.
explanation_options.b: 13.3 cm doesn't match the algebraic solution of the lens equation here.
explanation_options.c: -40 cm has the right magnitude but wrong sign — the image here is real (positive v), not virtual.
explanation_options.d: 20 cm is just the focal length itself, not the solved image distance.

subject: Physics
question_text: Total internal reflection occurs when light traveling in a denser medium strikes the boundary with a less dense medium at an angle:
explanation_short: Total internal reflection occurs at angles greater than the critical angle (denser to less-dense boundary).
explanation_long: When light traveling within a denser medium strikes the boundary with a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle, no refraction occurs at all — the light is completely (totally) reflected back into the denser medium, a phenomenon exploited in optical fibers.
explanation_trick: Below the critical angle, light partially refracts AND partially reflects; only ABOVE the critical angle does it become total internal reflection — the critical angle is the specific threshold where the refracted ray would graze exactly along the boundary (90 degrees).

explanation_options.a: Angles LESS than the critical angle result in normal (partial) refraction, not total internal reflection.
explanation_options.b: 0 degrees (straight-on incidence) doesn't produce total internal reflection at all.
explanation_options.c: Exactly 90 degrees describes the boundary itself (grazing incidence), not the general condition for TIR.
explanation_options.d: Correct — angles greater than the critical angle produce total internal reflection.

subject: Physics
question_text: The refractive index of a medium is defined as the ratio of:
option_a: The speed of light in that medium to the speed of light in vacuum
option_b: The speed of light in vacuum to the speed of light in that medium
option_c: The wavelength in vacuum to the frequency in the medium
option_d: The angle of incidence to the angle of reflection
explanation_short: Refractive index = speed of light in vacuum / speed of light in that medium.
explanation_long: The refractive index n of a medium is defined as n = c/v, where c is the speed of light in vacuum and v is the (always slower) speed of light within that medium — always giving n greater than or equal to 1.
explanation_trick: Since light always slows down entering a denser medium (v<c always), refractive index n=c/v is always >= 1 — a useful sanity check on any calculated refractive-index value.

explanation_options.a: This inverts the standard definition (v/c instead of c/v), which would give a fraction less than 1, contrary to convention.
explanation_options.b: Correct — refractive index is the vacuum speed divided by the medium's speed (c/v).
explanation_options.c: Wavelength-to-frequency ratio doesn't correspond to the standard refractive-index definition.
explanation_options.d: Angle of incidence to angle of reflection is unrelated to refractive index — that ratio isn't even generally meaningful (reflection angle always equals incidence angle).

subject: Physics
question_text: The bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium to another of different density is called:
explanation_short: The bending of light between media of different density is called refraction.
explanation_long: Refraction is the change in direction of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another with a different refractive index (density), due to the change in light's speed at the boundary.
explanation_trick: Reflection bounces light back into the SAME medium; refraction bends light as it CONTINUES into a NEW medium — two distinct phenomena that can even happen simultaneously at the same boundary (partial reflection + partial refraction).

explanation_options.a: Reflection is light bouncing back, not passing into a new medium.
explanation_options.b: Correct — refraction is the bending of light between media of different density.
explanation_options.c: Diffraction is the bending/spreading of light around obstacles or through small openings, a different phenomenon.
explanation_options.d: Polarization concerns the orientation of light's oscillation, unrelated to bending between media.

subject: Physics
question_text: The ray diagram shows a concave mirror with an object placed between the focal point (F) and the mirror's surface. Based on the diagram, the image formed is:
option_b: Virtual, upright, and magnified, formed behind the mirror
option_c: Real, upright, and the same size
explanation_short: Object between F and the mirror (within F) on a concave mirror gives a virtual, upright, magnified image behind the mirror.
explanation_long: Using the mirror formula 1/v+1/u=1/f with the object within the focal length (u<f), the resulting image distance v comes out negative (behind the mirror, i.e., virtual), and the magnification m=-v/u works out greater than 1 in magnitude and positive in sign (upright) — this matches the classic 'shaving/makeup mirror' use case of a concave mirror held close to a face.
explanation_trick: This is the ONE case where a concave mirror behaves like a plane or convex mirror in producing a virtual, upright image — but unlike those, it also MAGNIFIES the image, which is exactly why concave mirrors are used for close-up magnified views (shaving mirrors, dental mirrors).

explanation_options.a: Real, inverted, and diminished describes an object placed BEYOND the center of curvature, not within F.
explanation_options.b: Correct — virtual, upright, magnified, formed behind the mirror, for an object within F.
explanation_options.c: Real, upright, same-size doesn't match any single concave-mirror object position (real images from a concave mirror are always inverted).
explanation_options.d: Virtual, inverted images don't occur for concave mirrors — a concave mirror's virtual image (only possible when object is within F) is always upright, not inverted.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to the law of refraction (Snell's law), light bends toward the normal when it passes:
option_a: From a less dense medium into a denser medium
option_b: From a denser medium to a less dense medium
explanation_short: Light bends toward the normal when passing from a less dense medium into a denser one.
explanation_long: When light travels from an optically less dense medium (like air) into a denser medium (like glass or water), it slows down and bends TOWARD the normal (the line perpendicular to the surface); the reverse (denser to less dense) causes bending AWAY from the normal.
explanation_trick: 'Denser medium bends toward the normal' — pair this with its opposite: light going from denser to less-dense bends AWAY from the normal, as the two directions are exact mirror-image rules.

explanation_options.a: Correct — going into a denser medium, light bends toward the normal.
explanation_options.b: Going from denser to less dense actually bends light AWAY from the normal, the opposite of this scenario.
explanation_options.c: A vacuum-only restriction isn't accurate — this bending rule applies whenever light crosses between media of different densities/refractive indices.
explanation_options.d: Light traveling exactly along the normal (0-degree incidence) doesn't bend at all — there's no bending to describe in that special case.

subject: Physics
question_text: A concave mirror can form a real image when the object is placed:
option_a: Between the pole and the focal point
option_c: Never; concave mirrors only form virtual images
explanation_short: A concave mirror forms a real image when the object is placed beyond the focal point.
explanation_long: For a concave mirror, placing the object anywhere beyond the focal point F (between F and C, at C, or beyond C) produces a real, inverted image; only when the object is placed WITHIN the focal point (between the mirror and F) does a virtual image form instead.
explanation_trick: The focal point F is the dividing line for a concave mirror: object beyond F -> real image; object within F -> virtual image — remember this threshold clearly, as it's a very frequently tested optics distinction.

explanation_options.a: Between the pole and F (i.e., within F) produces a VIRTUAL image, not a real one.
explanation_options.b: Only at infinity is too restrictive — real images form for the entire range beyond F, not just at infinity.
explanation_options.c: Concave mirrors DO form real images (for objects beyond F) — this option is simply false.
explanation_options.d: Correct — beyond the focal point, a concave mirror forms a real image.

subject: Physics
question_text: The image formed by a plane mirror is:
option_a: Virtual, upright, and the same size as the object
explanation_short: A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright image the same size as the object.
explanation_long: Reflection in a flat (plane) mirror always produces a virtual image (behind the mirror, can't be projected on a screen), upright (same orientation as the object), and exactly the same size as the object — regardless of the object's distance from the mirror.
explanation_trick: Plane mirrors are the one case in optics where image size never changes with object distance — unlike curved mirrors or lenses, where magnification depends on where the object is placed.

explanation_options.a: Correct — virtual, upright, and same-size, for a plane mirror.
explanation_options.b: Real and inverted images require a curved (concave) mirror or a lens, not a flat mirror.
explanation_options.c: Real, upright, and magnified doesn't match a plane mirror's fixed same-size, virtual behavior.
explanation_options.d: A plane mirror doesn't diminish image size — the image is always the same size as the object.

subject: Physics
question_text: The binding energy of a nucleus represents:
option_a: The kinetic energy of the nucleus
option_c: The mass of a single proton
option_d: The energy required to completely separate all its nucleons
explanation_short: Binding energy is the energy required to completely separate all of a nucleus's nucleons.
explanation_long: Nuclear binding energy is the energy that would need to be supplied to break a nucleus apart into its individual, separated protons and neutrons — equivalently, it's the energy released when those nucleons originally combined to form the nucleus (via the mass defect, per E=mc^2).
explanation_trick: Higher binding energy PER NUCLEON generally means a MORE stable nucleus — this concept underlies why both fission (of very heavy nuclei) and fusion (of very light nuclei) release energy, moving toward the most stable (iron-56 region) configuration.

explanation_options.a: Kinetic energy of the nucleus is a separate, unrelated quantity from binding energy.
explanation_options.b: The nucleus's charge is a separate property (total proton charge), not related to binding energy's definition.
explanation_options.c: A single proton's mass is just a basic particle property, not the energy needed to separate ALL nucleons.
explanation_options.d: Correct — binding energy is the energy needed to completely separate all the nucleons.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to Einstein's mass-energy equivalence (E = mc^2), a small amount of mass converted entirely into energy would release:
option_c: An enormous amount of energy, since c^2 is very large
explanation_short: E=mc^2: even a tiny mass converts to an enormous amount of energy, since c^2 is huge.
explanation_long: The speed of light c is about 3x10^8 m/s, so c^2 is about 9x10^16 — multiplying even a very small mass by this huge factor yields an enormous energy release, which is why nuclear reactions (converting tiny fractions of mass to energy) can be so much more powerful than chemical reactions.
explanation_trick: This is precisely why nuclear reactions (fission/fusion) release vastly more energy per unit mass than chemical reactions — the mass converted is tiny, but c^2 is such an enormous multiplier that the resulting energy is still huge.

explanation_options.a: The energy released is anything but negligible — c^2's enormous size is exactly why it's significant.
explanation_options.b: Zero energy would contradict Einstein's own equation, which directly predicts a nonzero (and large) energy release.
explanation_options.c: Correct — an enormous amount of energy is released, since c^2 is a huge multiplying factor.
explanation_options.d: The released energy isn't restricted to only 'thermal' form — E=mc^2 describes the total energy released, which can appear as kinetic energy, radiation, heat, etc., depending on the process.

subject: Physics
question_text: Nuclear fusion, the process powering the Sun, involves:
option_a: Light nuclei combining to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
option_c: The emission of alpha particles only
option_d: No change in mass or energy
explanation_short: Nuclear fusion (powering the Sun) is light nuclei combining into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
explanation_long: In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse together (via a series of nuclear reactions) to form helium, releasing enormous energy due to the mass difference between reactants and products (per E=mc^2) — this is fusion, distinct from and requiring much higher temperatures/pressures than fission.
explanation_trick: Fusion combines LIGHT nuclei (like hydrogen) into something heavier; fission splits HEAVY nuclei (like uranium) into something lighter — opposite directions on the periodic table, but both release net energy.

explanation_options.a: Correct — light nuclei combining into a heavier one, releasing energy, describes fusion.
explanation_options.b: Splitting heavy nuclei describes FISSION, the opposite process.
explanation_options.c: Fusion isn't defined by alpha-particle emission specifically — that's a separate radioactive decay process.
explanation_options.d: Fusion definitely involves changes in both mass (a small amount converts to energy) and energy — that's the whole point of the process.

subject: Physics
question_text: Nuclear fission involves:
option_a: The decay of a single proton
option_b: The fusion of two light nuclei into a heavier one
option_c: The absorption of a neutron with no further effect
option_d: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy
explanation_short: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy.
explanation_long: In fission, a heavy, unstable nucleus (like Uranium-235) splits into two smaller nuclei (plus typically some neutrons), releasing a large amount of energy from the difference in nuclear binding energy — the basis of nuclear power plants and fission-based weapons.
explanation_trick: Fission (splitting heavy nuclei) and fusion (combining light nuclei) are opposite processes that BOTH release energy, because both move nuclei toward the most stable region of the binding-energy curve (around iron) — don't confuse the two despite their opposite mechanisms.

explanation_options.a: A single proton doesn't 'decay' in the process being described here — this describes something else entirely.
explanation_options.b: Fusing light nuclei describes FUSION, the opposite process from fission.
explanation_options.c: Simple neutron absorption 'with no further effect' doesn't describe fission, which involves the nucleus actually splitting.
explanation_options.d: Correct — fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter ones, releasing energy.

subject: Physics
question_text: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 6 hours. Starting with 800 g, how much remains after 18 hours?
explanation_short: 18 hours = 3 half-lives (6h each); remaining = 800/(2^3) = 800/8 = 100 g.
explanation_long: Number of half-lives elapsed = 18/6 = 3. Remaining amount = initial x (1/2)^n = 800 x (1/2)^3 = 800/8 = 100 g.
explanation_trick: Always convert elapsed time into a NUMBER of half-lives first (divide by the half-life value), then apply (1/2)^n — don't try to use the half-life duration directly in a different formula.

explanation_options.a: 200 g would correspond to only 2 half-lives, not 3.
explanation_options.b: 400 g corresponds to just 1 half-life.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 800/(2^3) = 100 g after 3 half-lives.
explanation_options.d: 50 g would correspond to 4 half-lives (24 hours), one too many.

subject: Physics
question_text: Gamma decay involves the emission of:
option_a: High-energy electromagnetic radiation, with no change in atomic or mass number
explanation_short: Gamma decay emits high-energy EM radiation, with no change in atomic or mass number.
explanation_long: Gamma decay involves a nucleus in an excited energy state releasing energy as a high-energy photon (gamma ray) to reach a lower energy state — unlike alpha or beta decay, this doesn't change the number of protons or neutrons, so both the atomic number and mass number stay the same.
explanation_trick: Gamma decay is purely an ENERGY release (no particle ejected from the nucleus in terms of protons/neutrons) — this is why it doesn't transmute the element, unlike alpha or beta decay.

explanation_options.a: Correct — high-energy EM radiation, no change in atomic/mass number.
explanation_options.b: A helium nucleus is emitted in alpha decay, not gamma decay.
explanation_options.c: An electron is emitted in beta-minus decay, not gamma decay.
explanation_options.d: A neutron isn't what's emitted in standard gamma decay.

subject: Physics
question_text: In beta-minus decay, a neutron in the nucleus transforms into a proton, emitting:
explanation_short: Beta-minus decay emits an electron and an antineutrino as a neutron becomes a proton.
explanation_long: In beta-minus decay, a neutron converts into a proton, an electron (the 'beta particle'), and an electron antineutrino — conserving charge, lepton number, and energy/momentum in the process.
explanation_trick: Beta-minus emits an ELECTRON (not a positron) — positron emission is a different process (beta-plus decay), where a proton converts into a neutron instead.

explanation_options.a: Correct — an electron and an antineutrino are emitted in beta-minus decay.
explanation_options.b: An alpha particle (helium nucleus) is emitted in alpha decay, a different process entirely.
explanation_options.c: Gamma rays alone don't accompany the neutron-to-proton conversion that defines beta-minus decay (though gamma emission can accompany other nuclear transitions).
explanation_options.d: A positron is emitted in beta-PLUS decay (proton to neutron), the opposite conversion from what's described here.

subject: Physics
question_text: The nucleus of an atom consists of:
explanation_short: The atomic nucleus consists of protons and neutrons.
explanation_long: Protons (positively charged) and neutrons (neutral) together make up the dense, central nucleus of an atom; electrons orbit outside the nucleus and are NOT part of it.
explanation_trick: Electrons are never part of the nucleus itself — they occupy the surrounding electron cloud/orbitals, a common point of confusion for beginners.

explanation_options.a: Correct — protons and neutrons make up the nucleus.
explanation_options.b: Electrons are outside the nucleus, not part of it.
explanation_options.c: Electrons again don't belong in the nucleus — only protons and neutrons do.
explanation_options.d: The nucleus (except for ordinary hydrogen) contains neutrons too, not just protons.

subject: Physics
question_text: Light of frequency 6 x 10^14 Hz strikes a metal with a work function of 2 x 10^-19 J. Using E = hf (h = 6.6 x 10^-34 Js), what is the approximate maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons?
explanation_long: First find the photon energy: E=hf=6.6x10^-34 x 6x10^14 = 3.96x10^-19 J. Then subtract the work function: KE_max = E - phi = 3.96x10^-19 - 2x10^-19 = 1.96x10^-19 J.
explanation_trick: Always calculate the photon energy (hf) FIRST, then subtract the work function — don't try to combine h, f, and phi in a single non-standard formula.

explanation_options.a: 3.96 x 10^-19 J is just the photon energy itself, before subtracting the work function.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 3.96e-19 minus 2e-19 = 1.96e-19 J.
explanation_options.c: 5.96 x 10^-19 J mistakenly adds the work function instead of subtracting it.
explanation_options.d: 0 J would only occur if the photon energy exactly equaled the work function (the threshold condition), which isn't the case here.

subject: Physics
question_text: The Planck constant relates a photon's energy to its:
explanation_short: Planck's constant relates photon energy inversely to wavelength and directly to frequency (E=hf=hc/lambda).
explanation_long: Combining E=hf with the wave relation c=f*lambda gives E=hc/lambda — so photon energy increases with frequency (direct proportionality) but decreases with wavelength (inverse proportionality), with Planck's constant h as the proportionality factor throughout.
explanation_trick: Remember BOTH relationships together: E is directly proportional to f AND inversely proportional to lambda — since f and lambda are themselves inversely related via c=f*lambda, these two statements are fully consistent with each other.

explanation_options.a: Photon energy formula (E=hf) doesn't involve mass at all — photons are massless.
explanation_options.b: Correct — E is inversely related to wavelength and directly related to frequency, via Planck's constant.
explanation_options.c: Charge isn't part of the photon energy relationship.
explanation_options.d: Speed of light (c) is a fixed constant in vacuum, not itself the direct energy-determining variable in E=hf (frequency is).

subject: Physics
question_text: Photons of light with higher frequency carry:
option_b: The same energy regardless of frequency
option_c: More energy, according to E = hf
explanation_short: Higher-frequency photons carry more energy, per E=hf.
explanation_long: Photon energy is directly proportional to frequency: E = hf, where h is Planck's constant. Higher frequency light (like blue/violet or UV) carries more energy per photon than lower-frequency light (like red or infrared).
explanation_trick: This direct relationship (E proportional to f) is the foundation of the whole photon concept — it's why, for instance, UV light can cause sunburn/DNA damage while lower-frequency visible light generally cannot.

explanation_options.a: Less energy would be the reverse (incorrect) relationship — higher frequency means MORE energy, not less.
explanation_options.b: Energy is NOT frequency-independent — E=hf directly ties them together.
explanation_options.c: Correct — E=hf means higher frequency carries more energy.
explanation_options.d: Photons always carry some energy proportional to their frequency — never zero (for any nonzero frequency).

subject: Physics
question_text: The emission spectrum of hydrogen consists of discrete spectral lines because:
option_a: Electrons move in continuous orbits at any energy
option_c: Light is absorbed uniformly at all wavelengths
option_d: Electrons can occupy only specific, quantized energy levels
explanation_short: Hydrogen's discrete spectral lines arise because electrons occupy only specific, quantized energy levels.
explanation_long: Since electrons in a hydrogen atom can only exist at specific, discrete energy levels, transitions between these levels release photons of only specific, discrete energies (and hence specific wavelengths/frequencies) — producing the characteristic sharp spectral lines, rather than a continuous spectrum.
explanation_trick: A CONTINUOUS spectrum would result from continuous (unquantized) energy levels — the fact that hydrogen's spectrum is DISCRETE (specific lines) is direct experimental evidence for quantization.

explanation_options.a: Continuous orbits at any energy would actually produce a continuous spectrum, not discrete lines.
explanation_options.b: Hydrogen atoms do contain electrons (one, specifically) — that's a false premise.
explanation_options.c: Uniform absorption at all wavelengths would also produce a continuous (not discrete-line) pattern.
explanation_options.d: Correct — quantized energy levels are why hydrogen shows discrete spectral lines.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, it is fundamentally impossible to simultaneously know with perfect precision a particle's:
explanation_short: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: position and momentum cannot both be known with perfect precision simultaneously.
explanation_long: The uncertainty principle states that there's a fundamental limit (not just a measurement-technology limitation) to how precisely both position and momentum of a particle can be simultaneously known: Δx x Δp ≥ h/(4 pi).
explanation_trick: This is a fundamental physical limit, not merely a practical limitation of imperfect instruments — even with 'perfect' measuring equipment, this trade-off would still exist.

explanation_options.a: Charge and mass aren't the pair of quantities linked by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.
explanation_options.b: Energy and charge aren't the standard Heisenberg uncertainty pair either (though there IS a related energy-time uncertainty relation).
explanation_options.c: Temperature and volume aren't quantum-mechanically linked by this principle.
explanation_options.d: Correct — position and momentum are the classic Heisenberg uncertainty pair.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to de Broglie's hypothesis, particles such as electrons exhibit:
option_c: Wave-particle duality, with an associated wavelength related to their momentum
explanation_short: De Broglie: particles like electrons show wave-particle duality with a wavelength tied to momentum.
explanation_long: De Broglie proposed that all matter has an associated wavelength, lambda = h/p (Planck's constant over momentum) — meaning particles like electrons can exhibit wave-like behavior (such as diffraction), alongside their familiar particle-like properties.
explanation_trick: Larger momentum corresponds to a SHORTER de Broglie wavelength (lambda = h/p, inverse relationship) — this is why everyday macroscopic objects have imperceptibly tiny wavelengths, while small, light particles like electrons show measurable wave effects.

explanation_options.a: Only particle-like behavior misses de Broglie's key insight about wave characteristics too.
explanation_options.b: 'No wave characteristics at all' directly contradicts de Broglie's hypothesis.
explanation_options.c: Correct — de Broglie's wave-particle duality, with wavelength tied to momentum.
explanation_options.d: The wavelength isn't infinite — it's finite and inversely related to the particle's momentum (lambda=h/p).

subject: Physics
question_text: X-rays are a form of:
option_b: Electromagnetic radiation with high energy and short wavelength
explanation_short: X-rays are electromagnetic radiation with high energy and short wavelength.
explanation_long: X-rays occupy a high-energy, short-wavelength portion of the electromagnetic spectrum (between ultraviolet and gamma rays) — like all EM radiation, they can travel through vacuum and require no medium.
explanation_trick: Being electromagnetic (not mechanical) is why X-rays can penetrate tissue and pass through vacuum in medical/astronomical imaging applications — a mechanical wave couldn't do either.

explanation_options.a: X-rays are electromagnetic, not sound (mechanical) waves.
explanation_options.b: Correct — X-rays are high-energy, short-wavelength electromagnetic radiation.
explanation_options.c: X-rays don't need a medium — they're electromagnetic, able to travel through vacuum.
explanation_options.d: X-rays are massless electromagnetic radiation (photons), not particles with significant rest mass.

subject: Physics
question_text: The work function of a metal is defined as:
option_a: The total energy of an incoming photon
option_b: The kinetic energy of an emitted electron
option_d: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the metal's surface
explanation_short: Work function: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a metal's surface.
explanation_long: The work function (phi) is a material-specific threshold energy that a photon must at least supply to liberate an electron from the metal's surface; any photon energy beyond this threshold becomes the ejected electron's kinetic energy (KE_max = hf − phi).
explanation_trick: Work function is a property of the METAL (fixed), not of the incoming light — don't confuse it with the photon's own energy (hf), which varies with the light source's frequency.

explanation_options.a: The photon's total energy is hf, a separate (light-dependent) quantity, not the metal's fixed work function.
explanation_options.b: The ejected electron's kinetic energy is what's LEFT OVER after overcoming the work function, not the work function itself.
explanation_options.c: The frequency of incoming light is a property of the light source, not of the metal's work function.
explanation_options.d: Correct — work function is the minimum energy needed to eject an electron from the metal surface.

subject: Physics
question_text: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light at a fixed frequency (above the threshold frequency) increases:
option_a: The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons
option_b: The work function of the metal
option_d: The number of photoelectrons emitted per second, not their maximum kinetic energy
explanation_short: Increasing light intensity (above threshold frequency) increases the NUMBER of photoelectrons emitted per second, not their max KE.
explanation_long: Each photon's energy (hf) determines the maximum kinetic energy of an ejected electron (via KE_max = hf − work function) — this depends only on frequency, not intensity. Increasing intensity means MORE photons arrive per second, ejecting more electrons per second, but each individual electron's max KE stays the same.
explanation_trick: Intensity affects the RATE (number of photoelectrons per second, i.e., photocurrent), while frequency affects the ENERGY (max KE) of each individual photoelectron — these are two separate, independently controllable variables in this experiment.

explanation_options.a: Maximum KE depends on frequency (via E=hf), not on intensity — this option describes the wrong variable's effect.
explanation_options.b: The work function is an intrinsic material property, unaffected by the incoming light's intensity.
explanation_options.c: The threshold frequency is also an intrinsic material property (tied to the work function), not changed by intensity.
explanation_options.d: Correct — intensity increases the number of photoelectrons per second, not their maximum kinetic energy.

subject: Physics
question_text: The photoelectric effect demonstrates that light behaves as:
option_a: A continuous wave only, with no particle nature
option_c: A stream of discrete energy packets called photons
option_d: A form of matter with rest mass
explanation_short: The photoelectric effect shows light behaves as discrete energy packets (photons).
explanation_long: Einstein's explanation of the photoelectric effect (electrons ejected from a metal only above a threshold FREQUENCY, regardless of intensity) could only be explained by treating light as quantized packets of energy (photons, E=hf), not as a purely continuous wave.
explanation_trick: A purely wave-based (classical) model of light predicts that even low-frequency, high-intensity light should eventually eject electrons — but experimentally it doesn't, below the threshold frequency, which is exactly the anomaly photon theory resolves.

explanation_options.a: A purely continuous wave model fails to explain the frequency threshold behavior seen in this effect.
explanation_options.b: A purely mechanical wave model doesn't apply to light at all in this context.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the photoelectric effect demonstrates light's particle-like photon nature.
explanation_options.d: Photons don't have rest mass — they're massless particles, even though they carry energy and momentum.

subject: Physics
question_text: When an electron transitions from a higher energy level to a lower one, the atom:
option_b: Emits a photon with energy equal to the difference between the two levels
explanation_short: An electron dropping to a lower energy level causes the atom to emit a photon with energy equal to the level difference.
explanation_long: When an electron transitions from a higher to a lower energy level, the atom releases the excess energy as a single photon, with photon energy E = hf = E_high − E_low (the difference between the two energy levels).
explanation_trick: Photon EMISSION happens when an electron drops to a LOWER level; photon ABSORPTION happens when an electron is excited UP to a higher level — opposite processes, easy to swap under exam pressure.

explanation_options.a: Absorbing a photon would correspond to a transition UP (to a higher level), not down.
explanation_options.b: Correct — a photon is emitted, with energy equal to the level difference.
explanation_options.c: The atom doesn't gain mass from this electronic transition.
explanation_options.d: The electron doesn't leave the atom entirely — it simply moves to a lower-energy orbital within the same atom.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to Bohr's model of the atom, electrons orbit the nucleus in:
option_a: Random paths with no fixed pattern
option_b: A continuous range of any possible orbit
option_c: Specific, quantized energy levels or orbits
option_d: Orbits identical to planetary orbits, with no quantum restriction
explanation_short: Bohr's model: electrons orbit in specific, quantized energy levels/orbits.
explanation_long: Bohr proposed that electrons can only occupy certain discrete, quantized orbits (with specific energies) around the nucleus, rather than any arbitrary orbit — a radical departure from classical (continuous) orbital mechanics, which explained hydrogen's discrete spectral lines.
explanation_trick: 'Quantized' is the key word — Bohr's key insight was restricting orbits to specific allowed energy levels, not letting electrons occupy any continuous range of orbits like a classical planet.

explanation_options.a: Random paths with no pattern contradicts Bohr's central postulate of specific, ordered orbits.
explanation_options.b: A continuous range of orbits describes classical (non-quantized) mechanics, the opposite of Bohr's model.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Bohr's model restricts electrons to specific, quantized energy levels.
explanation_options.d: Bohr's orbits are explicitly NOT unrestricted like planetary orbits — quantization is the whole point of the model.

subject: Physics
question_text: An AND logic gate produces a high (1) output only when:
option_a: At least one input is high
explanation_short: An AND gate outputs high (1) only when ALL its inputs are high.
explanation_long: The AND logic gate's truth table gives a high output only in the single case where every input is high (1); if even one input is low (0), the output is low.
explanation_trick: AND requires ALL inputs high (like a strict 'both must be true' condition), whereas an OR gate would output high if AT LEAST ONE input is high — don't mix up these two basic gates.

explanation_options.a: 'At least one high' describes an OR gate, not AND.
explanation_options.b: All inputs low would definitely give a low (not high) AND output.
explanation_options.c: Exactly one input high would still give a LOW AND output (since not ALL inputs are high).
explanation_options.d: Correct — AND requires ALL inputs to be high for a high output.

subject: Physics
question_text: Logic gates form the basic building blocks of:
explanation_short: Logic gates are the basic building blocks of digital electronic circuits and computers.
explanation_long: Logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, etc.) perform basic Boolean operations on binary (0/1) signals, and combinations of these gates form the fundamental building blocks of all digital circuits, from simple counters to full computer processors.
explanation_trick: Logic gates operate on discrete (digital) signals, fundamentally different from continuous (analog) signal processing — this digital/analog distinction is key to why they're specifically tied to 'digital' electronics.

explanation_options.a: Analog radio circuits work with continuous signals, not the discrete logic-gate operations described here.
explanation_options.b: Correct — logic gates underpin digital electronic circuits and computers.
explanation_options.c: Mechanical systems don't fundamentally rely on electronic logic gates.
explanation_options.d: Optical fibers are a signal-transmission medium, not built from logic gates.

subject: Physics
question_text: The three terminals of a bipolar junction transistor are the:
explanation_short: A BJT's three terminals are the emitter, base, and collector.
explanation_long: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has three doped regions/terminals: the emitter (emits charge carriers), base (thin control region), and collector (collects the carriers) — distinct from a field-effect transistor's source/drain/gate terminology.
explanation_trick: Emitter-Base-Collector (BJT) vs. Source-Drain-Gate (FET/MOSFET) — two different transistor families with different terminal names; don't mix them up.

explanation_options.a: Correct — emitter, base, and collector are a BJT's three terminals.
explanation_options.b: Anode, cathode, and gate describes something like a thyristor/SCR, not a basic BJT.
explanation_options.c: Source, drain, and gate describes a field-effect transistor (FET), not a bipolar junction transistor.
explanation_options.d: Positive, negative, and neutral aren't standard transistor terminal names at all.

subject: Physics
question_text: A transistor can act as an amplifier because:
option_a: A small change in base current produces a much larger change in collector current
option_b: A change in collector current causes a large change in base current
option_c: Emitter voltage has no effect on the circuit
explanation_short: A transistor amplifies because a small base-current change produces a much larger collector-current change.
explanation_long: In a bipolar junction transistor, the base current controls a much larger collector current (governed by the current gain, beta = Ic/Ib) — a small input signal at the base translates into a proportionally much bigger output signal at the collector, which is the basis of amplification.
explanation_trick: It's the BASE current controlling the (much larger) COLLECTOR current — reversing this causal direction (collector controlling base) would misdescribe how a transistor actually works as an amplifier.

explanation_options.a: Correct — small base-current changes produce much larger collector-current changes.
explanation_options.b: This reverses the actual control relationship — it's base current that controls collector current, not the other way around.
explanation_options.c: Emitter voltage very much does affect transistor operation — it's central to how the device is biased and functions.
explanation_options.d: Resistance doesn't simply make voltage 'disappear' — that phrasing doesn't describe how amplification works at all.

subject: Physics
question_text: A diode is used as a rectifier mainly because it:
option_a: Allows current to flow in both directions equally
option_c: Stores electrical charge like a capacitor
option_d: Allows current to flow predominantly in one direction, converting AC to pulsating DC
explanation_short: A diode rectifies because it allows current predominantly in one direction, turning AC into pulsating DC.
explanation_long: A diode's one-way conduction property (forward bias allows current, reverse bias blocks it) means an alternating current signal passing through a diode gets 'clipped' to flow in only one direction — producing pulsating DC, the basis of rectifier circuits.
explanation_trick: A diode isn't a perfect one-way valve in the amplification or storage sense — its usefulness for rectification comes purely from this asymmetric (one-direction-favored) current-passing behavior.

explanation_options.a: A diode does NOT allow current equally in both directions — that would defeat its rectifying purpose entirely.
explanation_options.b: Amplifying voltage signals is a transistor's function, not a basic diode's.
explanation_options.c: Storing charge like a capacitor isn't how a diode achieves rectification.
explanation_options.d: Correct — a diode passes current predominantly one way, converting AC to pulsating DC.

subject: Physics
question_text: A P-N junction diode allows current to flow easily when it is:
option_b: Forward biased, with the p-side connected to the positive terminal
option_c: Not connected to any voltage source
explanation_short: A P-N junction diode conducts easily when forward biased (p-side connected to positive terminal).
explanation_long: Forward bias (positive terminal to p-side, negative to n-side) narrows the depletion region and allows majority carriers to flow easily across the junction, letting current pass; reverse bias widens the depletion region and blocks current flow (except a tiny leakage current).
explanation_trick: 'Forward bias, p-side to positive' is the specific memorable configuration that makes a diode conduct — reversing this polarity (reverse bias) essentially blocks current instead.

explanation_options.a: Reverse bias blocks (rather than allows) current flow through the diode.
explanation_options.b: Correct — forward bias, with p-side connected to positive, allows easy current flow.
explanation_options.c: With no voltage source connected, there's no driving force for current at all.
explanation_options.d: A short circuit isn't the defining 'easy conduction' bias condition being described — that's specifically forward bias.

subject: Physics
question_text: Doping a semiconductor with an element having five valence electrons (such as phosphorus in silicon) creates a(n):
option_d: N-type semiconductor, with excess free electrons
explanation_short: Doping with a pentavalent element (5 valence electrons, like phosphorus) creates an N-type semiconductor.
explanation_long: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons; when it replaces a silicon atom (4 valence electrons) in the crystal lattice, it contributes one extra, loosely-bound electron — creating excess negative (electron) charge carriers, hence 'N-type' semiconductor.
explanation_trick: Remember: pentavalent (5 valence electrons) dopant -> N-type (extra electrons); trivalent (3 valence electrons) dopant -> P-type (creates 'holes,' i.e., positive charge carriers) — the numbers 5-and-N, 3-and-P are worth memorizing as a pair.

explanation_options.a: P-type comes from doping with a TRIVALENT (3 valence electron) element, not a pentavalent one.
explanation_options.b: An intrinsic semiconductor is undoped pure material, not the result of adding phosphorus.
explanation_options.c: Doping doesn't turn a semiconductor into an insulator — it enhances its conductivity, just with a specific majority carrier type.
explanation_options.d: Correct — pentavalent doping creates an N-type semiconductor with excess free electrons.

subject: Physics
question_text: A semiconductor's electrical conductivity lies between that of:
explanation_short: A semiconductor's conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator.
explanation_long: Semiconductors (like silicon, germanium) have electrical conductivity intermediate between good conductors (metals) and insulators — this intermediate, tunable conductivity (via doping) is what makes them useful for electronic devices.
explanation_trick: 'Semiconductor' literally hints at this in-between nature — neither as freely conducting as a metal nor as resistive as a true insulator.

explanation_options.a: Correct — semiconductor conductivity is between a conductor and an insulator.
explanation_options.b: Comparing two conductors doesn't capture the defining 'in-between' nature of a semiconductor.
explanation_options.c: Comparing two insulators likewise misses the point — a semiconductor conducts noticeably better than an insulator.
explanation_options.d: A superconductor (zero resistance) and vacuum (no charge carriers) is an unrelated, much more extreme comparison.

subject: Physics
question_text: Self-inductance of a coil opposes:
option_a: The current flowing in a neighboring coil only
option_d: Any change in the current flowing through it
explanation_short: Self-inductance opposes any change in the current flowing through the coil itself.
explanation_long: A coil's self-inductance creates a back-EMF that opposes whatever change is occurring in its own current (per Lenz's law applied to the coil's own changing flux) — this is why current in an inductor can't change instantaneously.
explanation_trick: Self-inductance is about the coil opposing changes in its OWN current, distinct from mutual inductance (where one coil's changing current affects a nearby, separate coil).

explanation_options.a: That describes mutual inductance (affecting a NEIGHBORING coil), not self-inductance.
explanation_options.b: Self-inductance opposes changes in current generally, not exclusively DC scenarios.
explanation_options.c: Self-inductance specifically responds to CHANGING current/flux, not static fields.
explanation_options.d: Correct — self-inductance opposes any change in the coil's own current.

subject: Physics
question_text: Eddy currents are:
option_a: Currents that only flow in insulators
option_b: Currents induced in a conductor due to a changing magnetic flux, often causing energy loss as heat
option_d: Currents that flow only in DC circuits
explanation_short: Eddy currents are induced currents in a conductor from changing flux, often causing heat loss.
explanation_long: Eddy currents are loop-like induced currents that form within a bulk conductor due to changing magnetic flux (e.g., in a transformer core or a moving conductor near a magnet) — they typically dissipate energy as resistive heating, which is often an undesirable loss (though sometimes useful, like in induction braking).
explanation_trick: Eddy currents are a specific case of electromagnetic induction acting WITHIN a solid conductor's own bulk (not just a wire loop) — engineers often use laminated cores specifically to reduce/minimize these energy-wasting eddy currents.

explanation_options.a: Eddy currents flow in CONDUCTORS, not insulators (insulators don't support free-flowing current).
explanation_options.b: Correct — eddy currents are induced conductor currents, often causing heat-loss.
explanation_options.c: Eddy currents aren't always beneficial — they often represent unwanted energy loss (though sometimes intentionally exploited, e.g., in braking systems).
explanation_options.d: Eddy currents arise from CHANGING flux, which can occur in both AC systems and situations with relative motion — not limited to DC circuits.

subject: Physics
question_text: An AC voltage has a peak value of 170 V. What is its approximate RMS (root-mean-square) value?
explanation_short: RMS voltage = peak/sqrt(2) = 170/1.414 ≈ 120 V.
explanation_long: For a sinusoidal AC voltage, RMS value = peak value / sqrt(2) ≈ peak x 0.707. So RMS = 170/1.414 ≈ 120 V — this matches the standard 120V household AC RMS value in regions using a 170V peak (~120V RMS) supply.
explanation_trick: RMS is always LESS than the peak value for a sinusoid (by a factor of about 0.707) — a very commonly referenced conversion (this is exactly the US household voltage relationship: 170V peak, 120V RMS).

explanation_options.a: 85 V would be peak/2, not peak/sqrt(2) — an incorrect conversion factor.
explanation_options.b: 170 V is just the peak value itself, not the RMS value.
explanation_options.c: 240 V would be roughly peak x sqrt(2), the reverse conversion (RMS to peak, not peak to RMS).
explanation_options.d: Correct — 170/sqrt(2) ≈ 120 V.

subject: Physics
question_text: An AC generator converts:
option_d: Mechanical energy into electrical energy, typically via electromagnetic induction
explanation_short: An AC generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy via electromagnetic induction.
explanation_long: A generator spins a coil within a magnetic field (or vice versa), and the resulting changing flux induces an alternating EMF — this is the reverse process of an electric motor, converting mechanical rotational energy into electrical energy.
explanation_trick: Generator (mechanical -> electrical) and motor (electrical -> mechanical) are reverse processes of each other, both relying on electromagnetic principles — easy to mix up which converts which way.

explanation_options.a: Electrical to mechanical describes a MOTOR, the reverse of a generator.
explanation_options.b: Chemical to electrical describes a battery/electrochemical cell, not a generator.
explanation_options.c: Nuclear to mechanical isn't the direct conversion an AC generator performs.
explanation_options.d: Correct — mechanical to electrical, via electromagnetic induction, is what an AC generator does.

subject: Physics
question_text: The diagram shows a step-up transformer with 100 turns on the primary coil and 400 turns on the secondary coil, connected to a 20 V AC source on the primary side. Based on the diagram, what is the secondary voltage?
explanation_long: The transformer voltage-turns relationship: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Vs = Vp x (Ns/Np) = 20V x (400/100) = 20 x 4 = 80 V.
explanation_trick: Since Ns > Np (400 > 100), this is confirmed as a step-UP transformer, and the output voltage should indeed be higher than the input — a useful sanity check on your answer's direction.

explanation_options.a: 5 V would be a step-DOWN result, inconsistent with Ns > Np here.
explanation_options.c: 400 V mistakenly uses Ns directly as if it were the voltage ratio itself.
explanation_options.d: 20 V (unchanged) would only apply if Np equaled Ns, which isn't the case here.

subject: Physics
question_text: A transformer is used to:
option_a: Change the voltage level of an alternating current
explanation_short: A transformer changes the voltage level of an alternating current.
explanation_long: Transformers use electromagnetic induction between primary and secondary coils (with different turn ratios) to step voltage up or down for AC — they cannot work with steady DC, since a constant flux induces no EMF.
explanation_trick: Transformers ONLY work with AC (or changing DC) precisely because they rely on a CHANGING flux to induce a secondary voltage — this is why they can't 'convert AC to DC' themselves (that requires a rectifier, a separate device).

explanation_options.a: Correct — a transformer changes AC voltage levels (step-up or step-down).
explanation_options.b: Converting AC to DC is done by a rectifier (often built from diodes), not a transformer itself.
explanation_options.c: A transformer doesn't generate current from nothing — it transfers/transforms existing AC power via induction.
explanation_options.d: A transformer doesn't store electrical energy the way a capacitor or battery does — it transfers power in real time via mutual induction.

subject: Physics
question_text: A coil with 100 turns experiences a change in magnetic flux of 0.02 Wb over 0.1 s. What is the magnitude of the induced EMF?
explanation_long: Using Faraday's law magnitude: EMF = N x (change in flux)/(time) = 100 x 0.02/0.1 = 100 x 0.2 = 20 V.
explanation_trick: Don't forget to multiply by the number of turns N — using just the single-loop flux-rate (0.2 V) without the x100 factor is a common oversight.

explanation_options.a: 2 V forgets to multiply by the number of turns (or divides by 10 extra).
explanation_options.c: 0.2 V is just the single-turn value, missing the x100 factor for N turns.
explanation_options.d: 200 V overshoots by a factor of 10.

subject: Physics
question_text: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current:
option_a: Reinforces the change in flux that caused it
option_b: Opposes the change in flux that caused it, consistent with conservation of energy
explanation_short: Lenz's law: induced current opposes the change in flux that caused it (conserving energy).
explanation_long: Lenz's law specifies the DIRECTION of induced current: it always flows so as to oppose the change in magnetic flux that produced it — this is required by energy conservation (otherwise, induction could create runaway self-amplifying energy from nothing).
explanation_trick: 'Opposes the change,' not 'opposes the flux itself' — the induced current creates its own magnetic field that fights against whatever CHANGE (increase or decrease) is occurring, in either direction as appropriate.

explanation_options.a: Reinforcing the change would violate energy conservation (a runaway feedback loop), which is exactly why Lenz's law exists to rule this out.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Lenz's law: induced current opposes the flux change, per energy conservation.
explanation_options.c: The direction IS well-defined — that's the entire point of Lenz's law.
explanation_options.d: The direction depends on the specific situation (increasing vs. decreasing flux, coil orientation), not fixed as always clockwise.

subject: Physics
question_text: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced EMF is proportional to:
option_b: The rate of change of magnetic flux
explanation_short: Faraday's law: induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux.
explanation_long: Faraday's law states EMF = -N(dPhi/dt) — the induced EMF depends on how FAST the magnetic flux is changing (and the number of turns N), not on the field strength or flux value alone.
explanation_trick: A rapidly changing SMALL flux can induce a larger EMF than a slowly changing LARGE flux — it's the rate of change, not the absolute flux, that determines EMF magnitude.

explanation_options.a: Field strength ALONE (without considering its rate of change) doesn't determine induced EMF.
explanation_options.b: Correct — EMF is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux.
explanation_options.c: Circuit resistance affects the resulting CURRENT (via Ohm's law) but isn't what determines the induced EMF itself.
explanation_options.d: Pre-existing current in the circuit isn't the source of the newly induced EMF.

subject: Physics
question_text: Electromagnetic induction refers to the generation of an EMF due to:
option_a: A changing magnetic flux through a circuit
explanation_short: Electromagnetic induction generates EMF due to a CHANGING magnetic flux through a circuit.
explanation_long: Faraday's law of induction: an EMF is induced whenever the magnetic flux through a circuit changes over time — whether from a changing field, changing area, or changing orientation. A constant (unchanging) flux, however strong, induces no EMF.
explanation_trick: It's specifically the CHANGE in flux that matters, not the flux's absolute magnitude — a strong but constant magnetic field through a stationary loop induces nothing.

explanation_options.a: Correct — a changing magnetic flux induces the EMF.
explanation_options.b: A constant magnetic field, with no change, induces no EMF at all.
explanation_options.c: Direct current flow isn't itself the defining condition — it's flux CHANGE that matters (even from AC or moving magnets).
explanation_options.d: Static electric charge doesn't directly cause electromagnetic induction — that requires changing magnetic flux.

subject: Physics
question_text: The magnetic field at the center of a current-carrying circular loop is:
option_b: Parallel to the plane of the loop
option_c: Maximum, perpendicular to the plane of the loop
option_d: Equal to the field far from the loop
explanation_short: The magnetic field at the center of a current loop is maximum and perpendicular to the loop's plane.
explanation_long: By the Biot-Savart law, the contributions from all points around a circular current loop add constructively at the center, producing the field's maximum value there, oriented perpendicular to the plane of the loop (along its axis), following the right-hand rule.
explanation_trick: The field strength decreases as you move away from the loop's center along its axis — the center is specifically where the field is strongest for this geometry.

explanation_options.a: The field isn't zero at the center — it's actually at its strongest there.
explanation_options.b: The field is perpendicular TO the loop's plane, not parallel to it.
explanation_options.c: Correct — maximum field, perpendicular to the loop's plane, at the center.
explanation_options.d: The field decreases with distance from the loop — it's not equal to the (weaker) far-field value at the center.

subject: Physics
question_text: A magnetic compass needle aligns with Earth's magnetic field because:
option_a: It is attracted directly to Earth's core
option_b: It has no interaction with Earth's magnetic field
option_c: It experiences a torque aligning it with the local magnetic field direction
option_d: It is repelled by all magnetic fields
explanation_short: A compass needle aligns with Earth's field because it experiences a torque toward the local field direction.
explanation_long: A compass needle is a small magnetic dipole; in an external magnetic field (Earth's), it experiences a torque that rotates it to align with the local field direction — this torque vanishes once aligned, giving a stable equilibrium orientation.
explanation_trick: The needle responds to Earth's magnetic field via torque (rotational alignment), not by being 'attracted' translationally to any single point like the core — it's a directional, not positional, effect.

explanation_options.a: The needle isn't attracted directly to Earth's core — it responds to the local magnetic field direction via torque.
explanation_options.b: The needle absolutely interacts with Earth's magnetic field — that's the entire basis of how a compass works.
explanation_options.c: Correct — torque aligns the needle with the local magnetic field.
explanation_options.d: The needle isn't uniformly repelled by all magnetic fields — it aligns with (rather than being repelled from) the ambient field.

subject: Physics
question_text: A charged particle moves in a circular path within a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force provides:
option_a: Centripetal force, keeping it in circular motion at constant speed
option_c: No net effect on its motion
option_d: A force in the direction of motion
explanation_short: In circular motion within a magnetic field, the magnetic force provides the centripetal force, keeping speed constant.
explanation_long: Since the magnetic force (F=qvB) is always perpendicular to velocity, it changes the particle's direction but never its speed — this perpendicular force acts exactly as the centripetal force needed to maintain uniform circular motion.
explanation_trick: Because the magnetic force does no work (it's always perpendicular to displacement/velocity), the particle's kinetic energy — and hence speed — never changes, only its direction does.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the magnetic force acts as centripetal force, at constant speed.
explanation_options.b: The magnetic force never increases speed since it's always perpendicular to velocity (does no work).
explanation_options.c: The magnetic force definitely affects motion — it's what curves the path into a circle.
explanation_options.d: The force is perpendicular TO the direction of motion, not along it.

subject: Physics
question_text: The force between two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction is:
explanation_short: Parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other.
explanation_long: Each current-carrying wire creates a magnetic field that exerts a force on the other wire (via F=IL x B); when the currents flow in the same direction, this mutual force is attractive; when in opposite directions, it's repulsive.
explanation_trick: Same direction -> attract; opposite direction -> repel — this is actually the OPPOSITE intuition from electric charges (like charges repel), so it's worth deliberately memorizing separately.

explanation_options.a: Repulsion occurs when the currents flow in OPPOSITE directions, not the same direction.
explanation_options.b: Correct — same-direction currents in parallel wires attract.
explanation_options.c: The force isn't zero — there is a genuine (attractive) force between them.
explanation_options.d: The force is along the line connecting the wires (attractive/repulsive), not perpendicular to both wires.

subject: Physics
question_text: A solenoid with a soft iron core has a stronger magnetic field than an air-core solenoid mainly because:
option_a: Iron has high magnetic permeability, which strengthens the field
option_b: Iron increases the resistance of the wire
explanation_short: An iron core strengthens a solenoid's field because iron has high magnetic permeability.
explanation_long: Magnetic permeability measures how easily a material supports the formation of a magnetic field within it; ferromagnetic materials like iron have very high permeability, greatly amplifying the field compared to an air core for the same current and winding.
explanation_trick: The iron core doesn't add current or resistance-related effects — its role is purely about permeability, concentrating and strengthening the magnetic field lines.

explanation_options.a: Correct — iron's high permeability strengthens the magnetic field.
explanation_options.b: The core's effect on the wire's electrical resistance isn't the reason for the stronger magnetic field.
explanation_options.c: Iron doesn't block the field — it actually concentrates and strengthens it.
explanation_options.d: The core doesn't increase the current flowing through the coil.

subject: Physics
question_text: The strength of the magnetic field inside a solenoid is increased by:
option_c: Increasing the current or the number of turns per unit length
explanation_short: A solenoid's field strength increases with more current or more turns per unit length.
explanation_long: The magnetic field inside a solenoid is given by B = mu0 x n x I, where n is turns per unit length and I is the current — so increasing either the current or the turn density increases the field strength.
explanation_trick: Adding a ferromagnetic (e.g., iron) core also increases the field further (higher effective permeability) — but among the given options, current and turn density are the direct solenoid-formula variables.

explanation_options.a: Decreasing turns would decrease (not increase) the field.
explanation_options.b: Removing the core material would actually decrease field strength if a ferromagnetic core was present.
explanation_options.c: Correct — increasing current or turns per unit length increases the solenoid's field.
explanation_options.d: Decreasing the current would decrease (not increase) the field.

subject: Physics
question_text: The diagram shows a straight wire carrying a current of 5 A, placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T, with 0.5 m of the wire's length inside the field. Based on the diagram, what is the magnitude of the force on the wire?
explanation_long: For a straight current-carrying wire perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, F = BIL = 0.2T x 5A x 0.5m = 0.5 N.
explanation_trick: Straightforward multiplication of the three given quantities (B, I, L) — this formula only applies directly when the wire is perpendicular to B, as stated here.

explanation_options.a: 5 N overshoots by a factor of 10.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 0.2 x 5 x 0.5 = 0.5 N.
explanation_options.c: 1 N overshoots by a factor of 2.
explanation_options.d: 0.05 N undershoots by a factor of 10.

subject: Physics
question_text: A charged particle moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences:
option_c: A force perpendicular to the field
option_d: A force equal to its weight
explanation_short: A charge moving parallel to B experiences no magnetic force (since sin(0 degrees)=0).
explanation_long: F=qvBsin(theta); when velocity is parallel to the magnetic field, theta=0 degrees, so sin(theta)=0, making the magnetic force exactly zero regardless of the charge's speed or the field strength.
explanation_trick: This is the flip side of the 'maximum at 90 degrees' fact — parallel motion to B gives zero force, a frequently paired concept.

explanation_options.a: Maximum force occurs at 90 degrees (perpendicular), not when parallel to the field.
explanation_options.b: Correct — parallel motion to B means zero magnetic force.
explanation_options.c: A perpendicular force would occur at some other, nonzero angle, not when moving exactly parallel to B.
explanation_options.d: The magnetic force has nothing to do with the charge's weight — these are entirely separate forces.

subject: Physics
question_text: The magnetic force on a moving charge is given by F = qvB*sin(theta), where theta is the angle between velocity and the field. This force is maximum when theta equals:
explanation_short: F=qvBsin(theta) is maximum when sin(theta)=1, i.e., theta=90 degrees.
explanation_long: Since sin(theta) reaches its maximum value of 1 at theta=90 degrees, the magnetic force on a moving charge is greatest when its velocity is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
explanation_trick: At theta=0 or 180 degrees (velocity parallel or antiparallel to B), sin(theta)=0, meaning ZERO force — the extremes of alignment give no force, while perpendicular alignment gives maximum force, the opposite of many force-law intuitions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — sin(90 degrees)=1, giving maximum force.
explanation_options.b: At 0 degrees, sin(0)=0, giving zero (not maximum) force.
explanation_options.c: At 180 degrees, sin(180)=0 too, again giving zero force.
explanation_options.d: At 45 degrees, sin(45)≈0.707, less than the maximum at 90 degrees.

subject: Physics
question_text: A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field that circles around it, as described by:
explanation_short: A current-carrying wire's circling magnetic field is described by the right-hand rule (Ampere's law).
explanation_long: Point your right thumb in the direction of conventional current flow; your curled fingers show the direction the magnetic field circles around the wire — this is the right-hand rule, consistent with Ampere's law for the field around a straight current-carrying conductor.
explanation_trick: Faraday's law is about INDUCED emf from CHANGING flux — a different (though related) phenomenon from the static field a steady current produces, which is what's being asked here.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the right-hand rule (Ampere's law) describes this circling field.
explanation_options.b: Faraday's law concerns induced EMF from changing flux, not the static field around a current-carrying wire.
explanation_options.c: Coulomb's law concerns electrostatic force between charges, unrelated to magnetic fields from current.
explanation_options.d: Ohm's law relates V, I, and R in a circuit, unrelated to magnetic field geometry.

subject: Physics
question_text: A battery with EMF 12 V and internal resistance 1 ohm is connected to an external resistor of 5 ohm. What is the current in the circuit?
explanation_long: For a circuit with internal resistance, total resistance = external R plus internal r: I = EMF/(R+r) = 12/(5+1) = 12/6 = 2 A.
explanation_trick: Always include the battery's own internal resistance in the total resistance of the circuit — forgetting it (using just 12/5) is a very common mistake.

explanation_options.a: 2.4 A would come from omitting the internal resistance (12/5).
explanation_options.b: 12 A ignores resistance almost entirely.
explanation_options.c: 1.7 A doesn't match the correct division.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 12/(5+1) = 2 A.

subject: Physics
question_text: Kirchhoff's current law (junction rule) states that:
option_a: Voltage is conserved around any loop
option_b: The sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum of currents leaving it
option_c: Current is always the same in every branch of a circuit
option_d: Resistance in a circuit is always constant
explanation_short: Kirchhoff's current law: current entering a junction equals current leaving it.
explanation_long: KCL is a statement of charge conservation at a circuit junction (node): the total current flowing IN must equal the total current flowing OUT, since charge can't accumulate indefinitely at a point in steady-state circuit operation.
explanation_trick: KCL (junction rule, about CURRENT) vs. KVL (loop rule, about VOLTAGE around a closed loop) are the two fundamental circuit-analysis laws — don't mix up which one applies to junctions versus loops.

explanation_options.a: Voltage conservation around a loop describes Kirchhoff's VOLTAGE law (KVL), not the current law.
explanation_options.b: Correct — KCL: current in equals current out at a junction.
explanation_options.c: Current isn't necessarily the same in every branch — it can split differently among parallel branches, which is exactly why KCL (conservation at the junction) is needed.
explanation_options.d: Resistance being 'always constant' isn't what Kirchhoff's current law states at all.

subject: Physics
question_text: The terminal voltage of a battery connected in a circuit is generally _____ its EMF, due to internal resistance.
explanation_short: Terminal voltage is generally less than EMF, due to voltage drop across internal resistance.
explanation_long: A real battery has internal resistance r; when current flows, some voltage is 'lost' driving current through this internal resistance (V_drop = Ir), so the terminal voltage delivered to the external circuit is EMF minus this internal drop: V_terminal = EMF − Ir, which is less than the EMF.
explanation_trick: Only in the idealized case of zero current draw (open circuit) does terminal voltage equal EMF exactly — under any actual current flow, it's always somewhat less.

explanation_options.a: Equal to the EMF only holds in the idealized no-current (open-circuit) case, not general circuit operation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — terminal voltage is less than EMF due to the internal resistance drop.
explanation_options.c: Terminal voltage isn't greater than EMF in a normal (non-charging) circuit.
explanation_options.d: Terminal voltage is directly related to EMF (via internal resistance), not unrelated.

subject: Physics
question_text: A wire of resistance 8 ohm is stretched to twice its original length, with its volume kept constant. What is its new resistance?
explanation_short: Stretched to 2x length, volume constant: area halves, so R_new = R x (2)^2 = 8 x 4 = 32 ohm.
explanation_long: R = rho L/A. Doubling length (L'=2L) while keeping volume constant (A'L'=AL) means A'=A/2. So R' = rho(2L)/(A/2) = 4 x (rho L/A) = 4R = 4x8 = 32 ohm.
explanation_trick: Stretching a wire affects resistance TWICE over: length doubles (directly increasing R) AND cross-sectional area shrinks (also increasing R) — combined, that's a factor of 4, not just 2.

explanation_options.a: 16 ohm only accounts for the length-doubling effect, missing the area-halving contribution.
explanation_options.b: 4 ohm would be the result of the wire getting THICKER and shorter, the opposite scenario.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 8 x 4 = 32 ohm, accounting for both length and area changes.
explanation_options.d: 8 ohm is just the original resistance, unchanged — but stretching definitely changes it.

subject: Physics
question_text: The resistivity of a typical conducting metal, as temperature increases, generally:
explanation_short: Resistivity of typical metals increases as temperature increases.
explanation_long: As a metal's temperature rises, increased thermal vibration of its lattice atoms causes more frequent electron collisions, increasing resistivity (and thus resistance) — this is why metal resistors have a positive temperature coefficient of resistance.
explanation_trick: This is the OPPOSITE behavior of semiconductors, whose resistivity typically DECREASES with increasing temperature — a frequently tested contrast.

explanation_options.a: Decreasing resistivity with temperature is typical of semiconductors, not metals.
explanation_options.b: Resistivity does change measurably with temperature for real metals — it's not constant.
explanation_options.c: Resistivity doesn't drop to zero just from ordinary heating (that would require superconductivity at very low temperatures, the opposite direction).
explanation_options.d: Correct — metal resistivity generally increases with temperature.

subject: Physics
question_text: Materials that allow electric current to flow easily are called:
explanation_short: Materials that let current flow easily are called conductors.
explanation_long: Conductors (like metals) have loosely bound outer electrons that move freely, allowing electric current to flow easily; insulators strongly resist current flow; semiconductors fall in between.
explanation_trick: Conductors, insulators, and semiconductors form a spectrum of increasing resistivity — know where each sits relative to the others.

explanation_options.a: Correct — conductors allow current to flow easily.
explanation_options.b: Insulators strongly resist current flow, the opposite of what's described.
explanation_options.c: Semiconductors have intermediate (not 'easy') conductivity.
explanation_options.d: Superconductors (zero resistance) are a special extreme case, not the general category described here.

subject: Physics
question_text: A 60 W bulb operates at 120 V. What current does it draw?
explanation_long: Using P = VI, rearranged: I = P/V = 60W / 120V = 0.5 A.
explanation_trick: Direct division from the power formula — a simple half-unit result that's easy to sanity-check.

explanation_options.a: 2 A would come from inverting/misapplying the division.
explanation_options.b: 7200 A would come from multiplying P and V instead of dividing.
explanation_options.c: 60 A is just the power value itself, ignoring the voltage division.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 60/120 = 0.5 A.

subject: Physics
question_text: Electrical power dissipated in a resistor can be found using P = I^2 R. A current of 2 A flows through a 10 ohm resistor. What power is dissipated?
explanation_long: Using the given formula, P = I^2 R = (2A)^2 x 10 ohm = 4 x 10 = 40 W.
explanation_trick: Square the current first (2^2=4), then multiply by resistance — don't multiply I by R first and then square.

explanation_options.a: 5 W is far too small.
explanation_options.b: 20 W forgets to square the current (uses 2 instead of 4).
explanation_options.c: 200 W overshoots, perhaps multiplying by an extra factor.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 4 x 10 = 40 W.

subject: Physics
question_text: The diagram shows a circuit in which resistors R1 (5 ohm) and R2 (5 ohm) are connected in series, and this series combination is connected in parallel with R3 (10 ohm). What is the total resistance of the circuit?
explanation_short: R1+R2 (series) = 10 ohm, in parallel with R3 (10 ohm): total = (10x10)/(10+10) = 5 ohm.
explanation_long: First combine the series branch: R1+R2 = 5+5 = 10 ohm. This combined 10 ohm branch is then in parallel with R3=10 ohm: R_total = (10x10)/(10+10) = 100/20 = 5 ohm.
explanation_trick: Always simplify series sub-combinations first, then apply the parallel formula to the resulting simplified network — tackling it step by step avoids errors in multi-resistor circuits.

explanation_options.a: 10 ohm is just the series-branch value itself, before combining with R3 in parallel.
explanation_options.b: 20 ohm would come from simple addition, ignoring the parallel combination rule.
explanation_options.d: 2.5 ohm undershoots the correct parallel-combination result.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two resistors of 6 ohm and 3 ohm are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
explanation_short: Parallel resistors: R = (6x3)/(6+3) = 18/9 = 2 ohm.
explanation_long: For two resistors in parallel, R_total = (R1 x R2)/(R1+R2) = (6x3)/(6+3) = 18/9 = 2 ohm.
explanation_trick: For exactly two resistors in parallel, the 'product over sum' shortcut avoids dealing with the full reciprocal formula (1/R = 1/R1+1/R2).
