explanation_options.a: 9 ohm is the SERIES combination of these same resistors, not the parallel one.
explanation_options.b: Correct — (6x3)/(6+3) = 2 ohm.
explanation_options.c: 4.5 ohm doesn't match the product-over-sum calculation.
explanation_options.d: 18 ohm is just the product alone, without dividing by the sum.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two resistors of 6 ohm and 3 ohm are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
explanation_short: Series resistors add directly: 6+3 = 9 ohm.
explanation_long: For resistors in series, the total resistance is simply the sum of individual resistances: R_total = R1+R2 = 6+3 = 9 ohm.
explanation_trick: Series resistors ADD directly (unlike parallel, which requires reciprocal combination) — the simpler of the two combination rules.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 6+3 = 9 ohm in series.
explanation_options.b: 2 ohm looks like a parallel-combination-style result, not series.
explanation_options.c: 18 ohm would come from multiplying instead of adding.
explanation_options.d: 3 ohm is just one of the two resistor values alone.

subject: Physics
question_text: A circuit has a voltage of 12 V and a resistance of 4 ohm. What current flows through it?
explanation_long: By Ohm's law, I = V/R = 12V / 4 ohm = 3 A.
explanation_trick: Direct application of I=V/R — just don't accidentally compute V x R instead.

explanation_options.a: 48 A would come from multiplying V and R instead of dividing.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 12/4 = 3 A.
explanation_options.c: 0.33 A inverts the division (R/V instead of V/R).
explanation_options.d: 8 A doesn't match 12/4.

subject: Physics
question_text: Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and:
explanation_short: Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance (V=IR).
explanation_long: Ohm's law states V = IR, connecting the three fundamental circuit quantities: voltage (V), current (I), and resistance (R).
explanation_trick: Memorize the V=IR triangle — it lets you instantly rearrange to I=V/R or R=V/I depending on what's asked.

explanation_options.a: Power (P=VI) is a related but separate formula, not what Ohm's law itself directly relates.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Ohm's law: V, I, and Resistance.
explanation_options.c: Charge isn't the third quantity in Ohm's law (that's resistance).
explanation_options.d: Capacitance belongs to capacitor-specific formulas, not Ohm's law.

subject: Physics
question_text: Electric current is defined as the rate of flow of:
explanation_short: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge.
explanation_long: Current I is defined as I = dq/dt, the amount of charge passing a point per unit time — measured in Amperes (Coulombs per second).
explanation_trick: Current measures charge FLOW RATE, distinct from charge itself (Coulombs) or voltage/energy per charge (Volts).

explanation_options.a: Energy flow relates to power, not current specifically.
explanation_options.b: Correct — current is the rate of flow of electric charge.
explanation_options.c: Voltage is potential difference, not a flow rate.
explanation_options.d: Resistance opposes current flow but isn't itself a flow rate.

subject: Physics
question_text: Grounding a charged conductor:
option_b: Allows excess charge to flow to or from the Earth, neutralizing it
option_c: Has no effect on its charge
explanation_short: Grounding lets excess charge flow to/from Earth, neutralizing the conductor.
explanation_long: Connecting a charged conductor to the (effectively infinite, neutral) Earth via a conducting path allows excess charge to flow away (if positively charged) or flow in from the Earth (if negatively charged) until the conductor reaches a neutral (zero net charge) state.
explanation_trick: Earth is treated as an essentially infinite reservoir of charge at zero potential — grounding a conductor drives it toward neutrality, not toward some arbitrary nonzero charge.

explanation_options.a: Grounding doesn't increase a conductor's charge — it neutralizes excess charge.
explanation_options.b: Correct — grounding allows charge to flow to/from Earth, neutralizing the object.
explanation_options.c: Grounding definitely changes the conductor's net charge state (toward neutral), not 'no effect.'
explanation_options.d: Grounding doesn't alter the conductor's fundamental material properties (conductor vs insulator) at all.

subject: Physics
question_text: The electric field inside a charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is:
explanation_short: The electric field inside a charged conductor at electrostatic equilibrium is zero.
explanation_long: In electrostatic equilibrium, all excess charge on a conductor resides on its outer surface, and the electric field inside the conducting material itself is exactly zero — otherwise, charges would still be experiencing a net force and moving (not in equilibrium).
explanation_trick: This is why a conductor acts as an electrostatic shield (Faraday cage) — any external field is exactly canceled inside the conducting material by the induced surface charge distribution.

explanation_options.a: Maximum field would contradict the equilibrium condition (charges would still be accelerating).
explanation_options.b: Correct — the field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is zero.
explanation_options.c: The field inside isn't generally equal to the field outside — inside is zero, outside can be nonzero.
explanation_options.d: Infinite field values don't occur in this physical scenario.

subject: Physics
question_text: Three capacitors of 2 microF, 3 microF, and 6 microF are connected in parallel. What is their total capacitance?
explanation_short: Parallel capacitors add directly: 2+3+6 = 11 microF.
explanation_long: For capacitors in parallel, the equivalent (total) capacitance is simply the sum of the individual capacitances: C_total = C1+C2+C3 = 2+3+6 = 11 microF (unlike resistors, where parallel combination requires reciprocal addition).
explanation_trick: Capacitors in PARALLEL add directly (like resistors in SERIES), while capacitors in SERIES combine reciprocally (like resistors in parallel) — this is the 'opposite' behavior compared to resistors, a frequent point of confusion.

explanation_options.a: 1 microF doesn't match direct addition of these values.
explanation_options.b: 6 microF is just one of the three capacitor values, not their sum.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 2+3+6 = 11 microF for capacitors in parallel.
explanation_options.d: 0.9 microF looks like a (incorrect) reciprocal-sum-style calculation, which doesn't apply to parallel capacitors.

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of electric charge is the:
explanation_short: The SI unit of electric charge is the Coulomb.
explanation_long: Electric charge is measured in Coulombs (C) in the SI system — related to current (Amperes) via charge = current x time (1 Coulomb = 1 Ampere-second).
explanation_trick: Ampere measures the RATE of charge flow (current); Coulomb measures the charge itself — these are related but distinct units, a very commonly tested pair.

explanation_options.a: Volt measures potential difference, not charge.
explanation_options.b: Ampere measures current (rate of charge flow), not charge itself.
explanation_options.c: Farad measures capacitance, not charge.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Coulomb is the SI unit of electric charge.

subject: Physics
question_text: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor increases when:
explanation_short: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor increases when the plate area increases.
explanation_long: From C = epsilon x A / d, capacitance is directly proportional to plate area A and inversely proportional to plate separation d — so increasing area (or decreasing separation, or increasing the dielectric constant) increases capacitance.
explanation_trick: Three ways to increase capacitance: increase area, decrease separation, or increase dielectric constant — memorize all three, as exam questions often test each independently.

explanation_options.a: Increasing plate separation DECREASES capacitance (inverse relationship with d).
explanation_options.b: Correct — increasing plate area increases capacitance.
explanation_options.c: Decreasing plate area would decrease capacitance, the opposite effect.
explanation_options.d: Decreasing the dielectric constant would decrease capacitance, the opposite effect.

subject: Physics
question_text: A capacitor stores electrical energy by:
option_a: Accumulating and separating positive and negative charge on its plates
option_b: Converting electrical energy into heat permanently
explanation_short: A capacitor stores energy by accumulating and separating positive and negative charge on its plates.
explanation_long: A capacitor consists of two conductive plates separated by an insulator (dielectric); applying a voltage causes positive charge to build on one plate and negative on the other, storing energy in the resulting electric field between them.
explanation_trick: Unlike a resistor, a capacitor doesn't dissipate energy as heat during charging — it stores the energy, which can later be released back into a circuit.

explanation_options.a: Correct — a capacitor stores energy via separated charge on its plates.
explanation_options.b: Converting energy permanently to heat describes a resistor's dissipative behavior, not a capacitor's energy-storage function.
explanation_options.c: Generating a magnetic field is characteristic of current-carrying coils/inductors, not the basic charge-storage mechanism of a capacitor.
explanation_options.d: Kinetic energy storage isn't how a capacitor works — it's electrical potential energy stored in the electric field.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two identical conducting spheres carrying charges of +6 microC and -2 microC are brought into contact and then separated. What is the charge on each sphere afterward?
explanation_short: Total charge (+6+(-2)=+4 microC) splits equally between identical spheres: +2 microC each.
explanation_long: When identical conducting spheres touch, the total charge redistributes equally between them (since they're identical in size/shape): total = +6 + (-2) = +4 microC, split equally gives +2 microC on each sphere.
explanation_trick: Add the charges algebraically (respecting sign) BEFORE dividing by 2 — a common mistake is to add the magnitudes without accounting for the negative sign.

explanation_options.a: +4 microC each would double-count — that's the TOTAL charge, not each sphere's share.
explanation_options.b: Correct — (+6-2)/2 = +2 microC on each sphere.
explanation_options.c: +3 microC each doesn't match the correct total-charge division.
explanation_options.d: -2 microC each doesn't match the correct (positive net) result.

subject: Physics
question_text: Electric potential at a point is defined as:
option_b: Work done per unit charge in moving a test charge from infinity to that point
explanation_short: Electric potential = work done per unit charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point.
explanation_long: Electric potential V at a point is defined as the work done per unit positive charge to bring a small test charge from infinity (reference zero potential) to that point, against (or with) the electric field.
explanation_trick: Electric potential (V, work/charge) is different from electric field (E, force/charge) — related but distinct quantities, often confused since both involve 'per unit charge.'

explanation_options.a: Field per unit charge doesn't correctly describe potential (that phrase doesn't correspond to a standard definition).
explanation_options.b: Correct — potential is work per unit charge from infinity to that point.
explanation_options.c: Force per unit area describes pressure, unrelated to electric potential.
explanation_options.d: Charge per unit volume describes charge density, not potential.

subject: Physics
question_text: Electric field lines around a positive point charge point:
option_a: Away from the charge, radially outward
option_d: Randomly in all directions with no pattern
explanation_short: Electric field lines point away from (radially outward from) a positive point charge.
explanation_long: By convention, electric field lines originate from positive charges and terminate on negative charges — a positive point charge has field lines radiating symmetrically outward in all directions.
explanation_trick: Field line DIRECTION convention: away from positive, toward negative — remembering this convention (not the physics itself, which is a human choice) is key to correctly reading field diagrams.

explanation_options.a: Correct — field lines point radially outward from a positive charge.
explanation_options.b: Pointing toward the charge would describe the field around a NEGATIVE charge instead.
explanation_options.c: Circular field lines around a point charge would describe a magnetic field pattern around a current-carrying wire, not an electric field from a point charge.
explanation_options.d: Field lines from a point charge follow a definite radial pattern, not a random one.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two point charges of 2 x 10^-6 C and 3 x 10^-6 C are separated by 0.1 m in vacuum (k = 9 x 10^9 Nm^2/C^2). What is the force between them?
explanation_trick: Be careful with the powers of ten — multiplying 10^9 x 10^-6 x 10^-6 gives 10^-3, then dividing by 10^-2 (from r^2=0.01) gives a net 10^-1 factor relative to the simple digit product.

explanation_options.a: 0.54 N is off by a factor of 10 (a power-of-ten slip).
explanation_options.b: 54 N is off by a factor of 10 in the other direction.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 5.4 N as computed via Coulomb's law.
explanation_options.d: 0.054 N is off by a factor of 100.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to Coulomb's law, the electric force between two point charges is inversely proportional to:
option_c: The square of the distance between them
explanation_short: Coulomb's law: force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between charges.
explanation_long: Coulomb's law states F = kq1q2/r^2 — the force is directly proportional to the product of the charges, but inversely proportional to the SQUARE of the separation distance r.
explanation_trick: This inverse-square relationship means doubling the distance reduces the force to 1/4, not 1/2 — a frequently tested numerical consequence.

explanation_options.a: The product of charges is a DIRECT (not inverse) proportionality factor.
explanation_options.b: The sum of charges doesn't appear in Coulomb's law at all — it's the product that matters.
explanation_options.c: Correct — force is inversely proportional to r^2.
explanation_options.d: Medium temperature isn't a variable in the basic Coulomb's law formula (though the medium's permittivity, via k, can matter).

subject: Physics
question_text: Like electric charges:
explanation_short: Like electric charges repel each other.
explanation_long: Coulomb's law and basic electrostatics tell us that charges of the same sign (both positive or both negative) exert a repulsive force on each other, while opposite charges attract.
explanation_trick: Like repels, unlike attracts — a foundational rule that underlies essentially all of electrostatics.

explanation_options.a: Attraction occurs between UNLIKE (opposite-sign) charges, not like charges.
explanation_options.b: Like charges definitely interact — via repulsion, not indifference.
explanation_options.c: Correct — like charges repel.
explanation_options.d: Charges of the same sign don't cancel out (that would require opposite signs of equal magnitude in direct contact).

subject: Physics
question_text: How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 degrees Celsius (specific heat of water = 4200 J/kg degreeC)?
explanation_long: Using Q = mcΔT: Q = 2kg x 4200 J/(kg·°C) x 10°C = 84000 J.
explanation_trick: Multiply all three factors together (mass, specific heat, temperature change) — a common slip is forgetting one of the three factors.

explanation_options.a: 8400 J is off by a factor of 10.
explanation_options.b: 42000 J is exactly half the correct value.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 2 x 4200 x 10 = 84000 J.
explanation_options.d: 420000 J overshoots by a factor of 5.

subject: Physics
question_text: Specific heat capacity is defined as the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of:
option_a: Any mass of a substance by any temperature
option_c: A substance to its melting point
option_d: 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree Celsius
explanation_short: Specific heat capacity: heat needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree Celsius.
explanation_long: Specific heat capacity (c) is defined per unit mass and per degree of temperature change: the heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C (in SI units, J/(kg·°C)).
explanation_trick: Don't confuse specific heat capacity (per kg) with heat capacity (for a specific object's total mass, not normalized) — specific heat is an intrinsic material property.

explanation_options.a: This is too vague/general — specific heat is precisely defined per unit mass and per degree.
explanation_options.b: Water specifically (1g) would describe the historical calorie definition, not the general concept of specific heat capacity.
explanation_options.c: Raising to the melting point involves latent heat too, not just specific heat capacity for temperature change.
explanation_options.d: Correct — specific heat capacity is heat per kg per degree Celsius.

subject: Physics
question_text: An isochoric (isovolumetric) process occurs at constant:
explanation_short: An isochoric (isovolumetric) process occurs at constant volume.
explanation_long: 'Iso-choric' (or isovolumetric) means the volume of the system doesn't change during the process, even as pressure and/or temperature vary.
explanation_trick: Since no volume change occurs, no work (W=PdV) is done in an isochoric process — all heat added goes directly into changing internal energy.

explanation_options.a: Correct — isochoric means constant volume.
explanation_options.b: Constant pressure describes an isobaric process.
explanation_options.c: Constant temperature describes an isothermal process.
explanation_options.d: Constant entropy describes an isentropic process.

subject: Physics
question_text: An isobaric process occurs at constant:
explanation_short: An isobaric process occurs at constant pressure.
explanation_long: 'Iso-baric' literally means 'same pressure' — throughout an isobaric process, the pressure of the system remains fixed while volume and/or temperature may change.
explanation_trick: Iso-baric (pressure), iso-choric (volume), iso-thermal (temperature) — the Greek/Latin roots directly tell you which variable is held constant in each named process.

explanation_options.a: Correct — isobaric means constant pressure.
explanation_options.b: Constant volume describes an isochoric process, not isobaric.
explanation_options.c: Constant temperature describes an isothermal process, not isobaric.
explanation_options.d: Constant entropy describes an isentropic (adiabatic reversible) process, not isobaric.

subject: Physics
question_text: A heat engine operates between a hot reservoir at 500 K and a cold reservoir at 300 K. What is its maximum possible (Carnot) efficiency?
explanation_short: Carnot efficiency = 1 − Tc/Th = 1 − 300/500 = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4 = 40%.
explanation_long: The maximum theoretical (Carnot) efficiency between a hot reservoir at Th and cold reservoir at Tc (both in Kelvin) is: efficiency = 1 − Tc/Th = 1 − 300/500 = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4, or 40%.
explanation_trick: Always use absolute (Kelvin) temperatures in the Carnot efficiency formula — using Celsius values directly would give a wrong answer.

explanation_options.a: 20% undershoots the correct Carnot efficiency.
explanation_options.b: 60% is actually 1 minus the WRONG ratio (Th/Tc inverted somehow) — doesn't match the formula.
explanation_options.d: 80% overshoots significantly beyond the correct efficiency.

subject: Physics
question_text: The second law of thermodynamics implies that in any energy transfer, the entropy of an isolated system:
option_d: Always increases or stays the same
explanation_short: The second law: entropy of an isolated system always increases or stays the same.
explanation_long: The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of an isolated system can never decrease over time — it either increases (for irreversible, real processes) or stays constant (only in the idealized case of a fully reversible process).
explanation_trick: 'Increases or stays the same' (not 'always strictly increases') is the precise wording — a perfectly reversible process is the special limiting case where entropy doesn't increase.

explanation_options.a: Entropy of an isolated system never spontaneously decreases.
explanation_options.b: It doesn't remain 'exactly constant' in general — only in the idealized reversible-process limit.
explanation_options.c: Entropy doesn't become zero as a general rule from the second law.
explanation_options.d: Correct — entropy always increases or (in the reversible limit) stays the same.

subject: Physics
question_text: Convection primarily transfers heat through:
option_c: The bulk movement of a fluid
explanation_short: Convection transfers heat via the bulk movement of a fluid.
explanation_long: In convection, heated fluid (liquid or gas) physically moves — carrying its thermal energy with it — usually driven by density differences (warmer, less dense fluid rises; cooler, denser fluid sinks), creating convection currents.
explanation_trick: Convection specifically requires actual fluid MOVEMENT (mass transport), unlike conduction (energy transfer without bulk movement) or radiation (no medium at all).

explanation_options.a: Direct molecular contact in solids describes conduction, not convection.
explanation_options.b: Electromagnetic waves through a vacuum describes radiation, not convection.
explanation_options.c: Correct — bulk fluid movement defines convection.
explanation_options.d: Sound waves are a distinct (acoustic) phenomenon, not the convection heat-transfer mechanism.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which method of heat transfer occurs through direct particle-to-particle contact, especially in solids?
explanation_short: Conduction transfers heat via direct particle-to-particle contact, especially in solids.
explanation_long: Conduction occurs when energetic particles (or free electrons in metals) transfer kinetic energy to neighboring particles through direct collisions, without the particles themselves undergoing bulk movement — dominant in solids where particles are tightly packed.
explanation_trick: Conduction (solids, direct contact) vs. convection (fluids, bulk movement) vs. radiation (electromagnetic waves, no medium needed) — three distinct mechanisms, easy to mix up under time pressure.

explanation_options.a: Convection involves bulk fluid movement, not direct particle contact.
explanation_options.b: Radiation doesn't require particle-to-particle contact at all — it can travel through vacuum.
explanation_options.c: Evaporation is a phase-change process, not a heat-transfer mechanism per se.
explanation_options.d: Correct — conduction is direct particle-to-particle heat transfer, especially in solids.

subject: Physics
question_text: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 150 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
explanation_long: Applying the first law: ΔU = Q − W, where Q=500J (heat absorbed) and W=150J (work done BY the gas on surroundings): ΔU = 500 − 150 = 350 J.
explanation_trick: Since the gas does work ON its surroundings (expanding), that work is subtracted from the heat added — don't add them together.

explanation_options.a: 650 J adds instead of subtracting.
explanation_options.b: -350 J has the correct magnitude but wrong sign — the internal energy increases here since Q>W.
explanation_options.d: 150 J is just the work value alone, ignoring the heat added.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to the first law of thermodynamics, the change in internal energy of a system equals:
option_a: Heat added plus work done by the system
option_c: Heat added minus work done by the system
explanation_short: First law: change in internal energy = heat added minus work done BY the system.
explanation_long: The first law of thermodynamics (energy conservation) is stated as ΔU = Q − W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done BY the system on its surroundings.
explanation_trick: Sign convention matters: work done BY the system is subtracted (it leaves the system), while work done ON the system would be added — always check which convention a problem uses.

explanation_options.a: Heat plus work would apply if using the 'work done ON the system' sign convention instead — but paired with the given wording ('by the system'), it should be subtracted.
explanation_options.b: Only heat added ignores any work interaction entirely.
explanation_options.c: Correct — ΔU = Q − W(by system).
explanation_options.d: Only work done ignores the heat transfer entirely.

subject: Physics
question_text: The zeroth law of thermodynamics establishes the concept of:
explanation_short: The zeroth law of thermodynamics establishes the concept of temperature and thermal equilibrium.
explanation_long: The zeroth law states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other — this is the logical foundation that makes 'temperature' a well-defined, comparable property.
explanation_trick: It's called the 'zeroth' law because it was recognized as a foundational necessity AFTER the first and second laws were established, but logically needed to come first.

explanation_options.a: Energy conservation is the first law's territory.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the zeroth law establishes temperature/thermal equilibrium.
explanation_options.c: Entropy is central to the second law, not the zeroth.
explanation_options.d: Absolute zero relates to the third law of thermodynamics.

subject: Physics
question_text: Heat naturally flows from a body of:
option_b: Higher temperature to lower temperature, until thermal equilibrium is reached
option_d: Higher pressure to lower pressure only
explanation_short: Heat naturally flows from hot to cold, until thermal equilibrium is reached.
explanation_long: Heat spontaneously moves from a region of higher temperature to lower temperature until both reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium) — this direction is a consequence of the second law of thermodynamics.
explanation_trick: Heat never flows spontaneously from cold to hot without external work being done (that's what a refrigerator does, but it consumes energy to force this 'backward' flow).

explanation_options.a: Heat doesn't spontaneously flow from lower to higher temperature.
explanation_options.b: Correct — heat flows hot to cold until thermal equilibrium.
explanation_options.c: Equal temperatures don't drive any net heat flow at all.
explanation_options.d: Heat flow is driven by temperature difference, not pressure difference.

subject: Physics
question_text: Ultrasonic waves have frequencies that are:
option_a: Below the range of human hearing
option_b: Exactly equal to the human hearing range
option_d: Above the range of human hearing (above about 20,000 Hz)
explanation_short: Ultrasonic waves have frequencies above the human hearing range, roughly above 20,000 Hz.
explanation_long: Human hearing typically spans about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; frequencies above this upper limit are called ultrasonic (used in medical imaging, sonar, etc.), while frequencies below 20 Hz are called infrasonic.
explanation_trick: Don't mix up 'ultra' (above range, high frequency) with 'infra' (below range, low frequency) — a common terminology mix-up.

explanation_options.a: Below the hearing range describes infrasonic waves, not ultrasonic.
explanation_options.b: Ultrasonic is specifically OUTSIDE (above) the normal hearing range, not equal to it.
explanation_options.c: Ultrasonic waves are sound (mechanical) waves, unrelated to the visible light spectrum.
explanation_options.d: Correct — ultrasonic waves are above about 20,000 Hz, beyond human hearing.

subject: Physics
question_text: Standing waves are formed when:
option_a: Two identical waves travel in opposite directions and interfere
option_b: Two waves of the same frequency travel in the same direction
option_c: A single wave travels through a vacuum
option_d: Waves have different frequencies and cancel entirely
explanation_short: Standing waves form when two identical waves traveling in opposite directions interfere.
explanation_long: A standing wave arises from the superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude traveling in opposite directions (e.g., an incident wave and its reflection) — creating fixed nodes and antinodes rather than a wave that appears to travel.
explanation_trick: 'Opposite directions' is the key ingredient — two identical waves traveling in the SAME direction just combine into a single traveling wave of the same type, not a standing wave pattern.

explanation_options.a: Correct — two identical waves traveling in opposite directions create standing waves.
explanation_options.b: Waves traveling in the same direction combine into a traveling wave, not a standing one.
explanation_options.c: A single wave alone (with nothing to interfere with) can't create a standing-wave pattern.
explanation_options.d: Waves of different frequencies don't cancel 'entirely' in a simple, sustained way — they'd produce a complex, non-standing interference pattern (like beats, not stationary nodes).

subject: Physics
question_text: A stretched string fixed at both ends vibrates in its fundamental mode with a frequency of 100 Hz. What is the frequency of the second harmonic (first overtone)?
explanation_short: For a string fixed at both ends, harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental: 2nd harmonic = 2x100 = 200 Hz.
explanation_long: A string fixed at both ends supports standing waves at frequencies f_n = n x f1 (n=1,2,3,...), where f1 is the fundamental. The second harmonic (also called the first overtone for this boundary condition) is 2 x f1 = 2 x 100 = 200 Hz.
explanation_trick: For a string fixed at BOTH ends (unlike a pipe closed at one end), all integer harmonics exist — so 'second harmonic' and 'first overtone' refer to the same frequency here (2f1), unlike some pipe-resonance cases where only odd harmonics appear.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the second harmonic is 2 x 100 = 200 Hz.
explanation_options.b: 50 Hz would be a sub-harmonic (half the fundamental), which doesn't physically occur for a string fixed at both ends.
explanation_options.c: 100 Hz is just the fundamental (first harmonic) itself, not the second harmonic.
explanation_options.d: 300 Hz would be the third harmonic, not the second.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
explanation_short: Pitch of a sound is determined by its frequency.
explanation_long: Higher frequency sound waves are perceived as higher pitch, and lower frequency as lower pitch — this is the standard frequency-pitch relationship in acoustics.
explanation_trick: Pairing with the previous fact: amplitude->loudness, frequency->pitch — keep these two mappings straight, as questions often swap them as distractors.

explanation_options.a: Amplitude determines loudness, not pitch.
explanation_options.b: Speed of sound in a medium is generally constant for a given medium and doesn't determine an individual sound's pitch.
explanation_options.c: Phase describes timing offset between waves, not the pitch of a given sound.
explanation_options.d: Correct — frequency determines pitch.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which property of a sound wave determines its loudness?
explanation_short: Loudness of a sound is determined by its amplitude.
explanation_long: A sound wave's amplitude corresponds to the energy/intensity of the vibration — larger amplitude means a louder sound, while frequency determines pitch (not loudness).
explanation_trick: Amplitude -> loudness; frequency -> pitch. These are two independent properties of a sound wave, often tested as a pair of related-but-distinct questions.

explanation_options.a: Frequency determines pitch, not loudness.
explanation_options.b: Correct — amplitude determines loudness.
explanation_options.c: Wavelength is related to frequency (via speed), not directly to loudness.
explanation_options.d: Speed of sound in a medium doesn't determine how loud a particular sound is perceived.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two sound waves of slightly different frequencies produce a periodic variation in loudness called:
explanation_short: Two close but slightly different frequencies produce beats — periodic loudness variation.
explanation_long: When two sound waves of nearly equal frequency overlap, their interference alternates between constructive (loud) and destructive (quiet), producing a periodic 'beat' pattern in loudness, with beat frequency equal to the difference between the two source frequencies.
explanation_trick: Beat frequency = |f1 - f2| — this is different from resonance (matching a natural frequency) or the Doppler effect (relative-motion frequency shift).

explanation_options.a: Resonance involves matching a system's natural frequency, not two close source frequencies beating together.
explanation_options.b: The Doppler effect concerns relative motion, not the interference of two close stationary frequencies.
explanation_options.c: Correct — this periodic loudness variation from close frequencies is called beats.
explanation_options.d: The waves don't cancel entirely — they alternate between constructive and destructive interference, producing the beat pattern, not total cancellation.

subject: Physics
question_text: A car horn emits sound at 500 Hz. As the car approaches a stationary listener, the listener hears a frequency that is:
explanation_short: An approaching sound source causes a higher perceived frequency (Doppler effect, blue-shift analog).
explanation_long: As the car approaches, successive sound wave crests are emitted from progressively closer positions, effectively 'compressing' the wavelength and raising the perceived frequency above the source's true 500 Hz — this is the classic Doppler effect for an approaching source.
explanation_trick: Approaching = higher pitch; receding = lower pitch — remember this direction, as it's frequently tested with car horns, sirens, and train whistles.

explanation_options.a: Lower frequency would occur if the car were moving AWAY, not approaching.
explanation_options.b: Exactly 500 Hz would only apply if there were no relative motion at all.
explanation_options.c: Zero frequency doesn't occur just from relative motion at normal speeds.
explanation_options.d: Correct — an approaching source causes the listener to hear a higher frequency than emitted.

subject: Physics
question_text: The Doppler effect describes the apparent change in:
option_a: The frequency (and pitch) of a wave due to relative motion between source and observer
option_b: The amplitude of a wave due to relative motion
option_d: The wavelength of a stationary source only
explanation_short: The Doppler effect describes the apparent change in frequency (and pitch) due to relative motion between source and observer.
explanation_long: When a sound source and observer move relative to each other, the observed frequency shifts from the source's actual emitted frequency — higher when approaching, lower when receding — this is the Doppler effect, commonly experienced with passing sirens.
explanation_trick: The Doppler effect changes perceived FREQUENCY/pitch, not the wave's fundamental speed through the medium — the speed of sound in the medium stays the same regardless of source/observer motion.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the Doppler effect concerns apparent frequency/pitch shifts from relative motion.
explanation_options.b: Amplitude relates to loudness, not what the Doppler effect describes.
explanation_options.c: The speed of light isn't what the (classical, acoustic) Doppler effect for sound waves concerns.
explanation_options.d: The effect applies to relative motion generally, not exclusively 'a stationary source' scenario.

subject: Physics
question_text: The speed of sound is generally fastest in:
explanation_short: Sound travels fastest through solids (denser, more rigid medium with stronger intermolecular coupling).
explanation_long: Sound speed depends on the medium's stiffness and density; solids, with their tightly-bound and rigid molecular structure, transmit sound vibrations fastest, followed by liquids, then gases — sound cannot travel through vacuum at all.
explanation_trick: This ordering (solids > liquids > gases > vacuum-impossible) is the reverse of what people sometimes intuitively expect, since gases seem 'freer' to move — but it's the strength of intermolecular coupling, not freedom of motion, that determines transmission speed.

explanation_options.a: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum at all — it needs a medium.
explanation_options.b: Correct — solids transmit sound fastest.
explanation_options.c: Gases transmit sound more slowly than solids or liquids.
explanation_options.d: Liquids transmit sound faster than gases but slower than solids.

subject: Physics
question_text: A wave has a frequency of 25 Hz and travels at 100 m/s. What is its wavelength?
explanation_short: wavelength = speed/frequency = 100/25 = 4 m.
explanation_long: The wave equation v = f lambda rearranges to lambda = v/f = 100 m/s / 25 Hz = 4 m.
explanation_trick: Simple direct division from the wave equation — just keep straight which quantity is being divided by which.

explanation_options.a: 0.25 m inverts the division (f/v instead of v/f).
explanation_options.b: 2500 m multiplies instead of dividing.
explanation_options.c: 125 m adds instead of dividing.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 100/25 = 4 m.

subject: Physics
question_text: Sound waves are classified as:
explanation_short: Sound waves are longitudinal waves.
explanation_long: In a sound wave, particles of the medium oscillate parallel (back and forth along the direction of propagation), creating compressions and rarefactions — this defines a longitudinal wave, as opposed to a transverse wave (like light or a wave on a string) where particle motion is perpendicular to propagation.
explanation_trick: Sound = longitudinal (compression waves); light = transverse (electromagnetic) — a fundamental classification often tested directly.

explanation_options.a: Transverse waves have perpendicular particle motion, unlike sound.
explanation_options.b: Sound is a mechanical wave, not an electromagnetic one.
explanation_options.c: Correct — sound waves are longitudinal.
explanation_options.d: Sound waves aren't restricted to only 'standing wave' form — they can also be traveling waves.

subject: Physics
question_text: A wave that requires a medium in order to travel is called a:
explanation_short: A wave that requires a medium to travel is a mechanical wave.
explanation_long: Mechanical waves (like sound, water waves) need a physical medium (particles) to transmit their disturbance — unlike electromagnetic waves (light, radio), which can travel through a vacuum.
explanation_trick: This is exactly why sound can't travel through the vacuum of space, but light can — sound is mechanical, light is electromagnetic.

explanation_options.a: Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum, needing no medium.
explanation_options.b: Light waves are a type of electromagnetic wave and also need no medium.
explanation_options.c: Correct — mechanical waves require a medium to propagate.
explanation_options.d: Radio waves are electromagnetic and travel through vacuum just fine.

subject: Physics
question_text: Resonance occurs when a system is driven at a frequency that:
option_a: Is much lower than its natural frequency
option_b: Matches its natural frequency, causing a large increase in amplitude
option_c: Has no relation to its natural frequency
explanation_short: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches the system's natural frequency, causing a large amplitude increase.
explanation_long: When an external periodic force drives a system at (or very near) its natural oscillation frequency, energy is transferred very efficiently into the system each cycle, building up to a dramatically larger amplitude than at other driving frequencies — this is resonance.
explanation_trick: Resonance can be destructive in real structures (bridges, buildings) if an external driving frequency happens to coincide with a natural frequency — a classic real-world application of this concept.

explanation_options.a: A frequency much lower than natural frequency generally produces only a modest, non-resonant response.
explanation_options.b: Correct — resonance occurs when driving frequency matches natural frequency, greatly amplifying oscillation.
explanation_options.c: Resonance specifically depends on the RELATIONSHIP to natural frequency — it's not frequency-independent.
explanation_options.d: Resonance amplifies oscillations dramatically — the opposite of dampening them.

subject: Physics
question_text: Damped oscillations occur when:
option_a: No energy is lost from the system
option_b: Energy is gradually lost from the system, usually due to friction or resistance
option_d: The system oscillates forever without any loss
explanation_short: Damped oscillations occur when energy is gradually lost from the system (e.g., friction/resistance).
explanation_long: In a damped oscillator, resistive forces (friction, air resistance, etc.) continuously remove mechanical energy from the system, causing the amplitude to decrease over time until oscillation eventually stops.
explanation_trick: An UNDAMPED (ideal) oscillator would maintain constant amplitude forever — damping is specifically the energy-loss mechanism that makes real-world oscillations eventually die out.

explanation_options.a: No energy loss describes an idealized undamped oscillator, the opposite of damping.
explanation_options.b: Correct — damping involves gradual energy loss, typically from friction/resistance.
explanation_options.c: Amplitude increasing over time would describe a driven, resonant, or unstable system, not simple damping.
explanation_options.d: Oscillating forever without loss describes an ideal undamped system, not a damped one.

subject: Physics
question_text: A mass-spring system has spring constant k and mass m. If the mass is doubled while k stays the same, the period of oscillation will:
option_d: Increase by a factor of sqrt(2)
explanation_short: T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k); doubling m gives T_new = 2 pi sqrt(2m/k) = sqrt(2) x original T.
explanation_long: For a mass-spring system, T proportional to sqrt(m). Doubling the mass gives T_new = 2 pi sqrt(2m/k) = sqrt(2) x [2 pi sqrt(m/k)] = sqrt(2) x T — an increase by a factor of sqrt(2) (about 1.41x), not a full doubling.
explanation_trick: Just like the pendulum-length case, this square-root dependence means doubling the mass does NOT double the period — it only increases it by a factor of sqrt(2).

explanation_options.a: Doubling would be the result if T were directly (not square-root) proportional to m.
explanation_options.b: Staying the same would only happen if T were independent of mass, which it isn't for a mass-spring system.
explanation_options.c: Halved would be the opposite (decreasing) effect, which doesn't happen when mass increases.
explanation_options.d: Correct — T increases by a factor of sqrt(2) when mass doubles.

subject: Physics
question_text: In simple harmonic motion, the velocity of the oscillating object is maximum:
option_b: Halfway between the mean and extreme positions
explanation_short: In SHM, velocity is maximum at the equilibrium (mean) position.
explanation_long: As an SHM object passes through equilibrium, all its energy is kinetic (zero displacement means zero elastic/gravitational PE relative to equilibrium), so its speed — and hence velocity magnitude — is at a maximum there. At the extremes, velocity momentarily drops to zero as the object reverses direction.
explanation_trick: Velocity and displacement are exactly out of phase in SHM: max displacement (extremes) corresponds to ZERO velocity, and zero displacement (mean position) corresponds to MAXIMUM velocity.

explanation_options.a: At the extreme positions, velocity is actually zero (momentarily at rest before reversing).
explanation_options.b: Halfway between mean and extreme isn't where the maximum occurs — that's at the mean position itself.
explanation_options.c: Correct — velocity is maximum at the equilibrium (mean) position.
explanation_options.d: Velocity absolutely changes throughout the SHM cycle — it's far from constant.

subject: Physics
question_text: The frequency of oscillation is related to the period by:
explanation_short: Frequency and period are reciprocals: f = 1/T.
explanation_long: Frequency (oscillations per second) and period (seconds per oscillation) are inverses of each other by definition: f = 1/T, or equivalently T = 1/f.
explanation_trick: This reciprocal relationship is used constantly to convert between the two — memorize it as a instant-recall fact.

explanation_options.a: f = T would make them directly equal, which contradicts their inverse relationship.
explanation_options.b: f = 2T doesn't match the definitional reciprocal relationship.
explanation_options.c: Correct — f = 1/T is the defining reciprocal relationship.
explanation_options.d: f = T^2 doesn't match the simple reciprocal definition.

subject: Physics
question_text: The maximum displacement of an oscillating object from its equilibrium position is called its:
explanation_short: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium in an oscillation.
explanation_long: Amplitude specifically measures how far the object swings from its equilibrium (rest) position at its extremes — distinct from frequency (oscillations per second) or period (time per oscillation).
explanation_trick: Amplitude relates to the 'size' of the oscillation, while frequency/period relate to its 'speed' — these are independent properties (you can have a fast, small-amplitude oscillation or a slow, large-amplitude one).

explanation_options.a: Correct — amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium.
explanation_options.b: Frequency measures oscillations per second, not displacement magnitude.
explanation_options.c: Period measures time per oscillation, not displacement magnitude.
explanation_options.d: Phase describes the oscillation's position within its cycle at a given time, not the maximum displacement.

subject: Physics
question_text: If the length of a simple pendulum is quadrupled, its period will:
explanation_short: Since T is proportional to sqrt(L), quadrupling L doubles T (sqrt(4)=2).
explanation_long: From T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g), T is proportional to sqrt(L). If L becomes 4L, then T_new = 2 pi sqrt(4L/g) = 2 x [2 pi sqrt(L/g)] = 2T — the period doubles, not quadruples.
explanation_trick: Because of the square root, the period scales more slowly than the length — quadrupling length only doubles the period, a common source of exam confusion (people expect a 4x change).

explanation_options.a: Correct — sqrt(4)=2, so the period doubles.
explanation_options.b: Quadrupling the period would require the length to increase by a factor of 16 (since T proportional to sqrt(L)).
explanation_options.c: Halved would be the opposite effect, occurring if length were quartered instead.
explanation_options.d: The period definitely changes since it depends directly on length.

subject: Physics
question_text: A simple pendulum has a length of 1 m. Using T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) with g = 10 m/s^2, what is its approximate period?
explanation_long: Plugging L=1m, g=10 m/s^2 into T=2 pi sqrt(L/g): sqrt(1/10)=sqrt(0.1)≈0.316, so T≈2 pi(0.316)≈1.987s, which rounds to approximately 2 seconds.
explanation_trick: This is a commonly memorized 'nice' result: a 1-meter pendulum with g=10 has a period of almost exactly 2 seconds — useful as a quick sanity-check benchmark.

explanation_options.a: 1 s undershoots — that would need a much shorter pendulum.
explanation_options.b: 0.5 s is far too short for a 1m pendulum.
explanation_options.c: Correct — approximately 2 seconds.
explanation_options.d: 4 s would need a pendulum roughly 4x longer.

subject: Physics
question_text: The time period of a simple pendulum depends on:
option_c: Its length and the local acceleration due to gravity
explanation_short: A simple pendulum's period depends on its length and local g (T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g)).
explanation_long: From T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g), the period depends only on the pendulum's length L and the local gravitational acceleration g — notably NOT on the mass of the bob or (for small angles) the amplitude.
explanation_trick: Mass is a deliberate distractor here — a heavier or lighter pendulum bob of the same length swings with the exact same period, a frequently tested counter-intuitive fact.

explanation_options.a: Mass doesn't affect a simple pendulum's period at all.
explanation_options.b: Amplitude (for small-angle oscillations) doesn't significantly affect the period either.
explanation_options.c: Correct — period depends on length and local g.
explanation_options.d: Mass alone, without length or g, isn't the relevant dependency.

subject: Physics
question_text: Simple harmonic motion is characterized by a restoring force that is:
option_c: Directly proportional to displacement and directed opposite to it
option_d: Directed in the same direction as displacement
explanation_short: SHM's restoring force is directly proportional to displacement and directed opposite to it (F = -kx).
explanation_long: The defining condition for simple harmonic motion is a restoring force F = -kx: proportional in magnitude to the displacement from equilibrium, and always directed back toward equilibrium (hence the negative sign).
explanation_trick: Both parts of this definition matter: proportionality (not just 'some' restoring force) AND the opposing direction — a force that's merely 'restoring' but not proportional to x isn't SHM.

explanation_options.a: A constant-magnitude force regardless of displacement would not produce SHM's characteristic sinusoidal motion.
explanation_options.b: A restoring force independent of displacement doesn't match Hooke's-law-like SHM behavior.
explanation_options.c: Correct — proportional to displacement, opposite in direction, is exactly SHM's restoring force.
explanation_options.d: A force in the SAME direction as displacement would push the object further away, not restore it.

subject: Physics
question_text: Surface tension in a liquid arises due to:
option_c: Cohesive forces between liquid molecules at the surface, pulling them inward
option_d: Air pressure acting on the liquid surface
explanation_short: Surface tension arises from cohesive forces between liquid molecules at the surface.
explanation_long: Molecules at a liquid's surface experience a net inward pull from cohesive forces with neighboring molecules (since they lack neighbors above them), creating a 'skin-like' tension that minimizes surface area.
explanation_trick: Surface tension is about molecules attracting EACH OTHER (cohesion), not repelling — this inward pull is what lets small insects walk on water and makes water droplets round.

explanation_options.a: Repulsive forces would push molecules apart, not create a cohesive surface tension effect.
explanation_options.b: Gravity alone doesn't create surface tension — it's a molecular-level cohesive effect.
explanation_options.c: Correct — cohesive forces between surface molecules, pulling them inward, cause surface tension.
explanation_options.d: Air pressure isn't the origin of surface tension, though it can interact with surface effects in other contexts.

subject: Physics
question_text: The property of a fluid that describes its internal resistance to flow is called:
explanation_short: Viscosity is the fluid property describing internal resistance to flow.
explanation_long: Viscosity measures how much a fluid resists deformation/flow due to internal friction between its layers — honey has high viscosity, water has low viscosity, by comparison.
explanation_trick: Don't confuse viscosity (a flow-resistance property) with density (mass per volume) — a fluid can be dense but not very viscous (like mercury) or viscous but not very dense (like honey vs. water, similar densities but very different viscosities... actually honey IS denser, but the key point is these are independent properties).

explanation_options.a: Density is mass per unit volume, a separate property from flow resistance.
explanation_options.b: Correct — viscosity describes internal resistance to flow.
explanation_options.c: Pressure is force per unit area, unrelated to flow resistance directly.
explanation_options.d: Buoyancy is the upward force from fluid displacement, unrelated to internal flow resistance.

subject: Physics
question_text: An airplane wing generates lift mainly because:
option_a: Air moves slower over the top surface than the bottom
option_b: The wing has no interaction with the airflow
option_d: Air moves faster over the curved top surface, lowering pressure there relative to the bottom, per Bernoulli's principle
explanation_short: An airplane wing lifts because air moves faster over its curved top, lowering pressure there (Bernoulli's principle).
explanation_long: The wing's curved upper surface makes air travel faster over the top than underneath, and by Bernoulli's principle, faster-moving air has lower pressure — the higher pressure below the wing than above creates a net upward lift force.
explanation_trick: 'Air moves SLOWER over the top' is the exact reverse of the truth — a classic trap answer testing whether you have the Bernoulli direction right.

explanation_options.a: This reverses the actual airflow speed relationship — air moves FASTER over the top, not slower.
explanation_options.b: The wing very much interacts with the airflow — that interaction is the entire basis of lift.
explanation_options.c: Gravity pulls the wing down, not upward — it's the pressure difference that provides lift against gravity.
explanation_options.d: Correct — faster air over the curved top lowers pressure there, per Bernoulli's principle, generating lift.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to Bernoulli's principle, in a horizontal pipe, as fluid speed increases, its pressure:
explanation_short: Bernoulli's principle: faster fluid speed corresponds to lower pressure (in a horizontal pipe).
explanation_long: Bernoulli's equation relates pressure and speed along a streamline: as speed increases (at the same height), pressure must decrease to keep the total energy per unit volume constant.
explanation_trick: This is the same physics behind airplane lift and the Venturi effect — 'fast flow, low pressure' is a recurring theme across fluid-mechanics questions.

explanation_options.a: Increasing pressure with increasing speed would violate Bernoulli's equation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — pressure decreases as speed increases, per Bernoulli's principle.
explanation_options.c: Pressure can't stay constant if speed changes, per Bernoulli's equation (at constant height).
explanation_options.d: Pressure doesn't become negative in this context — it just decreases relative to the slower-flow value.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to the continuity equation, as a fluid flows through a narrowing section of pipe, its speed:
explanation_short: Continuity equation: fluid speeds up as the pipe narrows.
explanation_long: The continuity equation (A1v1 = A2v2, for incompressible flow) means that as cross-sectional area A decreases, velocity v must increase to keep the volume flow rate constant.
explanation_trick: This directly sets up Bernoulli's principle questions too — faster flow through a narrow section also means lower pressure there (Venturi effect).

explanation_options.a: Decreases would violate the continuity equation for a narrowing pipe.
explanation_options.b: Correct — speed increases as the pipe narrows (continuity equation).
explanation_options.c: Speed can't stay constant if the cross-sectional area changes, for an incompressible fluid.
explanation_options.d: Speed doesn't become zero just because a pipe narrows — flow rate is conserved, not stopped.

subject: Physics
question_text: An object floats when the buoyant force acting on it is:
explanation_short: An object floats when the buoyant force on it equals its weight.
explanation_long: Floating equilibrium requires the upward buoyant force to exactly balance the downward weight of the object — net force zero, so it neither sinks further nor rises out further.
explanation_trick: If buoyant force exceeds weight, the object would accelerate upward (rising until it displaces less fluid and the forces balance) — 'greater than' isn't a stable floating condition, it's a transient one heading toward equilibrium.

explanation_options.a: Less than weight would mean the object sinks (net downward force).
explanation_options.b: Zero buoyant force would also mean the object sinks under its full weight.
explanation_options.c: Correct — floating equilibrium requires buoyant force = weight.
explanation_options.d: Greater than twice its weight would cause net upward acceleration, not steady floating.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to Archimedes' principle, the buoyant force on a submerged object equals:
option_a: The weight of the fluid displaced by the object
explanation_short: Archimedes' principle: buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.
explanation_long: An object submerged (fully or partially) in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces — this is Archimedes' principle, and it's independent of the object's own weight or density directly (those determine whether it floats or sinks, but the buoyant force formula itself only depends on displaced fluid weight).
explanation_trick: The buoyant force equals the displaced FLUID's weight, not the object's own weight — these are only equal for a floating object at equilibrium, not for a fully submerged sinking one.

explanation_options.a: Correct — buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced.
explanation_options.b: The object's own weight is a separate quantity — equal to buoyant force only when it's floating in equilibrium.
explanation_options.c: Fluid density alone (without volume) doesn't give a force.
explanation_options.d: Buoyant force is not zero for a submerged object — that would contradict Archimedes' principle itself.

subject: Physics
question_text: A hydraulic lift has a small piston of area 0.01 m^2 and a large piston of area 0.5 m^2. If a force of 100 N is applied to the small piston, what force is exerted by the large piston?
explanation_long: By Pascal's principle, pressure is the same throughout: F1/A1 = F2/A2, so F2 = F1 x (A2/A1) = 100 x (0.5/0.01) = 100 x 50 = 5000 N.
explanation_trick: The mechanical advantage of a hydraulic lift is exactly the ratio of the piston areas — a 50x area ratio gives a 50x force multiplication.

explanation_options.a: 2 N would come from inverting the area ratio.
explanation_options.b: 500 N undershoots by a factor of 10.
explanation_options.c: 50 N is far too small.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 100 x 50 = 5000 N.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to Pascal's principle, pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is:
option_a: Absorbed entirely at the point of application
option_b: Transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid in all directions
option_c: Lost as it moves through the fluid
explanation_short: Pascal's principle: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid.
explanation_long: Pascal's principle underlies hydraulic systems: pressure applied at any point in a confined, incompressible fluid is transmitted equally to all other points in the fluid, in all directions — not absorbed, not lost, and not limited to just downward.
explanation_trick: This principle is the whole basis of hydraulic lifts/brakes: a small force on a small-area piston creates the same pressure that, on a large-area piston, yields a much larger force.

explanation_options.a: Pressure isn't absorbed at the application point — it's transmitted throughout the fluid.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Pascal's principle: pressure is transmitted undiminished in all directions.
explanation_options.c: Pressure isn't lost as it moves through an ideal enclosed fluid.
explanation_options.d: Pressure is transmitted in ALL directions, not just downward — this is the key insight.

subject: Physics
question_text: Pressure is defined as force per unit:
explanation_short: Pressure is defined as force per unit area.
explanation_long: Pressure = Force / Area, giving units of Pa (N/m^2). This is distinct from force per unit volume (a density-like quantity) or force per unit length.
explanation_trick: Pressure spreads a force over a surface — a small area under the same force gives much higher pressure (why knives are sharp and snowshoes are wide).

explanation_options.a: Force per unit volume isn't the definition of pressure.
explanation_options.b: Correct — pressure is force per unit area.
explanation_options.c: Force per unit length isn't the definition of pressure.
explanation_options.d: Force per unit mass isn't the definition of pressure.

subject: Physics
question_text: Centrifugal force, as experienced by an object in a rotating reference frame, is best described as:
option_a: A real force pushing objects outward
option_c: A force that only exists in space
option_d: A fictitious (pseudo) force that appears to act outward in a rotating frame
explanation_short: Centrifugal force is a fictitious (pseudo) force that appears to act outward in a rotating reference frame.
explanation_long: In a rotating (non-inertial) reference frame, objects appear to experience an outward-pushing 'centrifugal force,' but this isn't a real interaction force — it's an artifact of analyzing motion from within the rotating frame; from an inertial (external) viewpoint, only the real centripetal force (inward) is acting.
explanation_trick: Centrifugal 'force' is real in the sense that you feel it (e.g., in a spinning car), but it's not a fundamental force from any object acting on you — it's a consequence of choosing a rotating reference frame.

explanation_options.a: It's not a real force pushing outward — it's a frame-dependent (fictitious) effect.
explanation_options.b: It is NOT the same as centripetal force — centripetal is real and points inward; centrifugal is fictitious and appears to point outward.
explanation_options.c: It's not limited to space — it appears in any rotating frame (e.g., a spinning carousel on Earth).
explanation_options.d: Correct — centrifugal force is a fictitious/pseudo force in a rotating frame.

subject: Physics
question_text: An astronaut in a satellite orbiting Earth appears to be weightless mainly because:
option_a: There is no gravity in space at that altitude
option_b: The satellite blocks the effect of gravity
option_c: The astronaut and satellite are both in continuous free-fall around Earth
option_d: The astronaut has zero mass in orbit
explanation_short: Astronauts feel weightless because they and the spacecraft are both in continuous free-fall around Earth.
explanation_long: Gravity still acts on an orbiting astronaut (it's what keeps them in orbit!) — the sensation of weightlessness arises because the astronaut and their spacecraft are falling toward Earth at the same rate, so there's no relative force between the astronaut and the cabin (no normal force from a floor).
explanation_trick: Weightlessness in orbit is NOT because gravity has vanished — a very common misconception; gravity is still very much present and is exactly what curves their path into an orbit.

explanation_options.a: Gravity is definitely still present at orbital altitudes — it's what keeps the satellite in orbit at all.
explanation_options.b: The satellite doesn't block gravity's effect on objects inside it.
explanation_options.c: Correct — both are in continuous free-fall, producing apparent weightlessness.
explanation_options.d: Mass doesn't become zero in orbit — mass is unaffected by location.

subject: Physics
question_text: A wheel completes 5 revolutions in 2 seconds. What is its angular velocity?
explanation_short: omega = (2 pi x revolutions)/time = (2 pi x 5)/2 = 5 pi rad/s.
explanation_long: Each revolution corresponds to an angle of 2 pi radians. Angular velocity = total angle/time = (5 x 2 pi)/2 = 10 pi/2 = 5 pi rad/s.
explanation_trick: Convert 'revolutions' to radians (multiply by 2 pi) before dividing by time — a common mistake is dividing revolutions/time directly and forgetting the 2 pi conversion factor.

explanation_options.a: 10*pi rad/s forgets to divide by the time (2s).
explanation_options.b: 2.5*pi rad/s divides twice instead of once.
explanation_options.c: 15.7 rad/s is actually the correct NUMERIC value (5*pi ≈ 15.7) but expressed in decimal instead of the exact pi-form the question expects as 'the' answer alongside option D.
explanation_options.d: Correct — (2 pi x 5)/2 = 5 pi rad/s (numerically about 15.7 rad/s).

subject: Physics
question_text: Angular velocity is measured in units of:
explanation_short: Angular velocity is measured in radians per second.
explanation_long: Angular velocity (omega) describes how fast an angle is swept out per unit time, with SI units of radians/second — distinct from linear velocity (meters/second).
explanation_trick: Don't confuse angular velocity's unit (rad/s) with linear speed's unit (m/s) — they're related by v = omega x r but are dimensionally distinct.

explanation_options.a: Correct — radians per second is the unit of angular velocity.
explanation_options.b: Meters per second is the unit of linear velocity/speed.
explanation_options.c: Newtons is the unit of force, unrelated to angular velocity.
explanation_options.d: Meters is a unit of length, not angular velocity.

subject: Physics
question_text: A satellite orbits Earth with a period equal to Earth's rotational period (24 hours), staying above the same point on Earth's surface. This type of orbit is called:
explanation_short: An orbit matching Earth's rotation, staying above the same point, is a geostationary orbit.
explanation_long: A geostationary orbit has a period of exactly 24 hours and lies in the equatorial plane, so the satellite appears to stay fixed above one point on Earth's surface — widely used for communication/weather satellites.
explanation_trick: Geostationary is a SPECIAL CASE of geosynchronous orbit (same 24-hour period) that is also equatorial and circular, making the satellite appear perfectly stationary over one ground point.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this describes a geostationary orbit.
explanation_options.b: Low Earth orbit has a much shorter period (about 90 minutes), not 24 hours.
explanation_options.c: A polar orbit passes over the poles and doesn't stay above one equatorial point.
explanation_options.d: An elliptical orbit has a varying distance from Earth, not a fixed point above the surface in general.

subject: Physics
question_text: The minimum speed needed for an object to permanently escape a planet's gravitational field is called:
explanation_short: Escape velocity is the minimum speed to permanently leave a planet's gravitational field.
explanation_long: Escape velocity is the speed at which an object's kinetic energy exactly equals the (negative) gravitational potential energy binding it, allowing it to escape to infinity without further propulsion.
explanation_trick: Don't confuse escape velocity (leaving the gravity well entirely) with orbital velocity (the speed needed to stay in a stable orbit, which is lower).

explanation_options.a: Orbital velocity keeps an object IN orbit, not escaping it.
explanation_options.b: Terminal velocity is the constant speed reached falling through a fluid (like air), unrelated to escaping gravity.
explanation_options.c: Correct — escape velocity is this minimum permanent-escape speed.
explanation_options.d: Angular velocity measures rotational speed (rad/s), unrelated to escaping gravity.

subject: Physics
question_text: If a planet has the same mass as Earth but a radius half of Earth's, the acceleration due to gravity at its surface would be:
explanation_short: g is proportional to M/R^2; same mass, half the radius -> g becomes 4 times Earth's.
explanation_long: g = GM/R^2. With M unchanged and R halved: g_new = GM/(R/2)^2 = GM x 4/R^2 = 4g_Earth.
explanation_trick: Since R is squared in the denominator, halving R doesn't just double g — it quadruples it (1/(1/2)^2 = 4).

explanation_options.a: Half of Earth's would result from doubling (not halving) the radius.
explanation_options.b: Correct — halving R with same M gives 4x the surface gravity.
explanation_options.c: The same as Earth's would only hold if radius were unchanged.
explanation_options.d: Twice Earth's undershoots — the R^2 dependence means the effect is squared, not linear.

subject: Physics
question_text: The value of acceleration due to gravity (g) at the surface of the Earth is approximately:
explanation_short: g at Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 m/s^2.
explanation_long: This is a standard reference value used throughout mechanics problems (often rounded to 9.8 or 10 m/s^2 for calculation simplicity).
explanation_trick: MDCAT problems often use g=10 m/s^2 for easy arithmetic, but the more precise standard value (9.8 m/s^2) is what this conceptual question is asking for.

explanation_options.a: 5 m/s^2 is roughly half the actual value.
explanation_options.b: 15 m/s^2 overshoots significantly.
explanation_options.c: Correct — g is approximately 9.8 m/s^2.
explanation_options.d: 3.5 m/s^2 is far too small.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two satellites orbit Earth at radii R and 4R. What is the ratio of their orbital periods (period at 4R divided by period at R)?
explanation_short: T proportional to r^1.5 (from Kepler's third law), so ratio = (4)^1.5 = 8.
explanation_long: From T^2 proportional to r^3, T proportional to r^(3/2). For r2/r1 = 4, T2/T1 = 4^(3/2) = (4^1)x(4^0.5) = 4x2 = 8.
explanation_trick: Remember to apply the 3/2 power (not just square or cube) when relating period ratios to radius ratios via Kepler's third law.

explanation_options.a: 2 undershoots — that would be 4^0.5, missing the extra factor from T^2=r^3.
explanation_options.b: 4 undershoots — that's just the radius ratio itself, not the period ratio.
explanation_options.c: 16 overshoots — that would be 4^2, squaring instead of using the 3/2 power.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 4^1.5 = 8.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to Kepler's third law, the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to:
option_c: The square of its orbital speed
option_d: The cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit
explanation_short: Kepler's third law: T^2 is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis (a^3).
explanation_long: Kepler's third law states T^2 proportional to a^3, where a is the semi-major axis of the orbit (essentially the average orbital radius for near-circular orbits) — not the planet's mass, radius, or speed directly.
explanation_trick: It's easy to misremember this as involving the planet's own mass — but Kepler's third law (for objects orbiting the same central body) is independent of the orbiting planet's own mass.

explanation_options.a: The planet's own radius (size) isn't the relevant variable — it's the orbital radius/semi-major axis.
explanation_options.b: The orbiting planet's mass doesn't appear in Kepler's third law.
explanation_options.c: Orbital speed isn't the direct proportionality variable in Kepler's third law.
explanation_options.d: Correct — T^2 is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis (a^3).

subject: Physics
question_text: A car of mass 1000 kg moves in a circle of radius 50 m at a constant speed of 10 m/s. What is the centripetal force acting on it?
explanation_long: Centripetal force formula: Fc = mv^2/r = 1000kg x (10 m/s)^2 / 50m = 1000 x 100 / 50 = 2000 N.
explanation_trick: Square the speed before dividing by radius — v^2, not v, goes in the numerator.

explanation_options.b: 200 N is off by a factor of 10.
explanation_options.c: 20000 N overshoots by a factor of 10.
explanation_options.d: 100 N is far too small.

subject: Physics
question_text: Centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion is directed:
option_c: Toward the center of the circle
explanation_short: Centripetal acceleration points toward the center of the circle.
explanation_long: In uniform circular motion, the velocity direction constantly changes (even though speed is constant), and this change requires an acceleration directed toward the center — this is centripetal ('center-seeking') acceleration.
explanation_trick: Centripetal acceleration doesn't change the object's speed (it's always perpendicular to velocity) — it only changes direction, keeping the object on its circular path.

explanation_options.a: Tangent to the path would describe the velocity direction, not the acceleration.
explanation_options.b: Away from the center would be centrifugal, a pseudo-force effect in a rotating frame, not the real centripetal acceleration.
explanation_options.c: Correct — centripetal acceleration points toward the center.
explanation_options.d: Along the velocity direction would imply changing speed, not just direction.

subject: Physics
question_text: A crane lifts a 200 kg load to a height of 10 m in 20 seconds (g = 10 m/s^2). What power does it deliver?
explanation_long: Power delivered = work done / time = mgh/t = (200 x 10 x 10)/20 = 20000/20 = 1000 W.
explanation_trick: Compute the work (mgh) first, then divide by time — don't divide by time before multiplying all three factors of mgh.

explanation_options.a: 100 W undershoots by a factor of 10.
explanation_options.c: 2000 W overshoots by a factor of 2.
explanation_options.d: 20000 W is just the work value itself, forgetting to divide by time.

subject: Physics
question_text: A machine's mechanical efficiency is defined as the ratio of:
explanation_short: Mechanical efficiency = useful output energy / input energy.
explanation_long: Efficiency measures how much of the input energy is converted into useful output, expressed as a ratio (often as a percentage): efficiency = output/input, always less than or equal to 1 (100%) for real machines due to losses.
explanation_trick: Don't invert the ratio — 'output over input' (not input over output) is the standard definition, always giving a value <= 1.

explanation_options.a: Correct — efficiency = output (useful) energy / input energy.
explanation_options.b: Input/output would be an inverted (and typically >1) ratio, not the standard efficiency definition.
explanation_options.c: Power/time isn't the definition of mechanical efficiency.
explanation_options.d: Force/distance isn't the definition of mechanical efficiency.

subject: Physics
question_text: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes and comes to rest over a distance of 50 m. What is the average braking force?
explanation_short: Using work-energy theorem: F = KE/d = (0.5x1000x400)/50 = 200000/50 = 4000 N.
explanation_long: The braking force does work equal to the car's initial kinetic energy over the stopping distance: F x d = (1/2)mv^2, so F = (0.5 x 1000 x 20^2)/50 = 200000/50 = 4000 N.
explanation_trick: Use the work-energy theorem directly (KE lost = work done by friction/braking force) rather than trying to find acceleration and time separately — it's a faster route to force.

explanation_options.a: 2000 N undershoots, perhaps forgetting to square the velocity.
explanation_options.b: 8000 N overshoots by a factor of 2.
explanation_options.c: 400 N is off by a factor of 10.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is an example of a (nearly) elastic collision?
option_a: Two cars colliding and sticking together
option_b: A lump of clay hitting a wall and sticking
option_c: A bullet embedding itself in a wooden block
option_d: A ball bouncing back to nearly its original height off a rigid surface, with little energy loss
explanation_short: A ball bouncing back to nearly its original height (little energy loss) is (nearly) an elastic collision.
explanation_long: In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is conserved (or nearly so) — a ball bouncing back to nearly its starting height demonstrates minimal KE loss, unlike a perfectly inelastic collision where the objects stick together and lose the most KE.
explanation_trick: 'Sticking together' (cars colliding, clay hitting a wall, a bullet embedding) is always the signature of a perfectly INelastic collision — the opposite of what's being asked here.

explanation_options.a: Cars sticking together is a perfectly inelastic collision.
explanation_options.b: Clay sticking to a wall is also perfectly inelastic.
explanation_options.c: A bullet embedding in wood is likewise perfectly inelastic.
explanation_options.d: Correct — a ball bouncing back to nearly its original height is (nearly) elastic.

subject: Physics
question_text: A spring with spring constant 200 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m. What is the elastic potential energy stored?
explanation_short: Elastic PE = 1/2 k x^2 = 0.5 x 200 x 0.01 = 1 J.
explanation_long: Spring PE formula: PE = (1/2)kx^2 = 0.5 x 200 N/m x (0.1m)^2 = 0.5 x 200 x 0.01 = 1 J.
explanation_trick: Square the compression distance (0.1^2=0.01) before multiplying by k and 1/2 — skipping the square is the most common error here.

explanation_options.b: 2 J double-counts, perhaps forgetting the 1/2 factor.
explanation_options.c: 20 J forgets to square x=0.1 (uses 0.1 instead of 0.01).
explanation_options.d: 0.5 J undershoots the correct value.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to the law of conservation of energy, energy:
option_a: Can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed
option_b: Can be created but not destroyed
option_c: Can be destroyed but not created
explanation_short: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed (conservation of energy).
explanation_long: The law of conservation of energy states that total energy in an isolated system remains constant — energy changes form (e.g., PE to KE to heat) but the total amount is conserved.
explanation_trick: Energy 'lost as heat' during real processes isn't actually destroyed — it's converted to thermal energy, which is exactly why the law holds even in lossy real-world systems.

explanation_options.a: Correct — conservation of energy: neither created nor destroyed, only transformed.
explanation_options.b: Energy can't be created either — this option gets only half the law right.
explanation_options.c: Energy can't be destroyed either — this also gets only half right.
explanation_options.d: Energy isn't ALWAYS lost as heat — many processes conserve useful energy forms.

subject: Physics
question_text: A pendulum bob of mass 0.5 kg swings from a height of 0.2 m above its lowest point. What is its speed at the lowest point (g = 10 m/s^2, ignoring air resistance)?
explanation_short: Energy conservation: mgh = 1/2 mv^2, so v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2x10x0.2) = sqrt(4) = 2 m/s.
