explanation_long: All gravitational PE converts to KE at the lowest point (ignoring air resistance): mgh = (1/2)mv^2, so v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.2) = sqrt(4) = 2 m/s. Mass cancels out entirely.
explanation_trick: Mass cancels in this energy equation — you never actually need the pendulum's mass (0.5 kg) to solve it, a deliberate distractor detail.

explanation_options.a: 1 m/s undershoots — check the square root of 4 again.
explanation_options.b: 4 m/s overshoots — that would need h=0.8m instead of 0.2m.
explanation_options.c: Correct — sqrt(2x10x0.2) = sqrt(4) = 2 m/s.
explanation_options.d: 0.5 m/s is far too small for this height.

subject: Physics
question_text: How much work does a 500 W motor do in 20 seconds?
explanation_long: Since Power = Work/time, Work = Power x time = 500W x 20s = 10000 J.
explanation_trick: Straightforward rearrangement of P=W/t into W=Pt.

explanation_options.a: 25 J divides instead of multiplying.
explanation_options.b: 500 J is just the power value itself, ignoring time.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 500 x 20 = 10000 J.
explanation_options.d: 2500 J doesn't match 500x20.

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of power is the:
explanation_short: The SI unit of power is the Watt.
explanation_long: Power is the rate of doing work (Watts = Joules/second). Joule is the unit of work/energy itself, Newton of force, Pascal of pressure.
explanation_trick: Power and energy are easy to conflate — Joule measures 'how much work,' Watt measures 'how fast that work is done.'

explanation_options.a: Joule is the unit of work/energy, not power.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Watt is the SI unit of power.
explanation_options.c: Newton is the unit of force.
explanation_options.d: Pascal is the unit of pressure.

subject: Physics
question_text: A 2 kg object moving at 6 m/s has a kinetic energy of:
explanation_long: Kinetic energy formula: KE = (1/2)mv^2 = 0.5 x 2kg x (6 m/s)^2 = 0.5 x 2 x 36 = 36 J.
explanation_trick: Don't forget to square the velocity before multiplying — a common slip is using v instead of v^2.

explanation_options.a: 12 J undercounts, perhaps forgetting to square v.
explanation_options.b: 18 J is half of the correct value.
explanation_options.d: 6 J is far too small.

subject: Physics
question_text: A force of 20 N moves an object 5 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
explanation_long: Since the force and displacement are in the same direction, W = Fd = 20N x 5m = 100 J.
explanation_trick: Simple direct multiplication when force and displacement are aligned — no angle/cosine factor needed.

explanation_options.a: 4 J divides instead of multiplying.
explanation_options.b: 25 J doesn't match 20x5.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 20 x 5 = 100 J.
explanation_options.d: 0.25 J divides by the wrong factor entirely.

subject: Physics
question_text: Work done by a force is defined as:
option_b: Force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force
explanation_short: Work = force x displacement in the direction of the force.
explanation_long: Work done by a constant force is W = F d cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the force and displacement — this reduces to force times displacement 'in the direction of the force' when they are aligned.
explanation_trick: If the force is perpendicular to the displacement (theta=90 degrees), zero work is done, even though a force is acting — a classic exam trap.

explanation_options.a: Force times time is impulse, not work.
explanation_options.b: Correct — work is force times displacement in the force's direction.
explanation_options.c: Mass times acceleration is Newton's second law (force), not work.
explanation_options.d: Force times velocity is power, not work.

subject: Physics
question_text: The centripetal force acting on a car turning a corner on a flat road is provided by:
option_c: Friction between the tires and the road
explanation_short: Centripetal force for a car cornering on a flat road comes from friction between tires and road.
explanation_long: On a flat (unbanked) road, the only horizontal force available to provide the necessary centripetal force for turning is static friction between the tires and the road surface — without enough friction (e.g., on ice), the car can't make the turn and skids outward.
explanation_trick: This is why icy or wet roads make turning dangerous — reduced friction directly reduces the maximum centripetal force available, and thus the maximum safe turning speed.

explanation_options.a: Engine power relates to forward propulsion, not the sideways centripetal force needed to turn.
explanation_options.b: Air resistance opposes forward motion, not a useful centripetal source.
explanation_options.c: Correct — friction between tires and road supplies the centripetal force on a flat road.
explanation_options.d: Weight acts vertically and doesn't directly provide horizontal centripetal force on a flat road.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two objects of mass 3 kg and 2 kg are connected by a string over a frictionless pulley (an Atwood machine). What is the acceleration of the system (g = 10 m/s^2)?
explanation_short: Atwood machine acceleration: a = (m1−m2)g/(m1+m2) = (3−2)(10)/5 = 2 m/s².
explanation_long: For two masses connected over a frictionless pulley, the net driving force is the weight difference (m1−m2)g, while the total inertia resisting acceleration is (m1+m2). So a = (m1−m2)g/(m1+m2) = (1)(10)/5 = 2 m/s².
explanation_trick: The heavier mass accelerates downward and the lighter one upward, both with the SAME magnitude of acceleration — the string constrains them together.

explanation_options.a: 10 m/s² would be free-fall acceleration, ignoring the counterweight.
explanation_options.b: 5 m/s² doesn't match the Atwood-machine formula here.
explanation_options.d: 1 m/s² undershoots the correct value.

subject: Physics
question_text: A rocket expels gas backward to propel itself forward. This is best explained by:
option_b: Newton's third law and conservation of momentum
explanation_short: A rocket's forward propulsion follows from Newton's third law and momentum conservation.
explanation_long: The rocket expels exhaust gas backward (action); by Newton's third law, the gas exerts an equal and opposite force on the rocket, pushing it forward (reaction). This is consistent with overall momentum conservation of the rocket+exhaust system.
explanation_trick: A rocket doesn't need anything to 'push against' externally (like air) — the expelled gas itself provides the reaction force, which is why rockets work in the vacuum of space too.

explanation_options.a: Newton's first law (inertia) doesn't explain the active propulsion mechanism itself.
explanation_options.b: Correct — third law reaction force + momentum conservation explain rocket propulsion.
explanation_options.c: Gravitation isn't the mechanism behind thrust generation.
explanation_options.d: Archimedes' principle concerns buoyancy in fluids, unrelated to rocket propulsion.

subject: Physics
question_text: Weight is defined as:
option_a: The amount of matter in an object
option_b: A measure of an object's inertia
option_c: The same as mass in all cases
option_d: The gravitational force acting on an object's mass
explanation_short: Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object's mass.
explanation_long: Weight = mg, the force exerted by gravity on a given mass. It's distinct from mass itself (which measures the amount of matter, and stays constant regardless of location).
explanation_trick: Weight changes with local gravity (different on the Moon, for instance) while mass does not — a classic conceptual distinction tested repeatedly.

explanation_options.a: That describes mass, not weight.
explanation_options.b: Inertia relates to mass's resistance to acceleration, not weight specifically.
explanation_options.c: Weight and mass are NOT the same in general — weight varies with local gravitational field strength.
explanation_options.d: Correct — weight is the gravitational force on a mass (W=mg).

subject: Physics
question_text: The impulse experienced by an object equals:
explanation_short: Impulse equals the change in momentum of an object.
explanation_long: The impulse-momentum theorem states that impulse (force × time, or the area under a force-time graph) equals the resulting change in an object's momentum: J = Δp = m(v_f − v_i).
explanation_trick: Impulse and 'mass times velocity' are related but not the same statement — impulse is specifically the CHANGE in mv, not mv itself.

explanation_options.a: Mass times velocity alone is just momentum itself, not impulse specifically.
explanation_options.b: Weight times time isn't the general definition of impulse (only in specific free-fall-like cases).
explanation_options.c: Correct — impulse equals the change in momentum.
explanation_options.d: Kinetic energy is a separate quantity (½mv²), unrelated to impulse.

subject: Physics
question_text: A 6 kg block is pushed with a horizontal force of 30 N across a surface with a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.2 (g = 10 m/s^2). What is the block's acceleration?
explanation_short: Friction force = μmg = 0.2×6×10=12N; net force = 30−12=18N; a = 18/6 = 3 m/s².
explanation_long: Friction force: f = μN = μmg = 0.2×6×10 = 12N. Net force = applied − friction = 30−12 = 18N. Acceleration = F_net/m = 18/6 = 3 m/s².
explanation_trick: Compute the friction force from μmg first, then treat it exactly like any other opposing force subtracted from the applied force.

explanation_options.a: Correct — (30−12)/6 = 3 m/s².
explanation_options.b: 5 m/s² would come from ignoring friction (30/6).
explanation_options.c: 1 m/s² undershoots the correct net-force division.
explanation_options.d: 2 m/s² also doesn't match the correct calculation.

subject: Physics
question_text: A 5 kg block on a horizontal surface experiences a friction force of 10 N when a horizontal force of 25 N is applied. What is the block's acceleration?
explanation_short: Net force = 25−10 = 15N; a = F_net/m = 15/5 = 3 m/s².
explanation_long: The applied force (25N) is partially opposed by friction (10N), so the net force driving acceleration is 25−10=15N. Then a = F_net/m = 15/5 = 3 m/s².
explanation_trick: Always subtract opposing friction from the applied force BEFORE dividing by mass to get acceleration — using the raw applied force alone is a common mistake.

explanation_options.a: 5 m/s² comes from ignoring friction entirely (25/5).
explanation_options.b: Correct — (25−10)/5 = 3 m/s².
explanation_options.c: 2 m/s² doesn't match the net-force calculation here.
explanation_options.d: 7 m/s² overshoots what the net force actually gives.

subject: Physics
question_text: Friction that opposes the start of motion between two surfaces in contact is called:
explanation_short: Static friction opposes the start (initiation) of relative motion.
explanation_long: Static friction acts between two surfaces at rest relative to each other and prevents motion from starting, up to some maximum value; once motion begins, kinetic friction takes over.
explanation_trick: Static friction is generally the maximum type of friction, often exceeding kinetic friction for the same surfaces — that's why it's harder to START pushing a heavy object than to keep it moving.

explanation_options.a: Kinetic friction opposes ongoing (already-started) relative motion.
explanation_options.b: Rolling friction applies specifically to rolling objects, not general sliding onset.
explanation_options.c: Fluid friction (drag) applies to objects moving through fluids, not solid-surface contact.
explanation_options.d: Correct — static friction opposes the onset of motion.

subject: Physics
question_text: A 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s collides head-on with a stationary 4 kg ball and sticks to it. What is their common velocity immediately after the collision?
explanation_short: Perfectly inelastic collision: v = (2×6)/(2+4) = 12/6 = 2 m/s.
explanation_long: Using conservation of momentum for a perfectly inelastic collision (objects stick together): m1u1 + m2u2 = (m1+m2)v. Here, (2)(6) + (4)(0) = (2+4)v → 12 = 6v → v = 2 m/s.
explanation_trick: 'Sticks to it' is the signal phrase for a perfectly inelastic collision — combine masses on the right side of the momentum equation.

explanation_options.a: 1 m/s doesn't satisfy the momentum-conservation equation.
explanation_options.b: 3 m/s overshoots the correct combined-mass division.
explanation_options.c: 4 m/s would require a much smaller combined mass.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 12/6 = 2 m/s.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to the law of conservation of momentum, in a closed system with no external forces, the total momentum:
explanation_short: In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum remains constant.
explanation_long: This is the law of conservation of momentum: as long as no net external force acts on a system, the total momentum of all its parts stays constant over time, even as momentum is exchanged internally (e.g., during collisions).
explanation_trick: 'Conserved' means constant, not necessarily zero — the total value just doesn't change over time.

explanation_options.a: Correct — total momentum remains constant (conserved).
explanation_options.b: Momentum doesn't spontaneously increase without external force.
explanation_options.c: It doesn't decrease either, absent external forces.
explanation_options.d: It doesn't need to become zero — it stays at whatever constant value it started with.

subject: Physics
question_text: The momentum of a 5 kg object moving at 4 m/s is:
explanation_short: Momentum = mv = 5×4 = 20 kg·m/s.
explanation_long: Momentum is simply mass times velocity: p = mv = 5kg × 4 m/s = 20 kg·m/s.
explanation_trick: Straightforward multiplication — just don't confuse momentum's formula (mv) with kinetic energy's (½mv²).

explanation_options.a: 1.25 kg·m/s would come from dividing instead of multiplying.
explanation_options.b: 9 kg·m/s doesn't match m×v for these values.
explanation_options.c: 0.8 kg·m/s also doesn't match m×v.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 5×4 = 20 kg·m/s.

subject: Physics
question_text: According to Newton's third law, when object A exerts a force on object B, object B:
option_b: Exerts an equal and opposite force on A
option_c: Exerts a smaller force back on A
explanation_short: Newton's third law: object B exerts an equal and opposite force back on A.
explanation_long: Newton's third law states that for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force. If A pushes on B, B simultaneously pushes back on A with the same magnitude but opposite direction.
explanation_trick: These two forces act on DIFFERENT objects (one on A, one on B) — they never cancel each other out for either object individually.

explanation_options.a: B doesn't necessarily remain stationary — it can still accelerate under the force from A.
explanation_options.b: Correct — by Newton's third law, B exerts an equal, opposite force on A.
explanation_options.c: The reaction force is exactly equal in magnitude, not smaller.
explanation_options.d: There's always a reaction force in a real interaction, per the third law.

subject: Physics
question_text: A net force of 15 N acts on a 3 kg object. What is its acceleration?
explanation_long: Newton's second law: F = ma, so a = F/m = 15N / 3kg = 5 m/s².
explanation_trick: Simple direct division from F=ma — just be careful not to invert it (m/F).

explanation_options.a: 45 m/s² would come from multiplying F and m instead of dividing.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 15/3 = 5 m/s².
explanation_options.c: 0.2 m/s² inverts the division (m/F instead of F/m).
explanation_options.d: 18 m/s² doesn't correspond to any simple combination of 15 and 3.

subject: Physics
question_text: Newton's first law is also known as the law of:
explanation_short: Newton's first law is the law of inertia.
explanation_long: Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force — this tendency to resist changes in motion is called inertia, giving the law its common name.
explanation_trick: Don't confuse it with the third law (action-reaction) or the second law (F=ma), which is about how force and acceleration relate quantitatively — the first law is purely qualitative.

explanation_options.a: Action and reaction describes the third law.
explanation_options.b: Conservation of momentum follows from Newton's laws but isn't the first law's name.
explanation_options.c: Gravitation is a separate law (universal gravitation), unrelated to inertia.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the first law is the law of inertia.

subject: Physics
question_text: A particle moves along a straight line with position x = 2t^2 - 3t + 1 (x in meters, t in seconds). What is its velocity at t = 2 s?
explanation_long: Differentiate the position function x=2t²−3t+1 with respect to time: v = dx/dt = 4t − 3. Substituting t=2: v = 8−3 = 5 m/s.
explanation_trick: Differentiate term-by-term (power rule): d/dt(2t²)=4t, d/dt(−3t)=−3, d/dt(1)=0 — the constant term always drops out for velocity.

explanation_options.a: Correct — v(2) = 4(2)−3 = 5 m/s.
explanation_options.b: 8 m/s would come from just using 4t without subtracting 3.
explanation_options.c: 4 m/s is only the 4t term at t=1, not t=2.
explanation_options.d: 1 m/s doesn't match the derivative evaluated at t=2.

subject: Physics
question_text: For an object moving with uniform velocity, its acceleration is:
explanation_short: Uniform velocity means zero acceleration.
explanation_long: 'Uniform velocity' means the velocity is constant — neither its magnitude nor direction changes — so by definition, the rate of change of velocity (acceleration) is zero.
explanation_trick: 'Uniform velocity' ≠ 'uniform acceleration.' The former means a=0; the latter means a is constant but can be nonzero.

explanation_options.a: Correct — uniform velocity implies zero acceleration.
explanation_options.b: Increasing acceleration would mean non-uniform (changing) velocity.
explanation_options.c: 'Constant but non-zero' acceleration describes uniformly accelerated motion, not uniform velocity.
explanation_options.d: Negative acceleration would mean the object is decelerating, contradicting uniform velocity.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two cars A and B start from the same point at the same time; A moves at a constant 20 m/s while B starts from rest with acceleration 4 m/s^2. After how many seconds will B catch up to A?
explanation_short: B catches up to A when 20t = ½(4)t² → t = 10 s.
explanation_long: Set A's distance equal to B's distance: 20t = ½(4)t² = 2t². Dividing both sides by t (t≠0): 20 = 2t, so t = 10 s.
explanation_trick: Always divide out the trivial t=0 solution (both start together) to find the meaningful catch-up time.

explanation_options.a: 5 s doesn't satisfy 20t=2t² (would need t=10).
explanation_options.b: 8 s is not a root of the equation.
explanation_options.c: Correct — solving 20t = 2t² gives t = 10 s.
explanation_options.d: 4 s is also not a root of the equation.

subject: Physics
question_text: A stone is dropped from a tower and takes 5 seconds to reach the ground (g = 10 m/s^2). What is the height of the tower?
explanation_short: Height of tower = ½gt² = ½×10×25 = 125 m.
explanation_long: Dropped from rest, so u=0: h = ut + ½gt² = 0 + ½(10)(5²) = ½×10×25 = 125 m.
explanation_trick: Same 'starts from rest, use ½at²' shortcut as other free-fall/uniform-acceleration problems — the ut term disappears.

explanation_options.b: 50 m forgets to square the time properly.
explanation_options.c: 25 m is way too small, missing the full multiplication.
explanation_options.d: 250 m double-counts, missing the ½ factor.

subject: Physics
question_text: The area under a velocity-time graph represents:
explanation_short: The area under a velocity-time graph gives the displacement.
explanation_long: Since velocity = displacement/time, integrating (i.e., finding the area under the curve) velocity over a time interval yields the net displacement covered.
explanation_trick: Area under v-t = displacement (can be signed/negative); area under a speed-time graph would instead give total distance.

explanation_options.a: Force isn't directly read off a v-t graph at all.
explanation_options.b: Acceleration is the SLOPE of a v-t graph, not the area.
explanation_options.c: Jerk (rate of change of acceleration) isn't represented by area either.
explanation_options.d: Correct — area under v-t graph = displacement.

subject: Physics
question_text: The slope of a velocity-time graph represents:
explanation_short: The slope (gradient) of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
explanation_long: Slope = Δv/Δt, which is exactly the definition of acceleration. This is analogous to how the slope of a position-time graph gives velocity.
explanation_trick: Slope of x-t graph → velocity; slope of v-t graph → acceleration; area under v-t graph → displacement. Keep this ladder straight.

explanation_options.a: Correct — slope of a v-t graph = acceleration.
explanation_options.b: Displacement is the AREA under a v-t graph, not its slope.
explanation_options.c: Speed is what's plotted on the y-axis itself, not the slope.
explanation_options.d: Distance relates to area, like displacement, not slope.

subject: Physics
question_text: A car travels at 20 m/s for 10 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s. What is the total distance traveled?
explanation_short: Total distance = (20×10) + (average speed × 5) = 200 + 50 = 250 m.
explanation_long: Phase 1: constant 20 m/s for 10s → 200 m. Phase 2: decelerating uniformly from 20 m/s to 0 in 5s → average speed = (20+0)/2 = 10 m/s, distance = 10×5 = 50 m. Total = 200+50 = 250 m.
explanation_trick: For uniform deceleration to rest, use the average-of-initial-and-final-velocity trick rather than needing the deceleration value itself.

explanation_options.a: 200 m only counts the first, constant-speed phase.
explanation_options.b: 150 m undercounts the deceleration-phase distance.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 200 m + 50 m = 250 m total.
explanation_options.d: 300 m overcounts, perhaps by not halving the average speed in phase 2.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
explanation_short: Velocity is a vector quantity (has direction); speed, distance, and time do not.
explanation_long: Velocity specifies both magnitude and direction, making it a vector. Speed is velocity's magnitude only (scalar); distance and time are also scalars.
explanation_trick: Time is never a vector in classical kinematics — a common trap answer, but it always describes only 'how much,' never 'which way.'

explanation_options.a: Correct — velocity is a vector.
explanation_options.b: Speed is the scalar magnitude of velocity.
explanation_options.c: Distance is a scalar (total path length).
explanation_options.d: Time is a scalar.

subject: Physics
question_text: A projectile is launched at 30 m/s at an angle of 30 degrees above the horizontal (g = 10 m/s^2). What is its maximum height?
explanation_short: Max height = u²sin²θ/(2g) = 900×0.25/20 = 11.25 m.
explanation_long: Only the vertical component of velocity (u sinθ = 30×sin30° = 15 m/s) matters for height. Using v²=u²-2gh at the top (v=0): h = (u sinθ)²/(2g) = 15²/20 = 225/20 = 11.25 m.
explanation_trick: Always resolve into vertical/horizontal components first for projectile problems — plugging the full speed into a vertical-motion formula (forgetting sinθ) is the classic mistake.

explanation_options.a: 15 m would result from using the full 30 m/s without resolving components correctly.
explanation_options.b: 22.5 m overestimates, possibly from a component-resolution slip.
explanation_options.c: 45 m greatly overestimates the height.
explanation_options.d: Correct — (15)²/20 = 11.25 m using the vertical component only.

subject: Physics
question_text: A ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s^2). How long does it take to return to its starting point?
explanation_short: Time to return to start when thrown up at 20 m/s: t = 2u/g = 2(20)/10 = 4 s.
explanation_long: For a vertically-thrown projectile returning to its launch height, total time of flight = 2u/g (time up equals time down by symmetry) = 2(20)/10 = 4 s.
explanation_trick: Don't just compute the time to reach the top (u/g = 2s) — the question asks for the full round trip, which is double that.

explanation_options.a: 2 s is only the time to reach the highest point, not the full round trip.
explanation_options.b: 1 s is far too short for either leg of the motion.
explanation_options.c: 10 s doesn't match u/g or 2u/g for these values.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 2u/g = 4 s for the complete up-and-down trip.

subject: Physics
question_text: An object starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s^2. How far does it travel in 5 seconds?
explanation_long: Starting from rest (u=0), use s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½(3)(5²) = ½×3×25 = 37.5 m.
explanation_trick: Since it starts from rest, the ut term vanishes entirely — just compute ½at².

explanation_options.a: 15 m forgets to square the time (uses 3×5 instead of 3×25/2).
explanation_options.b: 7.5 m is off by a factor of 5.
explanation_options.d: 75 m double-counts, missing the ½ factor.

subject: Physics
question_text: A car accelerates uniformly from 15 m/s to 35 m/s in 4 seconds. What is its acceleration?
explanation_long: Using the definition of average acceleration: a = (v_final − v_initial)/time = (35−15)/4 = 5 m/s².
explanation_trick: Simple subtraction-then-division — a very common exam setup, just don't swap initial and final velocities.

explanation_options.a: Correct — (35−15)/4 = 5 m/s².
explanation_options.b: 8.75 m/s² divides 35 by 4 without subtracting the initial velocity.
explanation_options.c: 20 m/s² is just the velocity change itself, forgetting to divide by time.
explanation_options.d: 4 m/s² doesn't match either the numerator or a sensible division here.

subject: Physics
question_text: Displacement is best defined as:
option_a: The shortest straight-line distance between initial and final position, with direction
explanation_short: Displacement is the straight-line distance (with direction) between start and end points.
explanation_long: Unlike distance (total path length, a scalar), displacement is a vector: it only cares about the net straight-line change in position, regardless of the path actually taken.
explanation_trick: An object can travel a large distance but have zero (or small) displacement if it ends up back near where it started — e.g., a full lap around a track.

explanation_options.a: Correct — displacement is the shortest path with direction, from start to end.
explanation_options.b: That describes distance, not displacement.
explanation_options.c: Speed×time gives distance under constant speed, not displacement directly.
explanation_options.d: Displacement is a vector, not purely a scalar.

subject: Physics
question_text: A car covers 40 km in 2 hours at constant speed. What is its speed?
explanation_short: Speed = distance/time = 40 km / 2 h = 20 km/h.
explanation_long: For constant speed, simply divide total distance by total time: 40/2 = 20 km/h.
explanation_trick: Straightforward unit-rate division — watch that the units (km, h) are already consistent, no conversion needed.

explanation_options.a: 10 km/h would come from dividing by 4 instead of 2.
explanation_options.b: 80 km/h would come from multiplying instead of dividing.
explanation_options.c: 5 km/h divides by 8, not 2.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 40 km ÷ 2 h = 20 km/h.

subject: Physics
question_text: The component of a force of 10 N along a direction making a 60-degree angle with the force is:
explanation_short: Component of a 10N force along a direction 60° from itself: 10cos60° = 5N.
explanation_long: The component of a vector along a given direction is found by multiplying its magnitude by the cosine of the angle between them: F_component = F cosθ = 10 × cos(60°) = 10 × 0.5 = 5 N.
explanation_trick: cos(60°) = 0.5 exactly — a value worth memorizing for quick component calculations.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 10cos(60°) = 5 N.
explanation_options.b: 10 N would be the full force, only correct if the angle were 0°.
explanation_options.c: 8.66 N = 10cos(30°), using the wrong angle.
explanation_options.d: 0 N would apply only if the angle were 90°.

subject: Physics
question_text: The diagram shows a vector A drawn on a coordinate grid, with its components labeled Ax = 6 and Ay = 8 along the horizontal and vertical axes. Based on the diagram, what is the magnitude of vector A and its angle from the x-axis?
explanation_short: With Ax=6, Ay=8: magnitude = √(6²+8²) = 10, angle = tan⁻¹(8/6) = 53.1°.
explanation_long: This is another 3-4-5-style Pythagorean triple scaled by 2 (6-8-10). Magnitude = √(36+64) = √100 = 10. The angle from the x-axis is tan⁻¹(Ay/Ax) = tan⁻¹(8/6) = tan⁻¹(1.333) ≈ 53.1°.
explanation_trick: Recognize 6-8-10 as a scaled 3-4-5 triangle to skip the square-root arithmetic entirely.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 10 and 53.1° from the diagram's components.
explanation_options.b: 14 would come from simply adding the components (wrong — magnitude isn't a linear sum).
explanation_options.c: 36.9° is the complementary angle (measured from the y-axis instead of the x-axis).
explanation_options.d: 2 is far too small and doesn't match either component.

subject: Physics
question_text: Three concurrent forces of 3 N, 4 N, and 5 N act on a body such that it remains in equilibrium. These forces must:
option_b: All act in exactly the same direction
option_c: Form a closed triangle when added head-to-tail
option_d: Have no relationship to each other
explanation_short: Concurrent forces in equilibrium form a closed polygon (triangle, for 3 forces) when added head-to-tail.
explanation_long: If three concurrent forces keep a body in equilibrium, their vector sum must be zero. Adding them head-to-tail graphically, this means the vectors must close up into a triangle — this is the basis of the 'triangle law' / Lami's theorem approach to force equilibrium problems.
explanation_trick: 3-4-5 shows up again here (3N, 4N, 5N) — a right-triangle of forces is exactly what 'closes' when arranged head-to-tail for equilibrium.

explanation_options.a: Parallel forces of different magnitudes generally can't sum to zero unless arranged oppositely, not simply parallel.
explanation_options.b: Identical direction forces would only add up, never canceling to zero.
explanation_options.c: Correct — a closed triangle (head-to-tail) is the graphical condition for equilibrium of three concurrent forces.
explanation_options.d: They absolutely must satisfy a specific vector relationship (summing to zero) to produce equilibrium.

subject: Physics
question_text: A rigid body is in complete equilibrium when:
option_a: The net force and net torque acting on it are both zero
option_c: It is moving with increasing speed
option_d: Only the net force is zero, regardless of torque
explanation_short: Complete equilibrium requires BOTH net force and net torque to be zero.
explanation_long: A rigid body can have zero net force but still spin up under a nonzero net torque (translational equilibrium without rotational equilibrium), or vice versa. True 'complete' equilibrium needs both conditions satisfied simultaneously.
explanation_trick: Don't assume 'equilibrium' automatically means 'at rest' — a body can be in dynamic equilibrium (moving at constant velocity with no rotation) and still satisfy both conditions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — both net force and net torque must be zero.
explanation_options.b: A body in complete equilibrium need not be at rest — constant-velocity translation with no rotation also qualifies.
explanation_options.c: Increasing speed means a nonzero net force, contradicting equilibrium.
explanation_options.d: Ignoring torque can leave a body accelerating rotationally even with zero net force.

subject: Physics
question_text: The cross product of two parallel vectors is:
explanation_short: The cross product of two parallel vectors is zero.
explanation_long: A×B has magnitude |A||B|sinθ. For parallel vectors, θ=0°, so sinθ=0, making the cross product the zero vector.
explanation_trick: This is the mirror-image rule to the dot-product one: cross product zero ↔ parallel/anti-parallel; dot product zero ↔ perpendicular.

explanation_options.a: Cross product is maximum at 90° (perpendicular vectors), not for parallel ones.
explanation_options.b: Cross product (a vector) isn't generally equal to dot product (a scalar) in any case.
explanation_options.c: Cross product is well-defined (zero) here, not undefined.
explanation_options.d: Correct — parallel vectors give zero cross product (sin 0° = 0).

subject: Physics
question_text: The dot product of two non-zero vectors A and B is zero. This means the vectors are:
explanation_short: Zero dot product between two non-zero vectors means they are perpendicular.
explanation_long: A·B = |A||B|cosθ. If A·B = 0 and neither vector is zero, then cosθ = 0, so θ = 90° — the vectors are perpendicular.
explanation_trick: Dot product zero → perpendicular; cross product zero → parallel (or anti-parallel). Don't mix up which product signals which relationship.

explanation_options.a: Parallel vectors give maximum (not zero) dot product.
explanation_options.b: Anti-parallel vectors give a maximum-magnitude negative dot product, not zero.
explanation_options.c: Equal magnitude alone says nothing about the angle between them.
explanation_options.d: Correct — zero dot product means the vectors are perpendicular.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two forces of equal magnitude F act on a point at an angle of 120 degrees to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is:
explanation_short: Resultant of two equal forces F at 120° = F (not 2F or F/2).
explanation_long: Using R = √(F²+F²+2F²cos120°) = √(2F² + 2F²(-0.5)) = √(2F² - F²) = √(F²) = F. Two equal-magnitude vectors at 120° to each other always combine to a resultant equal in magnitude to either one.
explanation_trick: 120° between two equal vectors is a special, memorable case: the resultant equals each individual vector's magnitude — worth remembering as a shortcut.

explanation_options.a: 2F would be the result only if they were at 0° (same direction).
explanation_options.b: Correct — the resultant magnitude is F at 120° separation.
explanation_options.c: F/2 doesn't match the vector addition formula here.
explanation_options.d: 0 would only occur if the two forces were exactly opposite (180°) and equal.

subject: Physics
question_text: The resultant of two vectors of magnitude 3 N and 4 N acting at right angles to each other is:
explanation_short: Resultant of 3N and 4N at right angles = √(3²+4²) = 5N (Pythagorean triple).
explanation_long: For two perpendicular vectors, the resultant magnitude is found via the Pythagorean theorem: R = √(F1² + F2²) = √(9+16) = √25 = 5 N.
explanation_trick: 3-4-5 is the classic Pythagorean triple — recognizing it instantly saves calculation time on the exam.

explanation_options.a: 1 N would be the difference, not the resultant, of perpendicular vectors.
explanation_options.b: 7 N would be the simple (wrong) sum, ignoring the angle.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 5 N via √(3²+4²).
explanation_options.d: 12 N would be if you multiplied instead of combining vectorially.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
explanation_short: Speed is a scalar quantity (magnitude only, no direction).
explanation_long: Speed tells you 'how fast' but not 'which way,' making it a scalar. Velocity, displacement, and acceleration are all vectors because they specify direction as well as magnitude.
explanation_trick: Speed and velocity are often used interchangeably in casual language but are physically distinct: speed = |velocity|, with the direction stripped away.

explanation_options.a: Velocity is a vector (has direction).
explanation_options.b: Displacement is a vector (has direction).
explanation_options.c: Acceleration is a vector (has direction).
explanation_options.d: Correct — speed is a scalar, magnitude only.

subject: Physics
question_text: A vector quantity has:
explanation_short: A vector has both magnitude and direction.
explanation_long: By definition, vector quantities (displacement, velocity, force, etc.) carry both a magnitude (size) and a direction, unlike scalars which have magnitude only.
explanation_trick: Just having a numeric value isn't enough to be a vector — direction is the defining extra ingredient.

explanation_options.a: Magnitude alone describes a scalar.
explanation_options.b: Direction alone isn't a complete physical description either.
explanation_options.c: Correct — a vector needs both magnitude and direction.
explanation_options.d: Every physical vector has both; 'neither' describes nothing physical.

subject: Physics
question_text: The order of magnitude of Avogadro's number (6.022 x 10^23) is:
explanation_short: 6.022×10^23 has order of magnitude 10^23 in the conventional exam sense.
explanation_long: Order of magnitude is usually read directly off the exponent of a number written in scientific notation (a×10^n, with 1≤a<10) — for 6.022×10^23, that gives 10^23, which is the answer expected here. Note: some stricter textbook definitions round to the nearest power of ten based on whether the mantissa exceeds √10≈3.16 (which 6.022 does), which would technically round up to 10^24 — but the exam-standard convention (matching the exponent as written) is 10^23.
explanation_trick: This is a genuinely two-convention topic: 'order of magnitude = the exponent as printed' (10^23, the expected answer) versus 'order of magnitude = nearest power of ten by log-rounding' (10^24, since 6.022 > √10). Both are defensible; this bank uses the more common exam convention.

explanation_options.a: Correct under the standard exam convention (exponent as printed in 6.022×10^23).
explanation_options.b: 10^20 is off by three orders — too small.
explanation_options.c: 10^22 is off by one order — too small.
explanation_options.d: 10^24 would follow the stricter nearest-power-of-ten rounding convention, since 6.022 > √10 ≈ 3.16 — a defensible alternative reading, not chosen here.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is a derived unit?
explanation_short: Newton is a derived unit (kg·m/s^2), unlike the base units meter, kilogram, and second.
explanation_long: The Newton is defined in terms of the base units as 1 N = 1 kg·m/s^2, making it a derived unit. Meter, kilogram, and second are themselves three of the seven SI base units.
explanation_trick: If you can write the unit as a combination of base units with an exponent structure, it's derived — this applies to Newton, Joule, Watt, Pascal, Volt, Ohm, etc.

explanation_options.a: Meter is a base unit (length).
explanation_options.b: Correct — Newton (kg·m/s^2) is a derived unit.
explanation_options.c: Kilogram is a base unit (mass).
explanation_options.d: Second is a base unit (time).

subject: Physics
question_text: A physical quantity Q is calculated as Q = A^2 * B / C^3. If the percentage errors in A, B, and C are 2%, 3%, and 1% respectively, what is the approximate percentage error in Q?
explanation_short: For Q = A²B/C³, the % error is 2(%A) + %B + 3(%C) = 2(2)+3+3(1) = 10%.
explanation_long: When a quantity is a product/quotient of powers, the percentage errors of each factor are multiplied by their power and added: for Q=A^2 B^1 C^-3, %error(Q) = 2×%error(A) + 1×%error(B) + 3×%error(C) = 2(2%)+1(3%)+3(1%) = 4%+3%+3% = 10%.
explanation_trick: The exponent on each variable (even in the denominator) becomes a positive multiplying factor on that variable's percentage error — errors always add, never subtract, when combining via error propagation.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 10% is the properly weighted sum (4+3+3).
explanation_options.b: 6% misses a term or under-weights an exponent.
explanation_options.c: 8% is likewise an undercount.
explanation_options.d: 12% overcounts one of the contributions.

subject: Physics
question_text: A vernier caliper has 20 divisions on its vernier scale matching 19 main scale divisions of 1 mm each. What is its least count?
explanation_short: Least count = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = 1mm − 19/20 mm = 0.05 mm.
explanation_long: With 20 vernier divisions matching 19 main-scale divisions of 1 mm each, one vernier division = 19/20 = 0.95 mm. The least count is the difference between one main-scale division and one vernier division: 1 − 0.95 = 0.05 mm.
explanation_trick: Least count formula: LC = (value of 1 MSD) − (value of 1 VSD), and value of 1 VSD = (n MSD)/(n VSD) where here it's 19 MSD spread over 20 VSD.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 0.05 mm is the least count here.
explanation_options.b: 0.01 mm would need 100 VSD matching 99 MSD, not this setup.
explanation_options.c: 0.1 mm would come from a coarser 10-division vernier scale.
explanation_options.d: 1 mm is just the main-scale division itself, not the least count.

subject: Physics
question_text: The instrument used to measure very small lengths, such as the diameter of a thin wire, with high precision is the:
explanation_short: The screw gauge (micrometer screw gauge) measures very small lengths, like wire diameter, to high precision.
explanation_long: A screw gauge uses a finely-threaded screw mechanism to give a least count as small as 0.01 mm, far more precise than a meter rule (1 mm) or measuring tape. It's the standard instrument for measuring thicknesses/diameters of thin objects like wires or sheets.
explanation_trick: Don't mix it up with the vernier caliper — both are precision tools, but the screw gauge is specifically best for very small diameters/thicknesses; the vernier caliper is more general-purpose.

explanation_options.a: A meter rule has only mm-level precision, not fine enough for a thin wire.
explanation_options.b: A measuring tape is for long lengths, with even coarser precision than a rule.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the screw gauge gives the finest precision for very small lengths.
explanation_options.d: A protractor measures angles, not lengths.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which pair of physical quantities has the same dimensions?
explanation_short: Work and Torque have identical dimensions ([ML^2T^-2]).
explanation_long: Work = Force × distance = [MLT^-2][L] = [ML^2T^-2]. Torque = Force × perpendicular distance, which gives the exact same dimensional combination, [ML^2T^-2] — even though physically one is a scalar (work) and the other a vector-like quantity (torque), their dimensions coincide, which is why torque is sometimes (confusingly) expressed in joules in some contexts, though N·m is preferred to avoid conflating them.
explanation_trick: Same dimensions don't always mean 'the same physical quantity' — work and torque are dimensionally identical but conceptually distinct (torque isn't 'stored' as energy the way work is).

explanation_options.a: Work=[ML^2T^-2], Power=[ML^2T^-3] — different.
explanation_options.b: Force=[MLT^-2], Pressure=[ML^-1T^-2] — different.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Work and Torque are both [ML^2T^-2].
explanation_options.d: Momentum=[MLT^-1], Force=[MLT^-2] — different.

subject: Physics
question_text: The dimensional formula of force is:
explanation_short: Force has dimensional formula [MLT^-2].
explanation_long: Force = mass × acceleration = mass × (length/time^2), giving dimensions [M][L][T^-2]. This matches Newton's second law, F = ma.
explanation_trick: Remember acceleration itself is [LT^-2]; multiplying by mass [M] just prepends M to get [MLT^-2].

explanation_options.a: [MLT^-1] is the dimension of momentum, not force.
explanation_options.b: [ML^2T^-2] is the dimension of energy/work/torque.
explanation_options.c: [ML^-1T^-2] is the dimension of pressure.
explanation_options.d: Correct — [MLT^-2] is the dimensional formula of force.

subject: Physics
question_text: The number of significant figures in the measurement 0.00420 is:
explanation_short: 0.00420 has 3 significant figures: 4, 2, and 0.
explanation_long: Leading zeros (before the first nonzero digit) are never significant — they just locate the decimal point. In 0.00420, the leading zeros before '4' don't count, but the trailing zero after '42' IS significant because it appears after the decimal point, following nonzero digits. So the significant figures are 4, 2, 0 — three total.
explanation_trick: A trailing zero after the decimal point is always significant, even if it looks like it 'adds nothing' to the value.

explanation_options.a: 2 undercounts — it ignores the significant trailing zero.
explanation_options.b: 5 overcounts — it treats a leading zero as significant.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 3 is the sig-fig count: digits 4, 2, and the trailing 0 are all significant.
explanation_options.d: 6 overcounts even further.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is a fundamental (base) quantity?
explanation_short: Mass is a fundamental (base) SI quantity; the other three are derived.
explanation_long: The seven SI base quantities are length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity. Force (=mass×acceleration), velocity (=displacement/time), and energy (=force×distance) are all derived from these base quantities.
explanation_trick: If a quantity's unit can be written as a combination of other units (like N = kg·m/s^2), it's derived, not fundamental.

explanation_options.a: Force is derived (from mass, length, time).
explanation_options.b: Velocity is derived (length/time).
explanation_options.c: Energy is derived (force x distance).
explanation_options.d: Correct — mass is one of the seven fundamental SI quantities.

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of electric current is the:
explanation_short: The SI base unit of electric current is the Ampere.
explanation_long: Electric current, the rate of flow of charge, is one of the seven SI base quantities, and its base unit is the Ampere (A). Volt is the unit of potential difference, Ohm of resistance, and Coulomb of charge (not its rate of flow).
explanation_trick: Don't confuse the unit of current (Ampere) with the unit of the charge it carries (Coulomb) — current is charge per unit time.

explanation_options.a: Volt measures potential difference (energy per charge), not current.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the Ampere is the SI base unit of electric current.
explanation_options.c: Ohm measures resistance, not current.
explanation_options.d: Coulomb measures charge itself, not the rate of its flow.

subject: English
question_text: Her ___ smile suggested she knew something we did not.
explanation_short: 'Enigmatic' fits the context of a smile suggesting hidden knowledge, implying mysterious or puzzling.
explanation_long: The context clue 'suggested she knew something we did not' signals mystery, matching 'enigmatic'.
explanation_trick: Link the sense of hidden knowledge/mystery in the sentence to a word meaning puzzling, ruling out plain descriptive emotion words.

explanation_options.a: 'Plain' implies an ordinary, unremarkable smile, contradicting the sense of hidden mystery.
explanation_options.b: 'Sad' describes an emotion unrelated to the implied secrecy or mystery.
explanation_options.c: 'Confused' implies not understanding, the opposite of someone who knowingly holds a secret.
explanation_options.d: Correct - enigmatic matches a smile that mysteriously suggests hidden knowledge.

subject: English
question_text: The evidence against him was ___ ; he had no chance of acquittal.
explanation_short: 'Irrefutable' fits the context of no chance of acquittal, implying the evidence was undeniable and conclusive.
explanation_long: The context clue 'no chance of acquittal' signals overwhelming, undeniable evidence, matching 'irrefutable'.
explanation_trick: Connect the outcome (no chance of acquittal) to strong, undeniable evidence, ruling out words meaning weak or uncertain.

explanation_options.a: Correct - irrefutable matches evidence so strong it left no chance of acquittal.
explanation_options.b: 'Weak' evidence would likely allow a chance of acquittal, contradicting the context.
explanation_options.c: 'Doubtful' evidence implies uncertainty, inconsistent with no chance of acquittal.
explanation_options.d: 'Flimsy' evidence is weak and unconvincing, inconsistent with a certain conviction.

subject: English
question_text: The politician gave a ___ speech that inspired the crowd.
explanation_short: 'Rousing' fits the context of a speech that inspired the crowd, implying an energizing, stirring delivery.
explanation_long: The context clue 'inspired the crowd' signals an exciting, motivating speech, matching 'rousing'.
explanation_trick: Match the described effect on the audience (inspired) to a word meaning exciting/energizing, ruling out words meaning dull.

explanation_options.a: Correct - rousing matches a speech energetic and inspiring enough to move a crowd.
explanation_options.b: 'Dull' implies a boring speech, contradicting one that inspired the crowd.
explanation_options.c: 'Boring' likewise contradicts a speech that successfully inspired listeners.
explanation_options.d: 'Monotonous' implies a flat, unvarying tone, inconsistent with an inspiring speech.

subject: English
question_text: The judge gave a ___ verdict after considering all the evidence.
explanation_short: 'Fair' fits the context of a verdict reached after carefully considering all the evidence, implying justice and impartiality.
explanation_long: The context clue 'after considering all the evidence' signals a careful, just decision, matching 'fair'.
explanation_trick: Careful consideration of evidence logically leads to a just outcome, ruling out words implying haste or bias.

explanation_options.a: 'Hasty' implies a rushed decision, contradicting the careful consideration described.
explanation_options.b: 'Biased' implies unfairness, contradicting a verdict based on considering all evidence.
explanation_options.c: 'Careless' implies inattentiveness, contradicting the careful evidence review described.
explanation_options.d: Correct - fair matches a verdict reached through careful, impartial consideration of evidence.

subject: English
question_text: She was ___ of praise for her son's achievements.
explanation_short: 'Lavish' fits the context of giving abundant praise for her son's achievements.
explanation_long: The context clue 'praise for her son's achievements' suggests generous, abundant praise, matching 'lavish'.
explanation_trick: A parent praising a child's achievements logically implies generosity, not stinginess or scarcity of praise.

explanation_options.a: 'Sparse' implies very little praise, inconsistent with a proud parent's likely generous praise.
explanation_options.b: Correct - lavish matches giving abundant, generous praise.
explanation_options.c: 'Stingy' implies withholding praise, inconsistent with the positive context of achievements.
explanation_options.d: 'Lacking' implies an absence of praise, inconsistent with the positive context described.

subject: English
question_text: The old man walked with a ___ pace due to his weak legs.
explanation_short: 'Sluggish' fits the context of weak legs, implying a slow, labored pace.
explanation_long: The context clue 'weak legs' signals slow, difficult movement, matching 'sluggish'.
explanation_trick: Connect the cause (weak legs) to its logical effect (slow movement), ruling out words meaning fast or energetic.

explanation_options.a: 'Brisk' implies a fast, energetic pace, contradicting the description of weak legs.
explanation_options.b: Correct - sluggish matches a slow pace caused by weak legs.
explanation_options.c: 'Quick' implies fast movement, inconsistent with weak legs causing slowness.
explanation_options.d: 'Lively' implies energetic movement, inconsistent with the weakness described.

subject: English
question_text: His argument was so ___ that no one could refute it.
explanation_short: 'Compelling' fits the context of an argument no one could refute, implying it was persuasive and strong.
explanation_long: The context clue 'no one could refute it' signals a strong, convincing argument, matching 'compelling'.
explanation_trick: Link the described effect (no one could refute it) to a word meaning persuasive, ruling out words meaning weak or confused.

explanation_options.a: 'Weak' would make the argument easy to refute, contradicting the context.
explanation_options.b: Correct - compelling matches an argument so persuasive that no one could refute it.
explanation_options.c: 'Confused' implies a poorly structured argument, inconsistent with one no one could refute.
explanation_options.d: 'Silly' implies a foolish argument, inconsistent with one that could not be refuted.

subject: English
question_text: The scientist made a ___ discovery that changed the field.
explanation_short: 'Groundbreaking' fits the context of a discovery that changed the field, implying major innovation.
explanation_long: The context clue 'changed the field' signals a significant, pioneering discovery, matching 'groundbreaking'.
explanation_trick: Match the scale of impact described ('changed the field') to a word of equally large significance, ruling out words meaning minor or unimportant.

explanation_options.a: Correct - groundbreaking matches a discovery significant enough to change an entire field.
explanation_options.b: 'Trivial' means unimportant, contradicting a discovery that changed the field.
explanation_options.c: 'Minor' implies small significance, contradicting the described major impact.
explanation_options.d: 'Insignificant' means lacking importance, the opposite of a field-changing discovery.

subject: English
question_text: The desert is a ___ region with very little rainfall.
explanation_short: 'Arid' fits the context of very little rainfall, describing an extremely dry region like a desert.
explanation_long: The context clue 'very little rainfall' matches the meaning of 'arid', which describes extreme dryness.
explanation_trick: Use the rainfall clue directly - 'very little rainfall' can only logically pair with a dryness word like arid.

explanation_options.a: 'Humid' implies high moisture in the air, contradicting the description of very little rainfall.
explanation_options.b: 'Lush' implies abundant vegetation from plentiful water, contradicting a desert's dryness.
explanation_options.c: 'Fertile' implies land good for growing crops, inconsistent with a region of little rainfall.
explanation_options.d: Correct - arid precisely describes a region with very little rainfall, like a desert.

subject: English
question_text: She spoke in a ___ voice so as not to wake the baby.
explanation_short: 'Soft' fits the context of not wanting to wake a sleeping baby, implying a gentle, quiet voice.
explanation_long: The context clue 'so as not to wake the baby' requires a quiet, gentle tone, matching 'soft'.
explanation_trick: Always use the surrounding clause as a clue - here, avoiding waking someone signals quietness, ruling out loud/harsh options.

explanation_options.a: Correct - a soft voice matches the need to avoid waking the baby.
explanation_options.b: A loud voice would wake the baby, contradicting the context.
explanation_options.c: A sharp voice suggests harshness, inconsistent with the gentle context needed here.
explanation_options.d: A harsh voice is the opposite of the gentle tone implied by not wanting to wake the baby.

subject: English
question_text: SCALPEL : SURGEON :: WRENCH : ?
explanation_short: A scalpel is the tool of a surgeon, just as a wrench is the tool of a mechanic.
explanation_long: This analogy relates a specialized tool to the professional who characteristically uses it.
explanation_trick: Focus on which professional specifically and characteristically uses this tool, not the object the tool works on.

explanation_options.a: A nut is an object a wrench works on, not the professional who uses the wrench.
explanation_options.b: A garage is where a mechanic works, not the professional who uses the wrench.
explanation_options.c: 'Tool' is too general a category, not the specific professional who uses it.
explanation_options.d: Correct - a mechanic is the professional who characteristically uses a wrench, paralleling surgeon with scalpel.

subject: English
question_text: THIRST : DRINK :: FATIGUE : ?
explanation_short: Thirst is relieved by drinking, just as fatigue is relieved by resting.
explanation_long: This analogy relates a physical need or discomfort to its specific remedy or relief.
explanation_trick: Focus on the remedy/action that relieves the condition, not another description of the same feeling.

explanation_options.a: 'Work' would cause or worsen fatigue, not relieve it.
explanation_options.b: 'Tired' is simply another word describing fatigue itself, not its remedy.
explanation_options.c: Correct - rest is the remedy for fatigue, paralleling drink as the remedy for thirst.
explanation_options.d: 'Sleepy' describes a state related to fatigue, not the remedy/action that relieves it.

subject: English
question_text: AUTHOR : NOVEL :: COMPOSER : ?
explanation_short: An author creates a novel, just as a composer creates a symphony.
explanation_long: This analogy relates a creative professional to the type of major work they produce.
explanation_trick: Match the creator to their signature type of finished creative work, not the tools or performing group involved.

explanation_options.a: Correct - a symphony is a major musical work a composer creates, paralleling novel for an author.
explanation_options.b: An instrument is a tool used to perform music, not the composer's created work.
explanation_options.c: An orchestra performs the composer's music, but is not the work the composer creates.
explanation_options.d: A music note is a basic unit of notation, not the composer's overall created work.

subject: English
question_text: CAR : GARAGE :: AIRPLANE : ?

explanation_long: This analogy relates a vehicle to its specific storage location when not in use.

explanation_options.b: 'Sky' is where an airplane flies, not where it is stored/parked.
explanation_options.c: A runway is where an airplane takes off and lands, not where it is stored.
explanation_options.d: Correct - a hangar is the airplane's storage location, paralleling garage for a car.

subject: English
question_text: LIBRARY : BOOKS :: GALLERY : ?

explanation_options.b: 'Walls' are part of the gallery's structure, not what it displays.
explanation_options.c: Correct - paintings are what a gallery displays, paralleling books in a library.

subject: English
question_text: PUPPY : DOG :: KITTEN : ?

question_text: PEN : WRITE :: KNIFE : ?

question_text: HOT : COLD :: DAY : ?

question_text: DOCTOR : HOSPITAL :: TEACHER : ?

question_text: BIRD : FLY :: FISH : ?
