explanation_options.d: Correct — the period of a simple pendulum depends on its length L and the acceleration due to gravity g, as given by T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g).

subject: Physics
question_text: In SHM, the velocity is maximum at the:
explanation_short: In SHM, velocity is maximum at the mean (equilibrium) position, where the restoring force and displacement are both zero.
explanation_long: In simple harmonic motion, velocity and displacement are out of phase: v = omega*sqrt(A^2 - x^2), which is maximum when displacement x = 0 (the mean position), giving v_max = omega*A. Conversely, at the extreme positions (x = +/-A), the body momentarily stops (v = 0) before reversing direction, converting all kinetic energy into potential energy at that instant.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes mistakenly think velocity should be maximum at the extremes (thinking of it like a swing 'moving fastest' there) — but the extremes are actually where velocity is exactly ZERO (turning points); it's the mean/equilibrium position where speed peaks.

explanation_options.a: Correct — velocity is maximum at the mean position in SHM, since that's where all the energy is kinetic and displacement (hence restoring force) is zero.
explanation_options.b: 'Quarter position' is not a standard SHM turning/reference point; velocity's maximum occurs specifically at the mean position (zero displacement).
explanation_options.c: At the extreme position, velocity is actually zero (momentarily at rest before reversing direction), not maximum.
explanation_options.d: Velocity is definitely not constant in SHM — it varies continuously between zero (at extremes) and maximum (at the mean position).

subject: Physics
question_text: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration is:
option_a: Directly proportional to displacement and directed toward mean position
explanation_short: In SHM, acceleration a = -omega^2 x, meaning it is directly proportional to displacement x from the mean position and always directed opposite to (toward) the mean position — i.e., it's a restoring acceleration.
explanation_long: Simple harmonic motion is defined precisely by this acceleration-displacement relationship: a = -omega^2 x. The negative sign indicates the acceleration (and hence the net restoring force, F = -kx) always points back toward the equilibrium (mean) position, opposing the displacement. This restoring nature is what causes the oscillatory back-and-forth motion characteristic of SHM, such as a mass on a spring or a simple pendulum for small angles.
explanation_trick: A common mix-up is forgetting the negative sign's significance — acceleration is not just proportional to displacement, it must be directed OPPOSITE to (restoring toward) the mean position; if it pointed away (positive, unstable), the motion would not be oscillatory SHM at all.

explanation_options.a: Correct — in SHM, acceleration is directly proportional to displacement and always directed toward the mean (equilibrium) position (a = -omega^2 x).
explanation_options.b: If acceleration were directed AWAY from the mean position, the motion would be unstable and diverge, not oscillate — this is the opposite of the true restoring nature of SHM.
explanation_options.c: Acceleration in SHM is NOT constant; it continuously varies with displacement (maximum at extremes, zero at the mean position).
explanation_options.d: Acceleration is actually zero AT the mean position (where displacement is zero) and MAXIMUM at the extreme position, the reverse of this option's claim.

subject: Physics
question_text: The orbital velocity of a satellite close to Earth surface is approximately:
explanation_short: The orbital velocity for a satellite in a circular orbit close to Earth's surface is approximately 7.9-8 km/s, obtained from v_o = sqrt(gR).
explanation_long: For a satellite in a low circular orbit just above Earth's surface, the required centripetal force is provided entirely by gravity: mv_o^2/R = mg, which gives v_o = sqrt(gR). Using g ≈ 9.8 m/s^2 and R ≈ 6.4 x 10^6 m, this evaluates to v_o = sqrt(9.8 x 6.4x10^6) ≈ sqrt(6.27x10^7) ≈ 7.9 km/s, commonly rounded to approximately 8 km/s.
explanation_trick: A common confusion is mixing up orbital velocity (≈8 km/s, needed to STAY in a low orbit) with escape velocity (≈11.2 km/s = sqrt(2) x orbital velocity, needed to LEAVE Earth's gravity entirely) — these are related by exactly a factor of sqrt(2), and mixing them up is a very frequent MDCAT-style trap.

explanation_options.a: 11.2 km/s is Earth's escape velocity, not the orbital velocity near the surface (escape velocity is sqrt(2) times larger than orbital velocity).
explanation_options.b: 22 km/s is far too large; it doesn't correspond to any standard near-Earth orbital or escape speed.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the orbital velocity for a satellite close to Earth's surface is approximately 8 km/s.
explanation_options.d: 3 km/s is too low for a near-surface circular orbit around Earth; that value is closer to some higher, more distant satellite orbital speeds.

subject: Physics
question_text: The value of g at the center of Earth is:
explanation_short: At the exact center of the Earth, the gravitational field (and hence g) is zero, because the mass of the Earth surrounding that point pulls equally in all directions, canceling out.
explanation_long: Inside a uniform spherical shell of mass, the gravitational field at any interior point is exactly zero (a consequence of the shell theorem) — the pull from mass on one side is exactly balanced by the pull from mass on the opposite side. At the very center of the Earth, by symmetry, all the mass surrounding that point pulls equally from every direction, so the net gravitational force (and hence g) is exactly zero. In general, g decreases as you go from the surface toward the center of a uniform-density sphere, reaching zero exactly at the center.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes think g should be at its MAXIMUM at the center (since 'that's where all the mass is concentrated conceptually') — but the shell theorem shows the opposite: as you descend below the surface, only the mass INSIDE your current radius contributes net pull, and that contribution shrinks to zero as your radius shrinks to zero at the very center.

explanation_options.a: g is actually zero at the center, not the same as its surface value (9.8 m/s^2); g decreases continuously from the surface to the center.
explanation_options.b: g does not become infinite at the center; by the shell theorem, the pull from surrounding mass cancels out to give exactly zero, not an unbounded value.
explanation_options.c: Correct — g is zero at the exact center of the Earth, since the gravitational pull from all directions cancels out by symmetry.
explanation_options.d: g is actually at its minimum (zero), not its maximum, at the center of the Earth — the maximum g occurs at the surface (for a uniform-density model).

subject: Physics
question_text: The value of g on the surface of Earth is approximately:
explanation_short: The standard value of gravitational acceleration g at Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 m/s^2.
explanation_long: The acceleration due to gravity, g, at Earth's surface is derived from Newton's law of gravitation: g = GM/R^2, where M is Earth's mass and R is Earth's radius. Plugging in Earth's actual mass (~5.97 x 10^24 kg) and mean radius (~6.37 x 10^6 m) gives g ≈ 9.8 m/s^2, a standard constant used throughout mechanics problems (often rounded to 9.8 or approximated as 10 m/s^2 for quick calculations).
explanation_trick: Students sometimes misplace a decimal point when recalling this value (writing 0.98 or 98 instead of 9.8) — always double check the order of magnitude: g is meant to be 'about 10', not 'about 1' or 'about 100'.

explanation_options.a: This is off by a factor of 10 (too small); 0.98 m/s^2 would be an unrealistically weak surface gravity.
explanation_options.b: Correct — g ≈ 9.8 m/s^2 at Earth's surface.
explanation_options.c: This is off by a factor of 10 (too large); 98 m/s^2 would make objects fall dangerously fast even over short distances.
explanation_options.d: This has an incorrect unit (m/s, not m/s^2) and an incorrect magnitude — g must have units of acceleration.

subject: Physics
question_text: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that the gravitational force between two masses is:
option_a: Directly proportional to the square of the distance
option_b: Inversely proportional to the product of masses
option_c: Directly proportional to product of masses and inversely proportional to square of distance
explanation_short: Newton's law of gravitation: F = G(m1 m2)/r^2 — the force is directly proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
explanation_long: Newton's universal law of gravitation states that every point mass attracts every other point mass with a force F = G(m1 m2)/r^2, where G is the universal gravitational constant, m1 and m2 are the two masses, and r is the distance between their centers. This is an inverse-square law: doubling the distance reduces the force to one-quarter, while doubling either mass doubles the force.
explanation_trick: A common error is mixing up 'directly proportional' and 'inversely proportional' between the mass-product term and the distance-squared term — remember: gravity gets STRONGER with more mass (direct), but WEAKER with more distance (inverse square), not the other way around.

explanation_options.a: This states the distance dependence backward — gravitational force decreases (not increases) with the square of the distance.
explanation_options.b: This states the mass dependence backward — gravitational force increases (not decreases) with the product of the masses.
explanation_options.c: Correct — F = G(m1 m2)/r^2: directly proportional to the product of masses, inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
explanation_options.d: Gravitational force is strongly dependent on distance (inverse-square law), so it is not independent of distance.

subject: Physics
question_text: The banking of a road on a curve is done to:
option_a: Reduce the weight of the vehicle
option_c: Provide the necessary centripetal force without relying entirely on friction
explanation_short: Roads are banked (inclined) at curves so that a component of the normal force provides the necessary centripetal force, reducing dependence on friction alone for the vehicle to safely turn.
explanation_long: When a vehicle goes around a curve, it needs a centripetal force directed toward the center of the curve to keep it on the circular path. On a flat road, this force comes entirely from friction between tires and road, which can fail at high speed or in wet/icy conditions. By banking (tilting) the road surface at an angle, the normal force from the road (which is now no longer purely vertical) gains a horizontal component that contributes directly to the centripetal force, reducing or even eliminating the reliance on friction — this allows safer cornering at higher speeds, especially important for highways and racetracks.
explanation_trick: A common misconception is thinking banking is done to 'reduce weight' or purely 'increase friction' — banking's actual physics purpose is to redirect part of the normal (support) force horizontally so it directly contributes to the centripetal force requirement.

explanation_options.a: Banking does not physically reduce the weight (mg) of the vehicle; weight remains determined by mass and gravity regardless of road angle.
explanation_options.b: Banking is not primarily about increasing speed; it is about safely providing the centripetal force needed for the speed a vehicle is already traveling.
explanation_options.c: Correct — banking provides part of the required centripetal force via the tilted normal force, reducing the need to rely solely on friction.
explanation_options.d: Banking does not increase the friction coefficient of the road surface; it changes the geometry so a component of the normal force helps provide centripetal force instead of, or alongside, friction.

subject: Physics
question_text: A geostationary satellite has an orbital period of:
explanation_short: A geostationary satellite orbits with a period of exactly 24 hours, matching Earth's rotation period, so it appears stationary relative to a fixed point on Earth's surface.
explanation_long: For a satellite to remain 'geostationary' (appearing fixed above one location on Earth), its orbital period must exactly match Earth's rotational period of approximately 24 hours (one sidereal day, ≈23 hours 56 minutes, commonly approximated as 24 hours), and it must orbit in the equatorial plane in the same direction as Earth's rotation. This requires a specific orbital radius (about 42,164 km from Earth's center, or roughly 35,786 km altitude), determined by equating gravitational force to the required centripetal force for that period.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse geostationary orbits (period = 24 hours, fixed point above equator) with low Earth orbit satellites (period ≈ 90 minutes to a few hours, moving visibly across the sky) — only the specific 24-hour equatorial orbit gives a truly 'stationary' appearance from the ground.

explanation_options.a: 1 hour is far too short; that period would require an impossibly close orbital radius and does not match Earth's rotation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — a geostationary satellite has an orbital period of 24 hours, matching Earth's rotation so it stays above the same point.
explanation_options.c: 12 hours corresponds to certain specific orbits (like some GPS satellites) but is half of Earth's rotation period, not the geostationary period.
explanation_options.d: 48 hours is twice Earth's actual rotation period and does not correspond to a geostationary orbit.

subject: Physics
question_text: Angular momentum is defined as:
option_c: Moment of inertia times angular velocity
option_d: Moment of inertia divided by angular velocity
explanation_short: Angular momentum L is defined as the moment of inertia multiplied by angular velocity: L = I*omega — the rotational analog of linear momentum p = mv.
explanation_long: Just as linear momentum is mass times velocity (p = mv), angular momentum for a rotating rigid body is defined as moment of inertia times angular velocity: L = I*omega. This quantity is conserved in the absence of external torques, which explains phenomena like a figure skater spinning faster when pulling in their arms (reducing I, so omega must increase to keep L constant).
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse this with torque (which is the rotational analog of FORCE, tau = I*alpha, using angular acceleration), not angular momentum (which uses angular VELOCITY, not acceleration) — remember: torque is rotational force, angular momentum is rotational momentum.

explanation_options.a: Torque times angular velocity is not a standard defined quantity matching angular momentum's definition.
explanation_options.b: Force times radius gives torque (in a simple case), not angular momentum.
explanation_options.c: Correct — angular momentum L = I*omega, the rotational analog of linear momentum p = mv.
explanation_options.d: Dividing (rather than multiplying) moment of inertia by angular velocity does not match the correct definition of angular momentum.

subject: Physics
question_text: Moment of inertia depends on:
option_b: Only the mass of the body
option_c: Mass and the distribution of mass about the axis
explanation_short: Moment of inertia depends on both the mass of a body AND how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation (I = sum of m*r^2 for each mass element).
explanation_long: Moment of inertia is the rotational analog of mass (inertia) in linear motion, defined as I = integral of r^2 dm, summing each mass element multiplied by the square of its distance from the rotation axis. This means two objects with identical total mass can have very different moments of inertia depending on how that mass is arranged relative to the axis — mass concentrated far from the axis contributes much more to I than mass near the axis (due to the r^2 dependence), and I also depends on WHICH axis is chosen for the same object.
explanation_trick: Students often think moment of inertia is just 'the mass' of a rotating body — but unlike ordinary mass, it critically depends on the mass DISTRIBUTION (via r^2) and the CHOICE of axis, which is why the same object can have very different moment-of-inertia values about different axes.

explanation_options.a: The axis alone is not sufficient; moment of inertia also depends on the mass and how it's distributed, not just which axis is chosen.
explanation_options.b: Mass alone is not sufficient; two bodies of equal mass distributed differently relative to the axis will have different moments of inertia.
explanation_options.c: Correct — moment of inertia depends on both the total mass and the distribution of that mass relative to the chosen rotation axis.
explanation_options.d: Moment of inertia is a property of the mass distribution (geometry), independent of the current angular velocity of rotation.

subject: Physics
question_text: The relation between linear velocity v, radius r, and angular velocity omega is:
explanation_short: The relation between linear and angular velocity for circular motion is v = r*omega, linear speed equals radius times angular velocity.
explanation_long: For a point moving in a circle of radius r with angular velocity omega, its linear (tangential) speed is v = r*omega. This comes from differentiating arc length s = r*theta with respect to time: ds/dt = r*(d theta/dt), i.e., v = r*omega. This relation shows that points farther from the axis of rotation (larger r) move faster linearly for the same angular velocity — like the outer edge of a spinning disc moving faster than points near its center.
explanation_trick: A common mix-up is inverting the relation (writing v = omega/r or r = v*omega, dimensional nonsense) — always remember v has units of r (metres) times omega (per second), consistent with v = r*omega.

explanation_options.a: This inverts the correct relationship; dividing r by omega does not give the correct linear velocity formula.
explanation_options.b: Correct — v = r*omega, linear velocity equals radius times angular velocity.
explanation_options.c: This incorrectly squares omega, which does not match the correct linear formula (that relation appears in centripetal acceleration, a=omega^2 r, not velocity).
explanation_options.d: This is dimensionally inconsistent with the correct v = r*omega relationship (it divides instead of multiplying).

subject: Physics
question_text: The centripetal force required to move a 2 kg body in a circle of radius 1 m at 3 m/s is:
explanation_short: Centripetal force F = mv^2/r = (2 x 3^2)/1 = (2 x 9)/1 = 18 N.
explanation_long: The centripetal force needed to keep a body moving in a circle is F = mv^2/r, where m is mass, v is speed, and r is the radius of the circular path. Substituting m = 2 kg, v = 3 m/s, r = 1 m: F = (2 x 3^2)/1 = (2 x 9)/1 = 18 N.
explanation_trick: A common mistake is forgetting to square the velocity (using v instead of v^2), which would give an incorrect answer of 6 N instead of the correct 18 N — always remember the v^2 term in the centripetal force formula.

explanation_options.a: This would result from forgetting to square v (using 2x3/1=6), a common formula-substitution error.
explanation_options.b: This equals mv (2x3x... not matching a clean derivation) or possibly from doubling 6 incorrectly rather than properly computing mv^2/r.
explanation_options.c: This equals mv^2 without dividing by r (2x9=18 is actually correct; this value 9 might come from v^2 alone without multiplying by m), an incomplete calculation.
explanation_options.d: Correct — F = mv^2/r = (2)(9)/1 = 18 N.

subject: Physics
question_text: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal acceleration is directed:
explanation_short: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal acceleration always points radially inward, toward the center of the circular path.
explanation_long: Even though the speed is constant in uniform circular motion, the velocity's DIRECTION is continuously changing, and any change in velocity requires acceleration. This acceleration, called centripetal acceleration, has magnitude v^2/r and is always directed toward the center of the circle — perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity (which is tangential). This inward acceleration is what continuously 'bends' the straight-line path into a circle.
explanation_trick: A common misconception (especially among beginners) is thinking centrifugal 'outward' force/acceleration is real in the inertial (non-rotating) frame — in reality, the true acceleration in circular motion is centripetal (inward); the outward-feeling 'centrifugal force' is a pseudo-force that only appears in the rotating reference frame.

explanation_options.a: The tangential direction describes the direction of velocity in circular motion, not the direction of centripetal acceleration.
explanation_options.b: Acceleration cannot be along the velocity vector for constant-speed circular motion; if it were, speed would change, contradicting 'uniform' circular motion.
explanation_options.c: Correct — centripetal acceleration is always directed radially inward, toward the center of the circular path.
explanation_options.d: Radially outward describes the (fictitious, frame-dependent) centrifugal effect, not the true (inertial-frame) centripetal acceleration.

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of angular velocity is:
explanation_short: Angular velocity, the rate of change of angular displacement, has SI unit radians per second (rad/s).
explanation_long: Angular velocity omega = d(theta)/dt, where theta (angular displacement) is measured in radians (a dimensionless ratio of arc length to radius) and t is in seconds. So the SI unit of angular velocity is rad/s. Note that since the radian is dimensionless, angular velocity's unit is effectively just 'per second' (s^-1), but it is conventionally written rad/s to distinguish it from ordinary frequency.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse angular velocity's unit (rad/s) with linear velocity's unit (m/s) or with rev/s (revolutions per second, a non-SI unit used practically but requiring conversion via 2*pi to get rad/s) — remember 1 revolution = 2*pi radians.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the SI unit of angular velocity is radians per second (rad/s).
explanation_options.b: m/s is the unit of linear velocity, not angular velocity.
explanation_options.c: m/s^2 is the unit of linear acceleration, not angular velocity.
explanation_options.d: rev/s (revolutions per second) is a commonly used but non-SI unit; the SI unit is rad/s (1 rev/s = 2*pi rad/s).

subject: Physics
question_text: The escape velocity from the surface of Earth is approximately:
explanation_short: The escape velocity from Earth's surface is approximately 11.2 km/s, given by v_e = sqrt(2gR) using Earth's radius and surface gravity.
explanation_long: Escape velocity is the minimum speed an object needs to completely escape a planet's gravitational field without further propulsion, derived by equating kinetic energy to gravitational potential energy: 1/2 mv_e^2 = GMm/R, giving v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) = sqrt(2gR). Using Earth's g ≈ 9.8 m/s^2 and R ≈ 6.4 x 10^6 m, this works out to approximately 11.2 km/s — a well-known standard physics constant.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse escape velocity (11.2 km/s, needed to leave Earth entirely) with low-Earth-orbit velocity (about 7.9-8 km/s, needed just to orbit near the surface) — these are related but numerically different values, escape velocity being higher by a factor of sqrt(2).

explanation_options.a: 2.4 km/s is far too low; that is roughly the escape velocity of the Moon, not Earth.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Earth's escape velocity is approximately 11.2 km/s.
explanation_options.c: 8 km/s is close to Earth's near-surface orbital velocity, not its escape velocity (which is sqrt(2) times larger).
explanation_options.d: 22.4 km/s is exactly double the correct escape velocity, an easy factor-of-two slip.

subject: Physics
question_text: A machine uses 500 J of energy to do 400 J of useful work. Its efficiency is:
explanation_short: Efficiency = (useful output/total input) x 100% = (400/500) x 100 = 80%.
explanation_long: Efficiency measures how much of the input energy is converted into useful work, expressed as a percentage: Efficiency = (Output energy / Input energy) x 100%. Here the machine uses 500 J but only 400 J does useful work (the rest, 100 J, is lost, e.g., to friction or heat). So efficiency = (400/500) x 100 = 80%.
explanation_trick: A common mistake is dividing input by output instead of output by input (500/400 = 125%, an impossible efficiency over 100%) — always put the USEFUL (smaller) output value in the numerator.

explanation_options.a: This would result from an incorrect ratio, such as computing the wasted fraction (100/500=20%... actually close to option c) rather than the useful fraction properly as 400/500.
explanation_options.b: 100% efficiency would mean no energy was wasted at all, but 100 J was lost here (500-400), so it cannot be 100%.
explanation_options.c: 20% represents the wasted fraction of energy (100/500), which is the complement of efficiency, not the efficiency itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — efficiency = (400/500) x 100% = 80%.

subject: Physics
question_text: The work-energy theorem states that work done by the net force equals:
explanation_short: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body by all forces equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_net = delta KE = KE_final - KE_initial.
explanation_long: This theorem follows directly from Newton's second law: integrating F = ma over a displacement gives W = integral(F ds) = integral(ma ds) = integral(mv dv) = 1/2 m v_final^2 - 1/2 m v_initial^2 = delta KE. It provides a powerful shortcut for solving problems: instead of tracking forces and accelerations throughout motion, you can relate total work directly to the change in speed.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse this with the relation between work and potential energy (W = -delta PE, which applies specifically to conservative forces) — the GENERAL work-energy theorem (for the NET/total force) always relates to kinetic energy change, not potential energy directly.

explanation_options.a: Power is the rate of doing work, a separate concept from what the work-energy theorem directly addresses.
explanation_options.b: The work-PE relationship (W = -delta PE) applies specifically to work done BY a conservative force alone, not the general work-energy theorem for net force.
explanation_options.c: Change in momentum relates to impulse (F delta t), a different theorem (impulse-momentum theorem), not the work-energy theorem.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the work-energy theorem states that net work done equals the change in kinetic energy.

subject: Physics
question_text: The gravitational PE of a 2 kg body at height 5 m (g = 10 m/s^2) is:
explanation_short: Gravitational PE = mgh = 2 x 10 x 5 = 100 J.
explanation_long: Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface is calculated as PE = mgh, where m is mass, g is the acceleration due to gravity, and h is the height above a chosen reference level. Substituting m = 2 kg, g = 10 m/s^2, and h = 5 m: PE = 2 x 10 x 5 = 100 J.
explanation_trick: A simple arithmetic slip (like multiplying only two of the three quantities, or misplacing a decimal) is the most common source of error here — always multiply all three: mass, g, and height together.

explanation_options.a: Correct — PE = mgh = 2 x 10 x 5 = 100 J.
explanation_options.b: This is far too small, likely from omitting a factor (e.g., using height alone x g without multiplying by mass properly, 10 vs 100 mismatch).
explanation_options.c: This is half the correct value, perhaps from a missed factor of 2 (using g=5 instead of g=10, or m=1 instead of m=2).
explanation_options.d: This is a quarter of the correct value, possibly from halving twice in error during the multiplication.

subject: Physics
question_text: The law of conservation of energy states that energy:
option_a: Is constant only in mechanical systems
option_b: Can be destroyed but not created
option_c: Can be created but not destroyed
option_d: Can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed
explanation_short: The law of conservation of energy states that the total energy of an isolated system remains constant — energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another (e.g., potential to kinetic, chemical to thermal).
explanation_long: This is one of the most fundamental principles in physics: in a closed/isolated system, the total energy (summed over all forms — kinetic, potential, thermal, chemical, etc.) never changes over time. Energy can be transformed between these forms (e.g., a falling object converts gravitational PE into KE), and can be transferred between objects, but the total quantity is always conserved. This applies universally, not just to mechanical systems — it also governs thermal, electrical, chemical, and nuclear processes.
explanation_trick: A common misconception is limiting this law to 'mechanical' systems only (ignoring heat, chemical, or other energy forms) — the law of conservation of energy is completely general and applies to ALL forms of energy in ALL types of physical systems.

explanation_options.a: This incorrectly restricts the law to mechanical systems only; conservation of energy is a universal principle covering all energy forms.
explanation_options.b: This states the law backward — energy can indeed be destroyed under this option's phrasing, which contradicts the actual law (energy is never destroyed).
explanation_options.c: This also states the law backward — energy cannot be created according to the actual law, contradicting this option.
explanation_options.d: Correct — energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another; this is the precise statement of the law.

subject: Physics
question_text: A machine lifts a 100 kg load to a height of 10 m in 20 s. The power (g = 10 m/s^2) is:
explanation_short: Work done = mgh = 100 x 10 x 10 = 10,000 J. Power = Work/time = 10,000/20 = 500 W.
explanation_long: First calculate the work done to lift the load against gravity: W = mgh, where m = 100 kg, g = 10 m/s^2, h = 10 m, giving W = 100 x 10 x 10 = 10,000 J. Power is then work done per unit time: P = W/t = 10,000 J / 20 s = 500 W.
explanation_trick: A common mistake is forgetting to compute the work done first (mgh) and instead dividing mass or height directly by time — always compute total work first, then divide by time to get power.

explanation_options.a: This would result from an arithmetic error, such as using a height of 5 m instead of 10 m in the calculation.
explanation_options.c: This is double the correct value, e.g., from forgetting to divide by the time of 20 s properly (or using 10 s instead).
explanation_options.d: This is far too small, perhaps from dividing mgh by 200 instead of 20, an order-of-magnitude slip.

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of power is:
explanation_short: The SI unit of power is the watt (W), defined as one joule of energy transferred or work done per second.
explanation_long: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred: P = W/t. Since work is measured in joules and time in seconds, the SI unit of power is joules per second, given the special name watt (1 W = 1 J/s). Horsepower is a non-SI unit sometimes used for power in everyday/engine contexts, but it is not the SI unit.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes mix up power's unit (watt, a rate) with work's unit (joule, a total amount) — remember power always implies 'per unit time', which the watt captures but the joule does not.

explanation_options.a: The newton is the SI unit of force, not power.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the watt is the SI unit of power (1 W = 1 J/s).
explanation_options.c: Horsepower is a commonly used but non-SI unit of power; the SI unit is the watt.
explanation_options.d: The joule is the SI unit of work/energy, not power (which additionally involves a rate over time).

subject: Physics
question_text: If the velocity of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes:
explanation_short: Kinetic energy KE = 1/2 mv^2 depends on the square of velocity; doubling v means KE scales by 2^2 = 4, so it becomes four times as large.
explanation_long: Since kinetic energy is proportional to the square of velocity (KE = 1/2 mv^2), any change in velocity is amplified quadratically in the kinetic energy. If v becomes 2v, then the new KE = 1/2 m(2v)^2 = 1/2 m(4v^2) = 4 x (1/2 mv^2) = 4 times the original KE. This is why high-speed collisions are disproportionately more dangerous — doubling speed doesn't just double impact energy, it quadruples it.
explanation_trick: A common error is assuming KE scales linearly with velocity (so doubling v just doubles KE) — this ignores the crucial 'squared' term in the formula, leading to a significant underestimate of the actual energy increase.

explanation_options.a: This would be true if KE were inversely related to velocity, which it is not — KE increases (not decreases) when velocity increases.
explanation_options.b: This assumes a linear relationship between KE and velocity, ignoring that KE depends on v-squared.
explanation_options.c: This wrongly assumes velocity has no effect on kinetic energy, contradicting the KE = 1/2 mv^2 formula entirely.
explanation_options.d: Correct — doubling velocity leads to a fourfold increase in kinetic energy, since KE is proportional to v^2 (2^2 = 4).

subject: Physics
question_text: Work done by a force is zero when the angle between force and displacement is:
explanation_short: Work done, W = Fd cos(theta), is zero when cos(theta) = 0, which occurs at theta = 90 degrees — i.e., when force and displacement are perpendicular.
explanation_long: Work depends on the component of force along the direction of displacement: W = Fd cos(theta). When the force is applied exactly perpendicular to the direction of motion (theta = 90 degrees), it has no component along the displacement direction, so no work is done, even though both force and displacement are individually nonzero. A classic example is carrying a bag horizontally while gravity acts vertically downward — gravity does zero work on the horizontally-moving bag.
explanation_trick: A common confusion is thinking zero work only occurs when force or displacement themselves are zero — but work is also zero whenever they are perpendicular (90 degrees), even if both are large in magnitude.

explanation_options.a: Correct — at 90 degrees, cos(90) = 0, so no work is done despite nonzero force and displacement.
explanation_options.b: At 180 degrees, cos(180) = -1, giving maximum negative work, not zero work.
explanation_options.c: At 45 degrees, cos(45) ≈ 0.707, giving positive (nonzero) partial work, not zero.
explanation_options.d: At 0 degrees, cos(0) = 1, giving maximum positive work (force fully along displacement), not zero.

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of work is:
explanation_short: The SI unit of work is the joule (J), defined as a force of one newton acting through a displacement of one metre.
explanation_long: Work is defined as W = F.d = Fd cos(theta), the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force. Since force is measured in newtons and displacement in metres, the SI unit of work is newton-metre, which is given the special name joule (1 J = 1 N·m). Energy, being the capacity to do work, shares the same unit.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse work's unit (joule) with power's unit (watt = joule/second) — remember power involves a rate (per unit time), while work/energy does not.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the joule is the SI unit of work (and energy).
explanation_options.b: The pascal is the SI unit of pressure (N/m^2), not work.
explanation_options.c: The watt is the SI unit of power (J/s), not work itself.
explanation_options.d: The newton is the SI unit of force, not work — work is force multiplied by displacement.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two projectiles are fired with the same speed at angles 30 and 60 degrees. Their horizontal ranges are:
explanation_short: Since R = (v^2 sin(2 theta))/g, and sin(2x30) = sin(60) = sin(2x60's complement)... specifically sin(60 degrees) = sin(120 degrees) (since sin(180-x)=sin(x)), the ranges for 30 degrees and 60 degrees are equal.
explanation_long: The range formula R = (v^2 sin(2 theta))/g depends on sin(2 theta). For theta = 30 degrees, 2 theta = 60 degrees, so sin(60 degrees) ≈ 0.866. For theta = 60 degrees, 2 theta = 120 degrees, so sin(120 degrees) = sin(180-120) = sin(60 degrees) ≈ 0.866 — the same value. This is a general result: any pair of complementary launch angles (theta and 90-theta) that sum to 90 degrees produces equal horizontal ranges for the same launch speed, because sin(2theta) = sin(180 - 2theta) = sin(2(90-theta)).
explanation_trick: Students sometimes assume a steeper angle (60 degrees) must always give a greater range than a shallower one (30 degrees) since it seems 'more powerful', but range depends on sin(2theta), and complementary angles (which sum to 90 degrees) always give identical ranges, just with different times of flight and maximum heights.

explanation_options.a: A 1:3 ratio does not correctly reflect that sin(60) = sin(120), which produces equal, not unequal, ranges.
explanation_options.b: A 2:1 ratio is incorrect; the correct relationship for complementary angles (30+60=90) is that the ranges are equal.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 30 and 60 degrees are complementary angles (summing to 90 degrees), so sin(2x30)=sin(60)=sin(120)=sin(2x60), giving equal ranges.
explanation_options.d: A 1:2 ratio is incorrect; complementary launch angles produce identical ranges, not a 1:2 ratio.

subject: Physics
question_text: A body freely falls from rest. The distance covered in the first 3 seconds (g = 10 m/s^2) is:
explanation_short: Using s = 1/2 g t^2 with g=10 m/s^2, t=3s: s = 0.5 x 10 x 9 = 45 m.
explanation_long: For a body released from rest and falling freely under gravity, the distance fallen after time t is given by s = 1/2 g t^2 (derived from s = ut + 1/2 at^2 with u=0). Substituting g = 10 m/s^2 and t = 3 s: s = 0.5 x 10 x (3)^2 = 0.5 x 10 x 9 = 45 m.
explanation_trick: A common mistake is forgetting to square the time (using t=3 instead of t^2=9), which would give an incorrect answer of 15 m instead of the correct 45 m.

explanation_options.a: Correct — s = 1/2 g t^2 = 0.5 x 10 x 9 = 45 m.
explanation_options.b: This is double the correct value, perhaps from omitting the factor of 1/2 in the formula (using g t^2 instead of 1/2 g t^2).
explanation_options.c: This equals g x t (10 x 3 = 30), an incorrect combination that doesn't match the s = 1/2 g t^2 formula.
explanation_options.d: This equals half of g x t (a partial/incorrect calculation), forgetting to square the time properly.

subject: Physics
question_text: A rocket propels forward because of:
option_d: Newton's third law (action-reaction of exhaust gases)
explanation_short: A rocket moves forward due to Newton's third law: as the rocket expels exhaust gases backward (action), the gases exert an equal and opposite reaction force pushing the rocket forward.
explanation_long: Rocket propulsion works by expelling mass (hot exhaust gases) at high velocity out of the rear of the rocket. By Newton's third law, for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction — the force the rocket exerts on the expelled gases (pushing them backward) is matched by an equal force the gases exert on the rocket (pushing it forward). This is also consistent with conservation of momentum: the total momentum of rocket + expelled gas remains constant (starting at zero if starting from rest), so as gas gains backward momentum, the rocket must gain forward momentum.
explanation_trick: A common misconception is thinking a rocket 'pushes off' the surrounding air (like an oar pushing off water) — this is wrong, since rockets work perfectly well in the vacuum of space where there is no air to push against; the true mechanism is the reaction to expelled propellant mass.

explanation_options.a: Newton's first law (inertia) explains why a rocket, once moving, continues moving, but not the actual mechanism by which it is propelled forward in the first place.
explanation_options.b: Conservation of energy is a general principle present in the process but doesn't specifically explain the forward thrust mechanism; that requires the action-reaction pairing.
explanation_options.c: Bernoulli's principle relates to fluid pressure and speed, not to rocket thrust generation, which is a momentum/reaction-force phenomenon.
explanation_options.d: Correct — rocket propulsion is a direct application of Newton's third law: the reaction to the backward-ejected exhaust gases propels the rocket forward.

subject: Physics
question_text: A body of mass m collides elastically head-on with an identical stationary body. After collision:
option_a: Moving body stops and stationary body moves with the initial velocity of moving body
option_c: They move together with half the initial velocity
explanation_short: For a head-on elastic collision between a moving body and an identical stationary body, the moving body comes to rest and the previously stationary body moves off with the initial velocity of the first — a complete 'transfer' of velocity.
explanation_long: Using the elastic collision formulas for equal masses (m1 = m2 = m): v1' = ((m1-m2)/(m1+m2))u1 + (2m2/(m1+m2))u2 and v2' = (2m1/(m1+m2))u1 + ((m2-m1)/(m1+m2))u2. With m1=m2 and u2=0, these simplify to v1' = 0 and v2' = u1. This is a classic and elegant result of elastic collisions between equal masses, commonly illustrated with Newton's cradle.
explanation_trick: A common misconception is assuming the two bodies end up moving together after collision (as in a perfectly inelastic collision) — that only happens when kinetic energy is NOT conserved; in an elastic collision between equal masses, they exchange velocities completely instead.

explanation_options.a: Correct — for equal masses in a head-on elastic collision, the incoming body stops and the target body moves off with the incoming body's original velocity.
explanation_options.b: Both bodies stopping would violate conservation of momentum (final momentum would be zero, but the initial momentum was nonzero).
explanation_options.c: Moving together with half the velocity describes a perfectly INELASTIC collision (they stick together), not an elastic one.
explanation_options.d: Both bodies ending with equal (nonzero, same-direction) velocities after collision doesn't satisfy the elastic-collision equations for equal masses.

subject: Physics
question_text: In an elastic collision between two bodies, which quantity is conserved besides momentum?
explanation_short: In an elastic collision, both linear momentum AND total kinetic energy are conserved — this is the defining feature that distinguishes elastic from inelastic collisions.
explanation_long: All collisions (elastic or inelastic) conserve total momentum, as long as no external forces act. What makes a collision specifically 'elastic' is that kinetic energy is ALSO conserved — none is converted to heat, sound, or permanent deformation. In inelastic collisions, momentum is still conserved, but kinetic energy is not (some is lost to other energy forms).
explanation_trick: A common confusion is thinking momentum alone defines 'elastic' — but momentum conservation applies to ALL collisions; it is specifically the additional conservation of kinetic energy that makes a collision elastic.

explanation_options.a: Velocity alone is not conserved in a collision (each body's velocity generally changes); only combined quantities like momentum and, here, kinetic energy are conserved.
explanation_options.b: Angular momentum applies to rotational systems, not the standard linear-collision context implied here; it is not the answer being tested.
explanation_options.c: Correct — kinetic energy, in addition to momentum, is conserved specifically in an elastic collision.
explanation_options.d: Mass of each individual object is trivially conserved in any everyday collision (no mass-energy conversion), so it isn't the special/distinguishing conserved quantity being asked about.

subject: Physics
question_text: Impulse is defined as:
option_a: Force multiplied by time of action
explanation_short: Impulse is defined as the product of the force applied and the time interval over which it acts: J = F x delta t.
explanation_long: Impulse quantifies the total effect of a force acting over a duration of time, and by the impulse-momentum theorem, it equals the resulting change in momentum: J = F x delta t = delta p = m delta v. This is why a small force acting for a long time (like a cushioned landing) or a large force acting briefly (like a sudden impact) can produce the same impulse and momentum change.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse impulse with force alone or with momentum alone — impulse specifically combines force AND the duration of its action (F multiplied by time), and equals the resulting momentum change.

explanation_options.a: Correct — impulse = force x time of action (J = F delta t), which equals the change in momentum.
explanation_options.b: Force divided by time would give a rate of change of force, not impulse.
explanation_options.c: Rate of change of force is not a standard named quantity related to the definition of impulse.
explanation_options.d: Momentum divided by force has units of time, not the correct definition of impulse (which is force multiplied by time).

subject: Physics
question_text: The rate of change of momentum of a body is equal to:
explanation_short: By Newton's second law in its general form, the rate of change of momentum of a body equals the net applied force acting on it: F = dp/dt.
explanation_long: Newton originally stated the second law in terms of momentum: the net external force on a body equals the time rate of change of its linear momentum, F = dp/dt = d(mv)/dt. For constant mass, this reduces to the familiar F = ma. This form is more general and correctly applies even when mass is changing (e.g., rockets).
explanation_trick: Impulse (force x time) is the CHANGE in momentum over an interval, not the same as the rate (per unit time) of that change — don't confuse the instantaneous rate (force) with the total accumulated change (impulse).

explanation_options.a: Power is the rate of doing work (dW/dt), not the rate of change of momentum.
explanation_options.b: Impulse is the total change in momentum (F x delta t), not its instantaneous rate of change.
explanation_options.c: Kinetic energy is a different quantity (1/2 mv^2) unrelated to the rate of change of momentum.
explanation_options.d: Correct — by Newton's second law, F = dp/dt, the applied force equals the rate of change of momentum.

subject: Physics
question_text: A force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg body. Its acceleration is:
explanation_short: Using F = ma: a = F/m = 10 N / 2 kg = 5 m/s^2.
explanation_long: By Newton's second law, F = ma, so the acceleration produced by a given force is a = F/m. Here a force of 10 N acts on a mass of 2 kg, giving a = 10/2 = 5 m/s^2.
explanation_trick: A common slip is inverting the formula (computing m/F instead of F/m), which would give an incorrect value of 0.2 instead of 5 — always keep force in the numerator when solving for acceleration.

explanation_options.a: This is the value of the force itself (10 N), not the acceleration.
explanation_options.b: This would result if you divided the mass by the force incorrectly reversed, or used a different mass value.
explanation_options.c: This would result from doubling the correct value, e.g., mistakenly multiplying instead of dividing (10x2).
explanation_options.d: Correct — a = F/m = 10/2 = 5 m/s^2.

subject: Physics
question_text: A ball is projected with velocity 20 m/s at 30 degrees. Its horizontal component of velocity is (approx):
explanation_short: Horizontal component = v cos(theta) = 20 x cos(30 degrees) = 20 x 0.866 = 17.3 m/s.
explanation_long: The horizontal component of a projectile's initial velocity is found using v_x = v cos(theta), where theta is the launch angle from the horizontal. Here v = 20 m/s and theta = 30 degrees, and cos(30 degrees) ≈ 0.866, giving v_x = 20 x 0.866 ≈ 17.3 m/s. This horizontal component remains constant throughout the flight since gravity acts only vertically.
explanation_trick: A common mix-up is using sin instead of cos for the horizontal component (sin(30)=0.5, giving 10 m/s, which is actually the VERTICAL component) — remember horizontal pairs with cosine when the angle is measured from the horizontal axis.

explanation_options.a: This is just the full launch speed, ignoring the angle entirely.
explanation_options.b: This is actually the vertical component (20 sin 30 = 10 m/s), mistakenly labeled as horizontal.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 20 cos(30 degrees) ≈ 20 x 0.866 ≈ 17.3 m/s.
explanation_options.d: This does not correspond to either the correct horizontal or vertical component calculation for this launch.

subject: Physics
question_text: For a projectile, the vertical component of velocity at the highest point is:
explanation_short: At the highest point of a projectile's path, the vertical component of velocity is momentarily zero, since the body has stopped rising and is about to start falling.
explanation_long: During projectile motion, the vertical velocity decreases continuously under gravity (v_y = u sin(theta) - gt) until it reaches zero exactly at the highest point of the trajectory — this is the condition that defines 'highest point'. After this instant, gravity continues to act, and the vertical velocity becomes negative (downward) as the projectile falls. The horizontal component of velocity, in contrast, remains constant throughout (ignoring air resistance) since gravity has no horizontal component.
explanation_trick: A common error is thinking the TOTAL velocity is zero at the highest point — it isn't; only the vertical component is zero, while the horizontal component (u cos theta) continues unchanged, so the projectile is still moving horizontally at the peak.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the vertical velocity component becomes zero at the highest point, which is precisely why that point is 'highest' (the body momentarily stops rising).
explanation_options.b: The vertical component is at its minimum (zero), not maximum, at the highest point; it was maximum at launch.
explanation_options.c: The vertical velocity at the highest point is zero, not equal to the initial (launch) velocity, which included both vertical and horizontal parts.
explanation_options.d: The vertical component (zero) is generally not equal to the horizontal component (which stays at u cos theta, non-zero) at the highest point.

subject: Physics
question_text: The horizontal range of a projectile is maximum when the angle of projection is:
explanation_short: The horizontal range of a projectile, R = (v^2 sin(2 theta))/g, is maximum when sin(2 theta) = 1, i.e., 2 theta = 90 degrees, so theta = 45 degrees.
explanation_long: The range formula for projectile motion (launched and landing at the same height) is R = (v^2 sin(2 theta)) / g. Since sin has a maximum value of 1 at an angle of 90 degrees, sin(2 theta) is maximized when 2 theta = 90 degrees, giving theta = 45 degrees as the launch angle that maximizes horizontal range for a given launch speed.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes think 90 degrees (straight up) gives maximum range because it seems like the 'most energetic' launch, but that actually gives zero horizontal range (all vertical motion) — 45 degrees optimally balances horizontal and vertical velocity components.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 45 degrees maximizes sin(2 theta), giving the maximum horizontal range.
explanation_options.b: 30 degrees gives the same range as 60 degrees (complementary angles), but neither is the maximum — only 45 degrees is.
explanation_options.c: 90 degrees sends the projectile straight up with zero horizontal range, the opposite of maximum range.
explanation_options.d: 60 degrees gives the same range as 30 degrees (complementary pair) but is not the maximum, which occurs only at 45 degrees.

subject: Physics
question_text: A car travelling at 20 m/s decelerates uniformly at 4 m/s^2. The distance covered before it stops is:
explanation_long: Since the car decelerates uniformly to rest, use the third kinematic equation v^2 = u^2 - 2as (deceleration taken as negative acceleration, or subtracted explicitly). With final velocity v = 0, initial velocity u = 20 m/s, and deceleration a = 4 m/s^2: 0 = (20)^2 - 2(4)s => 0 = 400 - 8s => s = 400/8 = 50 m.
explanation_trick: A common mistake is forgetting to square the initial velocity (using 20 instead of 400), or dividing by 2a incorrectly — always carefully substitute u^2, not u, into the equation.

explanation_options.a: This would result from an arithmetic slip, e.g., dividing 400 by 16 instead of 8.
explanation_options.b: This is 400/5, an incorrect denominator not matching 2a = 8.
explanation_options.c: This is exactly double the correct distance, possibly from using 'a' instead of '2a' in the denominator.

subject: Physics
question_text: A body starting from rest accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s^2. Its velocity after 5 s is:
explanation_short: Using v = u + at with u = 0, a = 2 m/s^2, t = 5 s: v = 0 + (2)(5) = 10 m/s.
explanation_long: Since the body starts from rest, initial velocity u = 0. Applying the first kinematic equation v = u + at with a constant acceleration of 2 m/s^2 over 5 seconds gives v = 0 + 2 x 5 = 10 m/s.
explanation_trick: A common slip is multiplying acceleration by time incorrectly or confusing this with the distance formula (s = ut + 1/2 at^2), which would give a different (and here irrelevant) numeric answer.

explanation_options.a: Correct — v = u + at = 0 + (2)(5) = 10 m/s.
explanation_options.b: This would result from doubling the correct answer, perhaps by miscalculating 2 x 2 x 5 instead of just 2 x 5.
explanation_options.c: This is the value you'd get from s = 1/2 a t^2 (a distance formula, 0.5 x 2 x 25 = 25), incorrectly applied here as if it were velocity.
explanation_options.d: This matches just the time value (5) rather than correctly multiplying by acceleration.

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of linear momentum is:
explanation_short: Momentum = mass x velocity, so its SI unit is kilogram-metre per second (kg m/s).
explanation_long: Linear momentum p is defined as p = mv, the product of mass (kg) and velocity (m/s). Multiplying these base/derived units together gives kg m/s as the SI unit for momentum. Note this is dimensionally equivalent to force x time (N·s), which is the unit of impulse — consistent with the impulse-momentum theorem.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse momentum's unit with force's unit (Newton, which is kg m/s^2) by forgetting momentum has no acceleration (time^-2) term — momentum only involves velocity (time^-1).

explanation_options.a: Correct — momentum's SI unit is kg m/s (mass in kg times velocity in m/s).
explanation_options.b: kg m/s^2 is the unit of force (from F=ma), not momentum.
explanation_options.c: Newton (N) is the unit of force, not momentum, though it is dimensionally related via impulse = force x time.
explanation_options.d: Joule (J) is the unit of energy/work, not momentum.

subject: Physics
question_text: The law of inertia is:
explanation_short: Newton's first law is called the law of inertia because it states a body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force — describing the body's inherent resistance (inertia) to changes in motion.
explanation_long: Newton's first law: 'An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion with the same speed and direction, unless acted upon by an unbalanced (net) force.' This property of resisting a change in the state of motion is called inertia, hence the law's common name. It contrasts with the second law (which quantifies how force changes motion) and the third law (action-reaction pairs).
explanation_trick: A common mix-up is calling the second law (F=ma) the 'law of inertia' since it also deals with force and motion — remember: first law = inertia (qualitative, no force needed for constant velocity), second law = F=ma (quantitative).

explanation_options.a: The law of gravitation is Newton's separate universal gravitation law, unrelated to the label 'law of inertia'.
explanation_options.b: Newton's third law describes action-reaction force pairs, not the concept of inertia.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Newton's first law is known as the law of inertia.
explanation_options.d: Newton's second law (F=ma) quantifies force and acceleration; it is not called the law of inertia.

subject: Physics
question_text: Newton's second law of motion states that force equals:
explanation_short: Newton's second law states F = ma: the net force on a body equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration.
explanation_long: Newton's second law quantifies how a net external force changes a body's motion: F_net = dp/dt, which for constant mass simplifies to F = ma. This means a larger force produces a proportionally larger acceleration, while a larger mass (more inertia) produces a proportionally smaller acceleration for the same force.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse this with momentum (mass x velocity) — remember F = ma uses acceleration (rate of change of velocity), not velocity itself.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Newton's second law: force = mass x acceleration (F = ma).
explanation_options.b: Mass times velocity is the definition of momentum, not force.
explanation_options.c: Mass divided by acceleration has no standard physical meaning matching force; this inverts the correct relationship.
explanation_options.d: Weight divided by mass equals g (acceleration due to gravity), not force in general — this is a special case misapplied generally.

subject: Physics
question_text: The slope of a displacement-time graph gives:
explanation_short: The slope of a displacement-time graph, ds/dt, is by definition the velocity of the body.
explanation_long: Velocity is defined as the rate of change of displacement with respect to time, v = ds/dt. On a displacement-time (s-t) graph, this rate of change is exactly the gradient/slope of the curve at any point — a steeper slope means higher velocity, a flat (zero) slope means the body is momentarily at rest, and a negative slope means the body is moving in the negative direction.
explanation_trick: Remember the hierarchy of graph slopes: slope of (s-t) graph = velocity; slope of (v-t) graph = acceleration. Confusing these two levels is one of the most common kinematics graph errors.

explanation_options.a: Force is not read directly from a displacement-time graph slope; that would require the slope of a momentum-time graph or mass times the slope of a v-t graph.
explanation_options.b: Displacement is the quantity plotted on the y-axis itself, not the slope of the graph.
explanation_options.c: Acceleration is obtained from the slope of a velocity-time graph, not a displacement-time graph (that would be a second derivative here).
explanation_options.d: Correct — the slope (gradient) of a displacement-time graph gives the instantaneous velocity.

subject: Physics
question_text: The area under a velocity-time graph represents:
explanation_short: The area under a velocity-time graph equals the change in position, i.e., displacement.
explanation_long: Displacement is the integral of velocity with respect to time: s = integral of v dt. Graphically, this integral corresponds exactly to the area enclosed between the velocity-time curve and the time axis. So for any v-t graph (uniform or non-uniform motion), computing the area under the curve gives the displacement over that time interval.
explanation_trick: A common confusion is mixing up which graph gives which quantity: slope of v-t graph = acceleration, but area under v-t graph = displacement; students sometimes reverse these two relationships.

explanation_options.a: Acceleration is given by the SLOPE of a velocity-time graph, not the area under it.
explanation_options.b: Force is not directly read off a velocity-time graph; it would require multiplying acceleration (the slope) by mass.
explanation_options.c: Speed is the value plotted on the y-axis itself at any instant, not the area under the whole curve.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the area under a velocity-time graph represents the displacement (change in position) over that time interval.

subject: Physics
question_text: Three coplanar forces acting on a point are in equilibrium. They can be represented in magnitude and direction by the three sides of a:
explanation_short: Three coplanar forces in equilibrium can be represented, in magnitude and direction, by the three sides of a triangle taken in order — this is the triangle law/rule for concurrent forces in equilibrium.
explanation_long: When three forces acting at a point are in equilibrium, if you draw them as vectors head-to-tail in sequence, they form a closed triangle (the resultant is zero because the vectors return to the starting point). This is known as the triangle law of forces (an extension of the general polygon law of vectors), and it is the graphical/geometric test used to verify three-force equilibrium.
explanation_trick: Students often confuse this with the parallelogram law (used to find the resultant of two vectors, not to represent equilibrium of three) — for equilibrium of three concurrent coplanar forces specifically, the closed triangle (taken in order, i.e., head-to-tail) is the correct representation.

explanation_options.a: A rectangle does not represent the triangle law for three concurrent forces in equilibrium; that would require four sides/forces.
explanation_options.b: Correct — three coplanar forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle when their vectors are drawn head-to-tail in order.
explanation_options.c: A circle is not part of the vector representation of force equilibrium; it doesn't relate to the triangle law.
explanation_options.d: A square, like a rectangle, represents four sides/forces, not three — it doesn't apply to three-force equilibrium.

subject: Physics
question_text: A vector of magnitude 10 makes an angle of 60 degrees with the x-axis. Its x-component is:
explanation_short: The x-component of a vector is magnitude x cos(theta) = 10 x cos(60) = 10 x 0.5 = 5.
explanation_long: For a vector of magnitude V making angle theta with the x-axis, its horizontal (x) component is V cos(theta) and its vertical (y) component is V sin(theta). Here V = 10 and theta = 60 degrees, so the x-component = 10 x cos(60 degrees) = 10 x 0.5 = 5.
explanation_trick: A very common mix-up is swapping sine and cosine — remembering 'cos goes with the adjacent/x-axis side' when theta is measured from the x-axis helps avoid computing sin(60) = 8.66 by mistake for the x-component.

explanation_options.a: This value, 5 sqrt(3) ≈ 8.66, is actually the y-component (10 sin 60), not the x-component.
explanation_options.b: This is just the full magnitude of the vector, ignoring the angle entirely.
explanation_options.c: Correct — x-component = 10 cos(60 degrees) = 10 x 0.5 = 5.
explanation_options.d: This is the numeric value of the y-component (10 sin 60 ≈ 8.66), mistakenly given as the x-component.

subject: Physics
question_text: Torque is the vector product of:
explanation_short: Torque is defined as tau = r x F, the vector (cross) product of the position vector r and the applied force F.
explanation_long: Torque quantifies the turning effect of a force about a pivot. It is calculated as the cross product of the position vector r (from the pivot to the point of force application) and the force vector F: tau = r x F, with magnitude rF sin(theta) and direction given by the right-hand rule, perpendicular to the plane of r and F.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes confuse torque's formula with work (F.d, a dot product/scalar), but torque uses the position vector crossed with force, giving a vector result, not force dotted with displacement.

explanation_options.a: Force and velocity combine to give power-like or other quantities, not torque.
explanation_options.b: Momentum and velocity is not a standard cross-product definition used for torque.
explanation_options.c: Force and displacement combined as a dot product gives work (a scalar), not torque.
explanation_options.d: Correct — torque is the cross product of the position vector (from pivot to point of application) and the force.

subject: Physics
question_text: A body is in complete equilibrium if:
option_a: Net torque on it is zero only
option_b: Net force on it is zero only
option_c: Both net force and net torque are zero
explanation_short: Complete equilibrium requires BOTH the net force and net torque acting on a body to be zero.
explanation_long: There are two independent conditions for a rigid body to be in complete (static) equilibrium: translational equilibrium, where the vector sum of all forces is zero (so the center of mass has no linear acceleration), and rotational equilibrium, where the sum of all torques about any point is zero (so there is no angular acceleration). Satisfying only one condition (e.g., zero net force but nonzero torque) can still leave the body rotating, so both must hold simultaneously.
explanation_trick: A frequent mistake is to think zero net force alone guarantees equilibrium — a body can have zero net force but still spin (e.g., a couple/torque pair), so the torque condition is equally essential.

explanation_options.a: Zero net torque alone is not sufficient — the body could still accelerate linearly if the net force is nonzero.
explanation_options.b: Zero net force alone is not sufficient — the body could still have a net torque and start rotating (e.g., a force couple).
explanation_options.c: Correct — true equilibrium needs both translational (net force = 0) and rotational (net torque = 0) conditions satisfied together.
explanation_options.d: Being at rest describes a state, not the underlying physical condition; a body could momentarily be at rest yet not be in equilibrium if net force/torque are nonzero.

subject: Physics
question_text: The direction of the vector product A x B is given by:
option_a: Right-hand rule, perpendicular to the plane of A and B
option_c: Along the resultant of A and B
explanation_short: The direction of A x B is given by the right-hand rule: it points perpendicular to the plane containing A and B.
explanation_long: The vector (cross) product of two vectors A and B produces a new vector whose magnitude is |A||B|sin(theta) and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane formed by A and B, determined by curling the right-hand fingers from A to B — the thumb then points along A x B. This perpendicularity is why cross products are used to define quantities like torque and angular momentum.
explanation_trick: A common confusion is applying the right-hand rule for the dot product too — remember the dot product gives a scalar (no direction at all), while only the cross product needs a direction rule.

explanation_options.a: Correct — by the right-hand rule, A x B points perpendicular to the plane of A and B.
explanation_options.b: The cross product is perpendicular to both A and B, so it cannot be parallel to B itself (except in degenerate zero cases).
explanation_options.c: This describes vector addition (A+B), which is a different operation from the cross product.
explanation_options.d: The cross product is perpendicular to A, so it cannot be parallel to A (except when the product is zero).

subject: Physics
question_text: The scalar product of two perpendicular vectors is:
explanation_short: The scalar (dot) product is A.B = |A||B|cos(theta); at theta = 90 degrees, cos(90) = 0, so the dot product is zero.
explanation_long: The dot product measures how much one vector 'projects onto' another. When two vectors are perpendicular, neither has any component along the direction of the other, so their scalar product is exactly zero. This is why perpendicularity is often tested in physics via A.B = 0 (e.g., showing velocity is perpendicular to centripetal acceleration in circular motion).
explanation_trick: Do not confuse the dot product (scalar, uses cosine, zero when perpendicular) with the cross product (vector, uses sine, zero when parallel) — these are opposite conditions and are a very common mix-up.

explanation_options.a: This describes the case when the vectors are parallel (theta=0, cos=1), not perpendicular.
explanation_options.b: Correct — cos(90 degrees) = 0, so the scalar product of two perpendicular vectors is zero.
explanation_options.c: The dot product is maximum when vectors are parallel (theta=0), not perpendicular.
explanation_options.d: The dot product is negative when the angle between vectors exceeds 90 degrees, not equal to it.

subject: Physics
question_text: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at right angles to each other. Their resultant is:
explanation_short: For perpendicular vectors, the resultant magnitude is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9+16) = sqrt(25) = 5 N.
explanation_long: When two forces act at right angles, their resultant is found using the Pythagorean theorem (since the two components form the legs of a right triangle and the resultant is the hypotenuse): R = sqrt(F1^2 + F2^2). Substituting F1 = 3 N and F2 = 4 N gives R = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 N — the classic 3-4-5 right triangle.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes just add the magnitudes directly (3 + 4 = 7 N) forgetting that vector addition at an angle requires the Pythagorean rule, not simple arithmetic addition — that only applies when forces are exactly parallel.

explanation_options.a: Correct — using the Pythagorean theorem, sqrt(3^2+4^2) = 5 N, the classic 3-4-5 triangle.
explanation_options.b: This comes from wrongly adding the magnitudes directly (3+4=7), which is only valid for parallel (0 degree) vectors.
explanation_options.c: This would be the resultant if the two forces were antiparallel/subtracted (4-3=1), not perpendicular.
explanation_options.d: This comes from multiplying instead of properly combining the perpendicular components (3x4=12).

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
explanation_short: Speed has only magnitude (no direction specified), making it a scalar quantity.
explanation_long: A scalar quantity is fully described by magnitude alone, while a vector quantity requires both magnitude and direction. Speed tells you 'how fast' but not 'which way', so it is scalar. In contrast, velocity, displacement and acceleration all specify direction as part of their definition, making them vector quantities.
explanation_trick: Speed and velocity are often used interchangeably in casual language, but on MDCAT-style questions remember: speed = |velocity| = magnitude only = scalar; velocity includes direction = vector.

explanation_options.a: Correct — speed is the magnitude of velocity, with no direction component, so it is scalar.
explanation_options.b: Displacement is a vector; it specifies both the distance and direction from the initial to final position.
explanation_options.c: Velocity is a vector; it is speed with a specified direction.
explanation_options.d: Acceleration is a vector; it specifies the rate of change of velocity, which itself is directional.

subject: Physics
question_text: Which pair of quantities has the same dimensions?
explanation_short: Torque (r x F) and energy/work (F x d) both have dimensions of force times length, i.e. [M L^2 T^-2].
explanation_long: Torque is defined as force multiplied by the perpendicular distance (moment arm), giving units of N·m. Energy/work is also force multiplied by displacement, also in N·m (= Joules). Although torque is a vector and energy is a scalar (so they aren't the 'same quantity'), their dimensional formulas are identical: [M L^2 T^-2]. The other pairs listed have clearly different dimensions.
explanation_trick: Don't confuse 'same dimensions' with 'same physical meaning' — torque and energy share dimensional formula and even numeric units (N·m = J), but they are conceptually different (vector moment vs scalar energy transfer).

explanation_options.a: Force [M L T^-2] and momentum [M L T^-1] differ in the power of T, so they are not dimensionally equal.
explanation_options.b: Pressure [M L^-1 T^-2] and force [M L T^-2] differ (pressure divides by area), so they are not equal.
explanation_options.c: Correct — both torque and energy have dimensions [M L^2 T^-2] (force x distance).
explanation_options.d: Work [M L^2 T^-2] and power [M L^2 T^-3] differ by a factor of time, so they are not dimensionally equal.

subject: Physics
question_text: The least count of a vernier caliper with 10 vernier divisions coinciding with 9 main-scale divisions of 1 mm each is:
explanation_short: Least count = value of one main-scale division / number of vernier divisions = 1 mm / 10 = 0.1 mm.
explanation_long: The least count (LC) of a vernier caliper is calculated as LC = (smallest main-scale division) / (total number of vernier scale divisions). Here the main scale division is 1 mm and there are 10 vernier divisions coinciding with 9 main-scale divisions, so LC = 1 mm / 10 = 0.1 mm. This is the smallest length the instrument can reliably resolve.
explanation_trick: Students sometimes divide the main-scale division by the number of main-scale divisions matched (9) instead of the number of vernier divisions (10) — always divide by the vernier division count.

explanation_options.a: This is the least count of a screw gauge/micrometer, not a typical vernier caliper.
explanation_options.b: This is simply the main-scale division value, ignoring the vernier scale's finer resolution entirely.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 1 mm divided by 10 vernier divisions gives a least count of 0.1 mm.
explanation_options.d: This is off by a factor of 10, as if there were 100 vernier divisions instead of 10.

subject: Physics
question_text: The number 0.004560 has how many significant figures?
explanation_short: In 0.004560, the leading zeros are not significant, but the zero between the decimal digits and the trailing zero after 6 are significant, giving 4 significant figures (4, 5, 6, 0).
explanation_long: Rules for significant figures: all non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant; leading zeros (before the first non-zero digit) are never significant, as they only fix the decimal point; trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant because they indicate precision of measurement. In 0.004560, the digits 4, 5, 6 are significant, and so is the trailing 0 after 6, giving 4 significant figures total.
explanation_trick: The most common mistake is counting the three leading zeros (0.00...) as significant, which would incorrectly give 7; remember leading zeros are placeholders only, never significant.

explanation_options.a: This undercounts by ignoring the significant trailing zero after 6 (only counting 4, 5, 6).
explanation_options.b: This wrongly counts all seven digits including the non-significant leading zeros.
explanation_options.c: This overcounts by one, perhaps by miscounting the leading zeros as significant.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 4, 5, 6 and the trailing 0 are significant, giving 4 significant figures.

subject: Physics
question_text: The dimensions of pressure are:
explanation_short: Pressure = Force/Area = (M L T^-2)/(L^2) = [M L^-1 T^-2].
explanation_long: Force has dimensions [M L T^-2] from F = ma. Area has dimensions [L^2]. Dividing force by area gives [M L T^-2] / [L^2] = [M L^-1 T^-2], which is the dimensional formula of pressure (and also of stress, since both are force per unit area).
explanation_trick: A common error is forgetting to subtract the exponent of L correctly when dividing by area — students often write [M L T^-2] (force's own dimension) without dividing by L^2 at all.

explanation_options.a: This is the dimensional formula of force itself, not pressure — it is missing the division by area.
explanation_options.b: The L exponent is wrong; this would result from an incorrect area/length combination, not force/area.
explanation_options.c: Correct — dividing force's dimensions by area's dimensions gives [M L^-1 T^-2].
explanation_options.d: This is the dimensional formula of energy/work (force x displacement), not pressure (force / area).

subject: Physics
question_text: Which of the following is NOT a base quantity in the SI system?
explanation_short: Force is a derived quantity (mass x acceleration); mass, time and temperature are all SI base quantities.
explanation_long: The seven SI base quantities are: length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity. Force is derived from Newton's second law, F = ma, combining the base quantities mass, length and time, so it is not itself a base quantity.
explanation_trick: A common trap is assuming any 'fundamental-sounding' quantity like force must be basic; always check whether a quantity's unit can be built from simpler ones — if yes, it's derived.

explanation_options.a: Mass is one of the seven SI base quantities.
explanation_options.b: Time is one of the seven SI base quantities.
explanation_options.c: Temperature is one of the seven SI base quantities.
explanation_options.d: Correct — force is a derived quantity, expressed in terms of mass, length and time (kg·m/s^2).

subject: Physics
question_text: The SI unit of electric current is the:
explanation_short: The SI base unit of electric current is the ampere (A).
explanation_long: Electric current is one of the seven SI base quantities, and its base unit is the ampere, defined via the force between two current-carrying conductors (modern SI: via the elementary charge e). The ohm, coulomb and volt are all derived units built from the ampere, second, kilogram and metre.
explanation_trick: Students often confuse charge (coulomb) with current (ampere) because they are closely related (I = Q/t), but coulomb is the unit of charge, not current.

explanation_options.a: The ohm is the unit of electrical resistance, not current.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the ampere is the SI base unit of electric current.
explanation_options.c: The coulomb is the unit of electric charge, a derived quantity (A·s), not current itself.
explanation_options.d: The volt is the unit of electric potential difference, not current.
